longer directly resolves; the clean two-axis split (resolution vs build-observation)
is C3. Keep the change minimal here — do not delete the merge path yet, just stop
treating merge as the resolve trigger for issues that went through `resolving`.

**Emits** `issue_resolved` with `source='build-confirmed'` + `green_head_run_id`.
acceptance_criteria: 1) Green verdict for a resolving issue -> state resolving->resolved, resolved_at set, source=build-confirmed, event emitted. 2) Guard: transition only from state=resolving (muted/unresolved/resolved untouched). 3) Green-Head ordinal per (target,origin) recorded (green_head_run_id from port_status.last_success_run_id/build_runs.id). 4) last_confirmed_build_generation advanced, building_generation cleared (no re-enqueue). 5) Merge no longer directly flips resolved for issues that went through resolving (authority moves to the build; full split is C3; merge path not deleted yet). 6) Test: resolving+green -> resolved w/ green-head; muted+green -> untouched.
close_reason: Implemented + reviewed + committed. Green head implemented as a build_runs watermark (not port_status.last_success_run_id) because dsynth hooks are disabled in the dev-env so confirm builds never reach build_runs/port_status.

title: C1 Build intent (generation counter / build_requests)
description: C1 Build intent. The resolving transition writes desired build state — a generation counter on the issue (requested_build_generation) or a build_requests row. Crash-safe, self-dedup. Prior art: K8s observedGeneration.
design:
## Design

Record *desired build state* on the issue row when a fix is accepted, as a
monotonic generation counter — the level-triggered spine (K8s observedGeneration),
NOT an edge-triggered command.

**Schema (db/schema.py, `issues` table):**
- add `requested_build_generation INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0`
- add `last_confirmed_build_generation INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0`
- add `building_generation INTEGER` (NULL = no build in flight; single-flight marker, set by C2)

**Write point — `mark_issue_resolving` (tracker/routes/issue_actions.py:98):**
Extend the existing single UPDATE (the one that sets `state='resolving'`,
`delivery_bundle_id`) to also bump `requested_build_generation =
requested_build_generation + 1`, in the SAME statement / same txn. This is the
"record intent" half of the verify_requests pattern (agentic_api.py:533), but on
the issue row itself rather than an append table — so it is level-triggered and
self-dedups (a re-accept just bumps the counter; no duplicate queue rows — that is
C2's job).

**Read feed for C2:** a query helper (tracker/agentic_queries/issues.py) returning
issues where `state='resolving' AND requested_build_generation >
last_confirmed_build_generation AND (building_generation IS NULL OR
building_generation < requested_build_generation)`.

**Event:** extend the emitted `issue_resolving` event (issue_actions.py:117) to
carry `requested_build_generation`, or emit a companion `issue_build_requested`.

**Rejected alternative:** a `build_requests` append table mirroring verify_requests
exactly. Rejected because it is edge-triggered — it can drift (a request row says
done while state later regresses) and needs its own dedup. The counter-on-issue is
crash-safe by construction (one row, one UPDATE) and is what C2/A2 compare against.

**Why crash-safe:** the generation bump rides the same single UPDATE as the state
write, under the caller's BEGIN IMMEDIATE txn — a crash leaves either the old or the
new generation, never a half-written intent.
acceptance_criteria: 1) issues table gains requested_build_generation, last_confirmed_build_generation, building_generation. 2) mark_issue_resolving bumps requested_build_generation +1 in the same UPDATE that sets state=resolving (one statement, same txn). 3) Emits an event carrying the new generation. 4) A read helper returns issues where state=resolving AND requested>confirmed AND not in-flight. 5) Test: accept -> gen=1/state=resolving; re-accept newer bundle -> gen=2; crash between leaves old-or-new gen, never half.
close_reason: Implemented + unit-verified; committed 7eaa21a2624 (C1/C2) and d75906b8877 (A1 + C2 go-live). Real build path needs a live chroot to exercise.

title: Block C — Reconcile seam: level-triggered build trigger
description: Wire the build-trigger as level-triggered intent, not a command. The resolving transition writes desired state; the runner re-derives 'does a build need to exist?' each loop and stays sole queue writer. Same shape as verify_requests; tracker never touches the queue filesystem. Prior art: Kubernetes controllers, ArgoCD, Sentry.
close_reason: All four children delivered. The confirm-build trigger is level-triggered intent: the tracker bumps a generation counter, the runner re-derives what needs building each pass and stays sole queue writer, regressed is derived from the build record rather than stored, and the retries are counted and paced.

title: A1 Confirm-build execution
description: A1 Confirm-build execution — build (target,origin) with the accepted fix and report green/red, via a runner-dispatched job reusing dev-env apply-and-build / dsynth build. Cleaner once the build runs on Block B isolated worktree substrate (sequencing is a preference, not a hard dep).
design:
## Design

Execute the confirm-build and report a green/red verdict, REUSING the existing
in-process build-and-report machinery — no new build engine.

**Enqueue + dispatch:**
- `enqueue_confirm_build_job(queue_root, *, issue_key, bundle_id, origin, target,
  generation, env, requested_by)` — mirror `enqueue_verify_job` (runner.py:1850);
  new job `type=confirm`, carries `issue_key` + `generation` so the verdict can be
  tied back to the exact C1 intent.
- Runner dispatch arm handles `type=confirm` by calling
  `dportsv3.verify_fix.run_verify_fix` in-process (same path the verify job uses) —
  it applies the accepted fix (the `delivery_bundle_id` diff) and drives dev-env
  `apply-and-build` → dsynth build for (target, origin).

**Verdict source (dsynth-owned, read-only):** the build reports through the
existing hook path into `build_results` / `port_status` (schema.py:367/378) — we do
NOT write those core columns ourselves (the "dsynth owns build data" constraint).
Read `port_status.last_attempt_result` / `last_success_run_id` for the verdict, or
capture run_verify_fix's returned status.

**Report-back:** POST the verdict to a new tracker endpoint (mirror verify's
`POST /api/bundles/{id}/verification`), carrying `(issue_key, generation, verdict,
build_run_id)`. That endpoint hands off to A2 (green) / A3 (red).

**Generation bookkeeping:** whatever the outcome, set
`last_confirmed_build_generation = generation` and clear `building_generation` — so
the C2 loop stops re-enqueuing this generation. (A2 additionally resolves on green;
A3 reopens on red.)

**Block B note:** runs correctly on today's shared checkout; cleaner/safer on the
Block B per-job worktree substrate, but that is a preference, not a hard dependency.
acceptance_criteria: 1) enqueue_confirm_build_job + a type=confirm dispatch handler that runs the accepted fix through verify_fix.run_verify_fix (reused, no new build engine) for (target,origin). 2) Produces a structured green/red verdict tied to (issue_key, generation, target, origin, build_run_id). 3) Reads port_status read-only; does NOT write dsynth-owned build_* core columns. 4) Verdict POSTs back to a new tracker endpoint that routes to A2/A3. 5) Regardless of outcome, sets last_confirmed_build_generation=generation and clears building_generation. 6) Test: stubbed green -> verdict green vs generation; stubbed red -> verdict red.
close_reason: Implemented + unit-verified; committed 7eaa21a2624 (C1/C2) and d75906b8877 (A1 + C2 go-live). Real build path needs a live chroot to exercise.

title: C2 Runner reconcile loop (level-triggered)
description: C2 Runner reconcile loop (level-triggered). Each loop, re-derive needs-a-build (requested_gen > last_built_gen) and enqueue a confirm-build job; runner is sole queue writer. Mirrors process_verify_requests. Prior art: K8s level-triggered reconcile + resync.
design:
## Design

New `process_build_requests(queue_root)` in agent/runner.py, a near-clone of
`process_verify_requests` (runner.py:880), called from the main loop right next to
it (runner.py:3831). Level-triggered: each pass RE-DERIVES which issues need a build
rather than draining a command queue.

**Each pass:**
1. SELECT the C1 feed — issues with `state='resolving' AND
   requested_build_generation > last_confirmed_build_generation` and not already
   in flight (`building_generation IS NULL OR < requested_build_generation`).
2. For each, look up `delivery_bundle_id` → its origin/target (mirror the bundle
   lookup at runner.py:919).
3. Call a new `enqueue_confirm_build_job(...)` (mirror `enqueue_verify_job`,
   runner.py:1850; new job `type=confirm`).
4. Single-flight mark: set `building_generation = requested_build_generation` for
   that issue (mirror `_mark_verify_request`, runner.py:953) so the next loop pass
   does NOT re-enqueue while the build runs. A1/A2 clear/advance it on completion.

**Invariants preserved:**
- Runner is the SOLE writer to the queue filesystem; the tracker only wrote the
  intent counter (C1). Restores the tracker-is-read-only-for-queue rule, same as
  verify_requests.
- Env selection reuses `env_resolver` (per-job dev-env precedence).

**'env busy' vs real failure (MVP):** if no env is free, skip and retry next loop
(no penalty, no in-flight mark). Per-key exponential backoff for *real* failures is
C4 — not needed for the MVP.

**Resync:** because it re-derives from the counter every pass, a lost enqueue or a
runner restart self-heals — the issue still shows requested > confirmed next loop.
acceptance_criteria: 1) process_build_requests(queue_root) added, called from the runner main loop next to process_verify_requests. 2) Each pass re-derives issues needing a build (requested>confirmed, state=resolving, not in-flight) and enqueues one confirm-build job per (target,origin,delivery_bundle_id) via enqueue_confirm_build_job. 3) Runner is the sole queue-fs writer; tracker wrote only the counter. 4) Single-flight: two loop passes before the build finishes enqueue exactly ONE job (building_generation marker). 5) env-busy -> skip/retry next loop, no penalty, no in-flight mark. 6) Test: seeded resolving issue -> one job; second pass -> none.
notes: Mechanism implemented + smoke-verified (enqueue_confirm_build_job, process_build_requests, _mark_issue_building single-flight, _reset_building_markers crash-recovery). NOT wired into the runner main loop yet: the loop call + _reset_building_markers startup call land WITH A1 (DeltaPorts-rk0), because C1 already creates resolving issues and a type=confirm job has no dispatch handler until A1. Producer+consumer go live atomically. Confirm-specific lifecycle transitions (CONFIRM_START/GREEN/RED) are A1's.
close_reason: Implemented + unit-verified; committed 7eaa21a2624 (C1/C2) and d75906b8877 (A1 + C2 go-live). Real build path needs a live chroot to exercise.

title: Block A — Execution oracle: gate `resolved` on a build, not the merge
description: Stop trusting the PR-merge event; make `resolved` mean the port actually builds. Reuses verify_fix.py build-and-report machinery; reads dsynth-owned port_status read-only; joins on (target,origin,fingerprint). Prior art: ClusterFuzz progression, SWE-bench, Google TAP.

title: config_dir has only its highest-priority entry: an unset variable means 'no config exists', not 'look in the usual places'
description:
paths.config_dir() is:

    raw = os.environ.get("DPORTSV3_CONFIG_DIR", "").strip()
    return Path(raw) if raw else None

There is no search path. No directory means no file, and every setting
silently falls back to its table default. Nothing in the package ever
looks in /usr/local/etc/polytropos.

"Where config lives" is hardcoded in two places, NEITHER of them the
code:

  rc.d scripts          /usr/local/etc/polytropos   (services only)
  bin/dportsv3          <checkout>/config           (wrapper only)
  installed dportsv3    nothing -> table defaults

OBSERVED. An operator put [dev_env] cache_root in
/usr/local/etc/polytropos/polytropos.toml, ran ./bin/dportsv3 dev-env
list, and got the default /root/.cache/dports-dev. The file was correct
and never loaded: the wrapper had already pointed the variable at the
checkout's config/. So the outcome was not "no config found" but "a
DIFFERENT config won, silently" -- the worst of the three, and nothing
in the output says which file was read.

WHAT OTHER TOOLS DO. Supervisor -- a daemon with this same problem,
shipped in ports -- searches an ordered list, first match wins, and its
first two entries are relative to the executable:

    ../etc/supervisord.conf     (relative to the executable)
    ../supervisord.conf         (relative to the executable)
    $CWD/supervisord.conf
    $CWD/etc/supervisord.conf
    /etc/supervisord.conf
    /etc/supervisor/supervisord.conf

The hardcoded absolute path is the LAST resort, not the mechanism. XDG
is the same shape for user tools: $XDG_CONFIG_HOME, then
$XDG_CONFIG_DIRS, first match wins.

The pattern both share: an explicit variable is the highest-priority
ENTRY in a list, not a precondition for finding anything at all.
Polytropos has only that entry.

LOCALBASE. /usr/local is not universal -- it is set at ports level and
can be /opt/pkg or anything else. Deriving from the entry point handles
that for free: a port with PREFIX=/opt/pkg installs the binary at
/opt/pkg/bin/dportsv3, so <bindir>/../etc/polytropos follows it with
nothing to configure.
design:
Give config_dir the list it is missing:

  1. $DPORTSV3_CONFIG_DIR                    explicit, wins as today
  2. <dir of argv[0]>/../etc/polytropos      follows LOCALBASE for free
  3. /usr/local/etc/polytropos               documented default, last resort
  4. None -> table defaults, as today

Guard 2 and 3 on the directory existing, so a wrong derivation is
harmless and falls through. bin/dportsv3 keeps winning for checkouts
because it sets the variable before the package looks.

DO NOT resolve() argv[0]. deploy links <prefix>/bin/dportsv3 ->
<prefix>/lib/polytropos/bin/dportsv3, so resolving the symlink yields
the venv and derives the WRONG prefix. The unresolved parent is the
whole point.

THE RULE THIS BENDS, stated rather than buried: paths.py exists to
forbid Path(__file__).parents[N] walking out of the package. Step 2 is
that shape. The argument for allowing it is that it walks from the
INSTALLED ENTRY POINT, whose location the packaging system controls and
which is the same anchor supervisor uses -- not from __file__ inside
site-packages guessing at a surrounding repository, which is the thing
that broke when the tool moved out of DeltaPorts. Reviewers should
weigh that rather than take it as settled.

An earlier idea -- derive the prefix by reversing deploy's
VENV_RELATIVE (lib/polytropos) from sys.prefix -- was dropped: it needs
a constant kept in sync across two modules and assumes the venv layout,
where the binary's own location needs neither.

SEPARATE, NOT THIS BEAD: the rc.d scripts hardcode /usr/local
internally (polytropos_config_dir, polytropos_cmd, polytropos_path) and
deploy copies them verbatim with shutil.copyfile. On a non-default
LOCALBASE the services are already wrong today -- installed in the right
place, pointing at the wrong one. Needs its own fix.
notes:
IMPLEMENTED, and it took TWO changes -- the first alone did not fix the
reported symptom.

1. paths.config_dir() is now a search, first match wins:
     $DPORTSV3_CONFIG_DIR  ->  <bindir>/../etc/polytropos  ->
     /usr/local/etc/polytropos  ->  None
   2 and 3 guarded on existing. argv[0] is deliberately NOT resolved:
   deploy links <prefix>/bin/dportsv3 at <prefix>/lib/polytropos/bin/
   dportsv3, so following the symlink derives the venv as the prefix.

2. bin/dportsv3 now claims the checkout's config/ only when it actually
   holds configuration (a polytropos.toml, or secrets/).

Why 2 was necessary, found while re-reviewing against the original
report rather than against the design: config/ ships EMPTY on purpose
(its README says so). The wrapper's old test was `[ -d config ]`, which
is always true in a checkout -- so on the operator's host the variable
was set to a directory containing only README.md. Step 1 of the new
search then won with a directory that has no settings file, the search
never ran, and /usr/local/etc/polytropos stayed invisible. Change 1 on
its own only helps the INSTALLED binary, which previously found nothing
at all.

The `secrets/` clause matters: a dev checkout can legitimately hold keys
with every setting at its default. Testing only for polytropos.toml
would have stopped finding those.

config/README.md updated -- it claimed the directory is found "through
$DPORTSV3_CONFIG_DIR, and only through it", which this makes false.

Tests: tests/test_config_dir_search.py (14). The wrapper decision is
exercised as real shell rather than a Python restatement, over five
directory shapes. Mutation-verified: following the symlink fails 1,
dropping the existence guard fails 2. Suite 2986 passed.

Precedent, since the walk bends paths.py's rule: supervisor resolves its
own config the same way and lists the absolute path last --
../etc/supervisord.conf relative to the executable is its FIRST entry.
XDG has the same shape for user tools. The pattern both share is that an
explicit variable is the highest-priority entry in a list, not a
precondition for finding anything.
RE-REVIEW FINDING, fixed in a follow-up: the search made the test suite
read the host filesystem.

paths.config_dir now stats the filesystem below $DPORTSV3_CONFIG_DIR, so
any test that unsets that variable picks up whatever the machine has.
tests/test_paths.py:50 does exactly that
(test_config_falls_back_to_the_bundled_sample). It passed here only
because this laptop has no /usr/local/etc/polytropos -- the deploy host
does. Green locally, different on the build host, and the symptom would
have surfaced as an unrelated assertion.

Fixed with an autouse fixture in tests/conftest.py that points
DEFAULT_CONFIG_DIR at a nonexistent path and replaces argv[0]. It sits
next to _isolate_env_resolver, which exists for the identical hazard one
layer over (the env resolver auto-picking a real dev-env off the host).
Only argv[0] is replaced because cli.py reads argv[1:]; tests that
exercise the search set both themselves and win by running later.

Verified the fixture actually bites: pointing DEFAULT_CONFIG_DIR at /usr
instead of a nonexistent path fails the isolation test. A guard that
silently does nothing would be worse than none.

Suite 2987 passed.

title: agent and verify builds are invisible: the hooks flag suppresses all eight to stop one
description:
When the agent runs dsynth, and when verify runs apply-and-build, both
write /work/.dports-agent-hooks-disabled, which short-circuits
hook_common.sh for EVERY hook. Two call sites:

  dportsv3/agent/worker.py:3249   the agent's dsynth test
  dev-env/dports_dev_env/cli.py:514  apply-and-build (what verify runs)

Only ONE of the eight hooks does something we need to stop:

  hook_pkg_failure                 raises a bundle  <-- the problem
  hook_pkg_success/_ignored/_skipped  tracker_record_result
  hook_run_start / hook_run_end    open/close a build_run
  hook_pkg_start / hook_pkg_started  progress

Suppressing the bundle is correct -- without it every failed attempt
would raise a new bundle for a port the agent is already patching, an
unbounded loop in the worst case. But the other seven are pure
recording, and killing them makes every agent and verify build invisible
to the tracker. Over a full evening of agent work I could not answer
"what did the agent actually build", because build_results contains
nothing from any agent-driven build.

THE PLUMBING ALREADY EXISTS. Hooks read DPORTSV3_TRACKER_BUILD_TYPE from
dportsv3-hooks.conf -- a FILE they source, so it already survives the
env-var stripping that forced the disable flag to be a file
(hook_common.sh:419, default "test"; passed as --type to start-build at
:561). build_types today holds exactly {test, release} and there is a
_validate_build_type guard. All 115 build_runs on the box are "test".
design:
Replace the boolean sentinel with a typed one:

  /work/.dports-agent-build-type  containing "agent" or "verify"

hook_common.sh reads it, sets DPORTSV3_TRACKER_BUILD_TYPE from it, and
sets a flag that ONLY hook_pkg_failure honours (skip the bundle upload).
Every other hook runs normally. Add the two rows to build_types.

Keep the old flag working, or migrate both call sites together -- a
half-migrated pair would silently start raising bundles from agent
builds, which is the loop this exists to prevent.

SECOND BENEFIT, and it bit us today. hook_common.sh documents the
current failure mode itself: a flag left behind by an agent killed
uncatchably "disables tracking for every later operator build, and the
only symptom is an absence". Under a typed sentinel a stale file
mislabels runs as agent -- a wrong value that can be seen and alerted
on -- instead of silence.

DECIDE BEFORE IMPLEMENTING: what a failed agent build records. Plain
`failure` gives the cleanest visibility but puts failures in
build_results with no corresponding bundle, and "failing origins with no
bundle" is exactly the query used to find never-tried ports. Either pick
a distinct result value, or fix that query at the same time.

title: Meta muse-spark: supportable, but it cannot disable reasoning and our 'none'/'max' both 400
description:
An OpenAI-compatible endpoint at https://api.meta.ai/v1 serving
muse-spark-1.3-contributor. Measured against it through our own
llm.complete(), not just the raw SDK:

  routes through openai SDK   yes -- _use_openai_sdk already returns
                              True for "explicit api_base, no provider
                              name", so no routing code is needed
  bare model id               unchanged (no "/" to strip)
  reasoning=low / high        OK
  reasoning unset             OK
  tool calling                OK -- returned a well-formed
                              read_file(path="Makefile")
  reasoning tokens            real (761 on a one-line prompt)
  reasoning_content           NOT returned -- billed for thinking, no
                              chain-of-thought in the response, unlike
                              deepseek

Two failures, both in the reasoning translation:

1. reasoning="none" -> HTTP 400 `unknown parameter 'thinking'`.
   With no provider name the dialect table misses and we fall back to
   the DeepSeek spelling, extra_body={"thinking":{"type":"disabled"}}.
   The endpoint DOES support off -- its own error message lists `none`
   as a valid reasoning_effort variant. It just wants the plain OpenAI
   spelling.

   This is the one that bites: llm.triage.reasoning DEFAULTS to "none",
   so triage 400s on this model out of the box.

2. reasoning="max" -> HTTP 400. Endpoint accepts
   none|minimal|low|medium|high|xhigh. Our vocabulary is
   none|low|high|max, so `max` has no counterpart; xhigh is nearest.

Config-only operation is possible today by setting every role's
reasoning to low or high explicitly, but that is a trap: the triage
default silently 400s.
design:
Same shape as the existing nvidia entry, which is the precedent:

  - add "meta" to _OPENAI_COMPATIBLE
  - add its base to _PROVIDER_API_BASE
  - add a _REASONING_DIALECTS["meta"] that passes reasoning_effort
    straight through, including "none", and maps our "max" -> "xhigh"

A dialect keyed on the provider name is the only workable place: with
only an api_base the provider resolves to the empty string, so there is
nothing to key on until the operator names it
(llm.<role>.provider = "meta").

Open question before implementing: confirm the vocabulary against the
published API docs rather than against one 400 message. The error text
listed the variants, but a doc may say which are aliases and whether
`none` truly disables billing for reasoning tokens or merely asks for
less.
notes:
CORRECTION to the description above, from the published docs plus a
measurement. The description inferred from the 400 message that the
endpoint supports reasoning_effort="none" and merely wanted the plain
OpenAI spelling. That was WRONG.

dev.meta.ai/docs/protocols/chat-completions, reasoning_effort row:

  Accepted values: "none", "minimal", "low", "medium", "high", "xhigh".
  When omitted, the model reasons by default; set this parameter to
  control how much. "none" (disable reasoning) is **not supported by
  Muse Spark** and returns HTTP 400.

Default is "model-set" -- omit the parameter and the model decides.

Measured against the live endpoint, one level per request:

  none      400  '"reasoning_effort" does not support "none" with this model.'
  minimal   OK   completion=26   reasoning=14
  low       OK   completion=135  reasoning=123
  medium    OK   completion=246  reasoning=234
  high      OK   completion=134  reasoning=122
  xhigh     OK   completion=436  reasoning=424

(minimal/medium/high each answered 503 service_overloaded first and
succeeded on retry -- transient, not rejection. Worth knowing the
endpoint sheds load: llm.retry_* already covers 503.)

So thinking cannot be switched off on this model at all. The earlier
enum in the 400 message is the parameter's vocabulary, not this model's.

Also contradicting the doc summary: reasoning tokens ARE reported, in
usage.completion_tokens_details.reasoning_tokens. The traces themselves
stay private -- no reasoning_content -- so this model is billed for
thinking we cannot read, unlike deepseek.

Two model ids, and the difference is not cosmetic:
  muse-spark-1.3-contributor  "Used to improve our products."
  muse-spark-1.3              "Not used to improve our products."
The snippet we were handed names the -contributor one.

IMPLEMENTED (dportsv3/agent/llm.py):
  - "meta" added to _OPENAI_COMPATIBLE and _PROVIDER_API_BASE
  - _REASONING_DIALECTS["meta"] = _reasoning_meta: passes
    reasoning_effort through, maps our "max" -> "xhigh", and maps every
    off-spelling to "minimal" with a one-time warning, since silently
    spending reasoning tokens an operator switched off is what poly-r1g
    exists to prevent
  - "meta" ALSO added to _NAMESPACED_MODEL_IDS. This is the subtle one:
    _ROUTING_PREFIXES is derived as _OPENAI_COMPATIBLE minus that set,
    so adding meta to the compatible set alone would have made "meta/"
    a routing prefix and stripped it off NIM's "meta/llama-..." ids,
    404ing them -- the exact hazard _bare_model's docstring warns about.
    Membership keeps it out. Covered by a test that fails if the entry
    is removed.

Tests: tests/test_llm_meta_provider.py (16). Suite 2961 passed.

NOT done: no config change, no key moved, nothing deployed. Every value
the dialect can emit (minimal/low/medium/high/xhigh) is in the measured
-good set above, but the new code has not itself been run against the
live endpoint -- that needs a deploy.
Re-review finding, now pinned by a test: naming the provider is what
activates the dialect. Translating the vendor snippet literally gives
api_base and no provider, which routes through the SDK correctly but
leaves _provider_of returning "", so the dialect table misses and the
DeepSeek fallback sends `thinking` -- the field this endpoint 400s on.

So the working config is:

    [llm.triage]        # and/or [llm.patch] / [llm.chat]
    provider = "meta"
    model = "muse-spark-1.3"          # or -contributor
    api_key_file = "secrets/triage.key.meta"
    reasoning = "low"                 # "none" is honoured as "minimal"

api_base is then redundant: _PROVIDER_API_BASE supplies it.

This is a general property of the dialect table, not something this
change introduced -- an api_base-only config has always fallen back to
the DeepSeek dialect whatever is behind it. Fixing that generally would
mean resolving a provider from a known base URL, which is a bigger
change than this bead.

title: A failed restore_to_base is silent: github.py discards the bool it returns
description:
`_git.restore_to_base` is best-effort by design -- it runs in a finally
and must not mask the delivery exception, so it swallows everything and
reports via its return value. Its docstring: "Returns True on a clean
restore, False if any step failed (the caller can log it)."

The caller does not. `github.py` calls it as a bare statement in the
finally and drops the result. Nothing anywhere reads it.

So the one failure mode the return value exists to warn about -- the
restore itself failing -- produces no log line, no event, no row. The
clone stays on the feature branch with the diff applied, and the next
Accept fails with GitWrongBranch or GitDirtyClone pointing at a branch
whose delivery looked like it succeeded. The operator gets the same
symptom as poly-lt1 (concurrent Accepts) with none of the same cause,
and no way to tell them apart.

Latent, not observed: every restore on 2026-09-02 succeeded. Found while
reading the path for poly-lt1.
design:
Smallest fix: have github.py check the bool and log a warning naming the
clone and the branch it is stuck on. One if-statement.

Worth deciding, not assuming: whether a failed restore should also be
visible in the tracker rather than only in the log -- the next operator
to hit it is looking at a bundle page, not at tracker.log. Cheapest
version of that is wording the NEXT failure well: GitWrongBranch could
say "a previous delivery did not restore the clone" when the branch it
finds is an agentic/* one. That needs no new state.

Do not make restore_to_base raise. It runs in a finally and would mask
the real delivery error.
notes:
Implemented: github.py checks the return and logs a warning naming the
clone, the base it should be on, and the branch it is stuck on.

Dropped the second idea in the design note (rewording GitWrongBranch to
guess at an unrestored clone): with poly-lt1 landed the branch-mismatch
case is close to unreachable, so it would be speculative code for a
message nobody reads.

Found while writing the test: tests/test_delivery_github.py's _FakeGit
returned None from restore_to_base, so it was falsy -- the fake did not
match the real bool contract and would have made every existing test
emit the new warning. Fixed the fake, added restore_ok.

Tests: 2 in tests/test_delivery_github.py. Verified by mutation
(downgrading the warning to debug fails exactly one test).

title: dsynth_build and dsynth_test both exist, so every successful attempt compiles the port twice for ~3% of extra signal
description:
poly-8ni gave the agent dsynth_test as a separate acceptance gate,
kept dsynth_build as the cheap iteration loop, and told the prompt to confirm
once at the end. That design assumed the gate was expensive. It is not: `dsynth
test` IS a build, plus three cheap phases, and it force-rebuilds -- so the
second call throws away what the first produced and compiles the port again.

MEASURED, from tool_trace duration_ms on today's runs

  port                 build s   test s   overhead
  devel/level-zero        56.5     58.3       103%
  graphics/dcp2icc        32.6     19.3        59%
  devel/onetbb            26.6     16.7        63%
  x11/libinput            31.6     17.2        54%
  databases/fastdb        17.0      8.7        51%
  graphics/jbig2dec       12.9     11.5        90%
  TOTAL                  177.1    131.7        74%

level-zero is the honest number for a port that actually compiles: test costs
103% of build, i.e. the same work again plus ~3%. The sub-100% rows are ports
that died early (check-sanity, configure), where test never reached a compile.

WHAT THE EXTRA 3% BUYS

Phases observed across the env's dsynth logs:

  check-sanity patch configure build stage package install deinstall check-plist

install / deinstall / check-plist are the `test` additions. There is no `test`
phase -- the port's own test suite is NOT run, which was the worry that
justified keeping the two apart. It does not apply.

THE FIX

One build tool that runs `dsynth test`, always. Consequences:

- one compile per attempt instead of two on every success
- rebuild_ok comes to mean "passed the acceptance gate", which is what poly-8ni
  wanted; gate_ok (poly-qkp) becomes redundant as a separate field, though the
  recording machinery for report_complete stays useful
- the prompt loses its "confirm at the gate" step and its post-gate
  investigation guidance
- QA failures surface during iteration, where the agent can act on them,
  instead of at verify time where it cannot

THE ONE REAL CONSEQUENCE, STILL UNMEASURED

Ports carrying a latent check-plist defect will begin failing where they pass
today, because the loop currently never runs check-plist. poly-8ni deliberately
did not make the gate mandatory for exactly this reason. That argument stands;
what has changed is that it is now cheap to find out, because dtest costs what
dbuild costs. Worth a sweep before or shortly after the cutover rather than
holding the simplification hostage to it.

title: triage is serialised behind patching for no reason: it uses no tools and never touches dsynth
description:
The runner processes one job at a time. That is necessary for patch
jobs, which drive dsynth, and pointless for triage, which does not.

WHAT TRIAGE ACTUALLY DOES

dportsv3/agent/triage.py has no tool_loop, no tools.schemas, no whitelist. It
is a single LLM completion over a payload assembled from bundle artifacts. No
dsynth, no compose, no build. Measured today: ~90 seconds and 8-19k tokens,
against minutes and ~85k billable for a patch attempt.

Its only contact with the dev-env is three calls, and just one writes:

  is_slave_port(env, origin)        read a Makefile
  probe_health_cached(env, ttl)     cached, runner.health_cache_seconds=60
  ensure_overlay_or_abort(...)      WRITE: bootstraps a header overlay.dops

So triage never contends for the resource that actually serialises the system:
dsynth's exclusive lock on the build directory. Confirmed by observation today
-- a build launched while a patch job was running died instantly with
"main: Another dsynth is using /work/dsynth/build, exiting". Triage has no such
constraint.

THE COST, MEASURED

One worklist run raised 12 bundles. Each waited its turn in a serial loop whose
slow element is patching. The 12 triages together are a few minutes of work;
they instead trickled out across the whole run, because a triage could not
start until the previous port's patch attempt had finished.

WHY THIS IS NOT poly-s9m

poly-s9m (EPIC: multi-env concurrent building) is scoped to builds. Its
blockers are host-wide dsynth_active gating, env resolution refusing when more
than one env exists, and jobs having no env column -- and it explicitly parks
everything behind a decision between an in-process worker pool and multiple
runner processes.

Parallel triage needs none of that. No second env, no env scheduling, no lease
protocol. Its blocker #2 ("the runner loop is serial: one claim -> process_job
at a time, no pool") is the only part that applies, and it is stated there as a
build problem, so the cheap half is buried under an epic that cannot start.

WHAT WOULD NEED CARE

- ensure_overlay_or_abort writes into the shared DeltaPorts checkout. Per
  origin and small, but two triages bootstrapping at once need a lock or a
  serialisation point. Note that checkout is already the subject of poly-3sq
  (stubs left behind when a job does not land).
- The patch side must stay serial while dsynth is exclusive, so this is a
  per-job-type concurrency policy, not a global pool.
- Ordering: triage enqueues the patch job, so faster triage means a deeper
  patch queue, not more patch throughput. The win is latency to a
  classification and to escalation decisions, not more fixes per hour.

title: blobstore and blob_objects have drifted: 63% of files on disk have no row, and nothing detects it
description:
The artifact store and its index disagree, silently and by a wide
margin. Measured on the 2026Q3 builder, 2026-09-02:

  tracked files : 1,816    22.5 MiB   (have a blob_objects row)
  orphan files  : 3,120    30.9 MiB   (no row at all)
  total on disk : 4,936    53.5 MiB

So 63% of the files under paths.artifact_root/blobstore are invisible to the
database. Not unreferenced rows -- absent rows. Nothing can find, serve,
account for or reclaim them, and no check reports the divergence: the
mismatch only surfaced because the store was measured by hand against the
index.

NOT poly-326, THOUGH THEY MEET

poly-326 is the other half: blob_objects has no refcount, so a row that exists
cannot be proven unreferenced and therefore cannot be deleted. That same scan
found 59 such rows -- present in blob_objects, referenced by no artifact_refs.

Put together, reachability is unanswerable in both directions:

  row without a reference  ->  cannot be deleted safely   (poly-326)
  file without a row       ->  cannot be found at all     (this)

A fix for either alone still leaves the store unable to say what it holds.

LIKELY CAUSE

A state.db recreated while the blobstore persisted would produce exactly this
shape: the files outlive the index that named them. poly-cka documents one way
that happens -- wiping the evidence tree, where the runner and tracker race to
create state.db. That is a plausible origin rather than a demonstrated one; the
drift is not timestamped and nothing logged it.

WHY IT MATTERS BEFORE DISK DOES

At 31 MiB of orphans this costs nothing. The cost is epistemic: the index knows
about a third of what is on disk, so any statement the system makes about what
it has stored is currently wrong, and any future retention or migration work
would silently operate on the subset it can see.

Worth having regardless of the fix:

- a consistency check that walks the store against blob_objects and reports
  both directions of drift, so this is discovered by the system rather than by
  someone measuring it by hand
- a decision on the orphans: adopt them into the index, or delete them. They
  cannot be served today either way.

INCIDENTAL: poly-326'S NUMBERS ARE STALE

That bead records 49 blobs / 655.6 KB / zero dedup from 2026-08-27. The store
is now 1,816 objects / 22.5 MiB, and deduplication is real: 2,968 artifact_refs
resolve to 1,757 distinct blobs, 41% saved. port/pkg-plist alone is 10.7 MiB
across 148 refs -- 47% of all artifact bytes from 5% of the refs.

title: Explain the issue model in the UI: a welcome-and-help overlay
description:
The operator surface teaches nothing about its own model. An issue, an
occurrence and a job are three different things with three different
state machines; `regressed` is derived on read and never stored;
`resolving` means "a fix was accepted, a confirm build has not proved
it yet"; the worklist hides in-progress work on purpose. All of that
is written down only in the docstrings of issue_state.py,
fix_state.py, lifecycle.py and fingerprint.py.

Add one modal overlay -- opened on first visit, reachable afterwards
from a `?` in the agentic subnav -- that explains the model in six
chapters plus a glossary, over a blurred page rather than in a
separate doc nobody opens.

DESIGN

A working demo with the copy written and the diagrams drawn:

  https://claude.ai/code/artifact/c303466c-7b00-45bf-8642-626876444a92

It mocks /agentic and hovers the overlay over it. Chapters:

  1  issue / occurrence / job, and why they are not the same thing
  2  the fingerprint: what is canonicalised away, and the issue key
  3  who does what -- the runner lane and the operator lane
  4  the worklist bands and the one button each offers
  5  the issue lifecycle: resolving, Green Head, why two greens
  6  every occurrence status, its band, and its action gate
  +  glossary (origin, target, bundle, dops, dev-env, Green Head)

SCOPE

- one Jinja partial, `_welcome_modal.html`, included from `_base.html`
  so any tracker page can open it; no route, no query layer
- trigger: a `?` button in `_agentic_subnav.html`, plus auto-open on
  first visit keyed on localStorage['dportsv3.tour.v1']. Bump the key
  when the model changes and every operator gets the new tour once
- styles into progress.css using the existing tokens. The demo adds
  two webfonts (Bitter, IBM Plex Sans) to separate the handbook from
  the console; they are droppable, the fallbacks are Georgia and the
  system sans
- chapter 6's status table should be RENDERED from
  fix_state._RESOLUTION_STATUS and _WORKLIST_BUCKET rather than
  written by hand, so it cannot drift from the projection it
  documents. Everything else is static prose.

WHY THIS MATTERS

The UI presents a Sentry-shaped issue model without ever saying so,
and then departs from it in the one place that counts: something has
already tried to fix the issue before the operator sees it, so the
question on screen is "is this fix good" rather than "what broke".
An operator who reads it as a crash list will accept unverified fixes,
mistake `resolving` for done, and never learn that muting an issue
also stops the agent working new occurrences of it.

The action gates make this concrete. Accept is disabled until a
rebuild has proved the change, and nothing on the page says why the
button is dead.

NOT TRUE YET

Two open bugs make chapters 2 and 5 describe intent rather than
behaviour, and the guide should not ship claiming otherwise:

- poly-awz -- every failure fingerprints to the same value, so
  grouping by root cause does not currently happen at all
- poly-l9y -- a resolved issue that fails again does not read as
  regressed, so the dashed edge in chapter 5 never fires

title: A build result records nothing about the tree it was built from
description:
A result says "devel/libunwind failed at @2026Q3" and nothing about WHICH
@2026Q3 — which DeltaPorts commit, which freebsd-ports branch point, whether
the tree was dirty, which dev-env produced it. The result is therefore not
interpretable later and not reproducible at all.

THE PLUMBING ALREADY EXISTS AND HAS NEVER BEEN USED

  build_runs: 21 rows, 0 with commit_sha, 0 with commit_branch

The columns are there (commit_sha, commit_branch, commit_pushed_at),
finish_build_run accepts them (db.py:130), the client sends them
(client.py:27), the models declare them (models.py:71,97), and
`dportsv3 tracker finish-build` exposes --commit-sha / --commit-branch.
Nothing ever passes a value. Build provenance was designed in and never
wired up.

WHAT IDENTITY ACTUALLY MEANS HERE

Not the env NAME. "2026Q3" exists on every host and is recreated freely;
two envs sharing a name are not the same tree, and two envs with identical
inputs are interchangeable whatever they are called. The real identity is
the resolved input set, which `dports-dev-env status` already emits as one
JSON line:

  target, deltaports{branch,commit,dirty},
  freebsd_ports{branch,commit,dirty}, polytropos{branch,commit,dirty}

Env name + host are useful as a human breadcrumb, not as identity.

WHAT IT WOULD HAVE BOUGHT, FROM THIS WEEK

1. poly-e56, directly. /work/DeltaPorts is a symlink the agent repoints at
   its per-job worktree; a killed job left it on branch
   bundle/devel_llvm19@lite at ed604d3b3b6 while master was 3dbd7cebdad.
   Every compose and build from that env used the wrong overlays and
   nothing recorded it. Cost: three composes and several hours to find.
   A recorded commit would have made it one query.

2. Contradictory results become a fact instead of a mystery. Right now
   devel/libunwind, devel/libpciaccess and shells/bash-completion each show
   `success` as their last recorded result and FAILURE in the same day's
   sweep. With input fingerprints that reads "different trees"; without it,
   it reads "the tracker is wrong".

3. Dirty trees are invisible. The live env reports deltaports dirty=true
   (37 untracked files, including agent-authored overlay.dops). Results
   from a dirty tree are not reproducible and arguably are not evidence.
   Nothing marks them.

4. Issue fingerprints silently merge across drifted envs. Issues group by
   (target, origin, fingerprint). Two envs at @2026Q3 where one has
   GCC_DEFAULT=12 and one does not produce failures that fold into one
   issue: times_seen inflates, last_seen flips, the history stops meaning
   anything. This bites with a single host — no fleet required.

5. Verification claims are unfalsifiable. Every bundle currently has an
   empty verification_status. "Verified" is only a claim as "verified
   against tree X".

6. Prerequisite for poly-s9m. If envs are the unit of concurrency within a
   host (M hosts x N envs), scheduling needs env identity in the run record.

SCOPE

Cheapest useful step, no schema migration: populate the existing
commit_sha / commit_branch at hook_run_start from the env's DeltaPorts HEAD.
Already plumbed end to end; it is the single field that would have caught
poly-e56.

Beyond that, decide where the full input set belongs — build_runs (per
build) or build_results (per port) — and whether dirty should be a hard
flag on the row, since a dirty tree invalidates reproducibility regardless
of commit.

Distinct from poly-fij.8: that one is about attributing work to a BUILDER
and only matters once a fleet exists. This one is about what a result means
and is already wrong with one host and one env.

title: A build run has no source builder, and the schema forbids two at once
description:
The epic moves JOB dispatch to a claim endpoint and attributes jobs via
jobs.owner_id. Build runs get neither. Nothing in poly-fij or its six
children mentions build_runs, build_type or the active-build constraint —
checked, zero occurrences.

WHAT THE SCHEMA SAYS TODAY

  CREATE TABLE build_runs (
      id, target, build_type, started_at, finished_at,
      commit_sha, commit_branch, commit_pushed_at, total_expected )

  CREATE UNIQUE INDEX uq_build_runs_active
      ON build_runs(target, build_type) WHERE finished_at IS NULL

No host, runner_id or owner column. build_results attaches to
(build_run_id, origin) only, so a result carries no attribution either.
runs has run_id, profile, path, target — and path is empty in practice.

So a build is identified by (target, build_type), and the partial unique
index makes at most one active build of a target possible ANYWHERE.

WHY THIS IS NOT JUST A MISSING COLUMN

Attribution and concurrency are the same problem here. To tell two builders'
builds apart you must first be allowed to have two, and the index says no:
create_build_run raises ActiveBuildError (db.py:102, via get_active_run at
db.py:73) and the caller gets 409.

In a fleet that is the steady state, not an edge case: builder A starts
@2026Q3 test, builder B is refused and — per the current hook behaviour —
disables its own tracking for the whole run and keeps building. B's work
becomes invisible for as long as A holds the row.

ALREADY OBSERVED, ACCIDENTALLY (poly-0d6)

On 2026-08-31 a single build was killed by hand, leaving its row with
finished_at NULL. Every later build on the SAME host was then refused and
untracked for 2.5 hours — 137 ports built, 30 failures, 0 results recorded.
That is precisely the multi-builder failure mode, reached with one builder.
poly-0d6 covers detecting and recovering the stale row; it does not change
what a build is keyed by.

run_id DOES NOT HELP

current_run_id() reads ${evidence_root}/.current_run, a file on the builder
(hook_common.sh:133). Format run-<profile>-<ts>-<pid>. Minted locally, no
coordination, encodes no host. Probably collision-free across hosts by luck,
but it cannot be used for attribution.

SCOPE, to decide rather than assume

- What is a build in a fleet? Either (a) one logical build per target that
  several builders contribute results to — then build_runs stays singular
  and RESULTS need the builder attribution; or (b) a build per builder —
  then the unique index has to include the builder and every "the build for
  this target" reader needs revisiting. These are different products, and
  the UI (poly-fij.6) reflects whichever is chosen.
- Whichever way: build_results wants a source so "which builder saw this
  failure" is answerable, and issue fingerprints do not silently merge
  failures from different hosts.
- The 409 path needs a better answer than "disable tracking and keep
  building" regardless — see poly-0d6.

Blocks nothing today (single builder), but it should be settled before
poly-fij.6, whose acceptance criterion is "attributes every claimed job and
every bundle to a named builder" — build runs are absent from that sentence.
notes:
Correction: the single-builder occurrence of this constraint is tracked as poly-gd5 (filed 2026-08-27), not poly-0d6 — the latter was a duplicate I filed on 2026-08-31 before searching. Evidence merged into poly-gd5.
Cross-ref: poly-yh9 covers the other half — a build result records nothing about the TREE it was built from (dev-env inputs: DeltaPorts/freebsd-ports/polytropos commits + dirty). That one is already wrong with a single host and single env; this one needs a fleet before it bites.

title: A provider outage is recorded as agent_gave_up, so the agent is blamed for the API
description:
A patch job killed by the provider is resolved as `agent_gave_up`, which
says the agent tried and could not fix the port. It did neither.

MEASURED, overnight run 2026-08-31, 8 patch jobs on known-broken ports.
Four ended `dead`, and the bundle for every one of them reads
`resolution = agent_gave_up`:

  devel/nspr             Error code: 429
  x11/libinput           Error code: 500
  multimedia/libbluray   Error code: 504
  graphics/jbig2dec      Error code: 504

Those strings are the whole content of each job's `.error` note. The log
agrees: each port's last line before the move is an `[api_error]`, not a
patch verdict. None of the four reached a conclusion about the port.

WHY

steps.py `_err(..., JobEvent.PATCH_GAVE_UP, transient=...)` is used for
both cases. When the transient budget is spent, `record_transient_failure`
returns False and the call falls through to the terminal path carrying
PATCH_GAVE_UP. lifecycle.py:258 maps that event to the resolution string
`agent_gave_up`. So "the provider was down for the whole retry budget" and
"the agent could not fix this port" are indistinguishable downstream.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND THE LABEL

decision.py counts `failed_patch_attempts` from the `patch_gave_up` /
`patch_budget_exhausted` retire reasons — it is documented there as the
primary "is automation stuck?" signal. A provider outage therefore inflates
that count for a port the agent never actually failed on, and pushes the
next job on that port toward a higher tier or a manual handoff on false
evidence. The four ports above now each carry a failed attempt they did not
earn.

Note the inverse hazard already recorded on poly-4av: a job that is
*requeued* carries neither retire reason, so it is invisible to the same
signal. The two together mean the counter is wrong in both directions.

SCOPE

A distinct terminal event and resolution for "gave up because the provider
never answered" — e.g. PROVIDER_EXHAUSTED / `provider_unavailable` — so the
operator sees the truth and decision.py can exclude it from
failed_patch_attempts. The lifecycle already has PROVIDER_UNAVAILABLE for
the non-terminal case; this is its terminal sibling.

Companion to poly-4av. Found while exercising the in-call retry.

title: dsynth_build rebuilds every flavor, so verifying one fix recompiled a green flavor for 91 minutes
description:
dsynth_build rebuilds every flavor of a port, so verifying a fix for one
flavor can spend an hour and a half compiling flavors that were already
green.

MEASURED, devel/llvm19 patch attempt 1:

  18:32:06  T12 -> dsynth_build  origin=devel/llvm19
  20:04:12  [tool:dsynth_build] origin=devel/llvm19 rebuild_ok=False FAIL

  92 minutes for one tool call. What happened inside it:

    devel___llvm19@default.log     97 KB   mtime 18:33   FAILED 00:00:52
    devel___llvm19@lite.log       9.7 MB   mtime 20:04   full recompile

The flavor under test, @default, failed in 52 seconds -- the verdict was
available at 18:33. The remaining 91 minutes recompiled @lite, which had
built successfully in the main run an hour earlier and which the fix was
not about. It was rebuilt only because editing overlay.dops changes the
port's content CRC, so dsynth invalidates the cached package for every
flavor of the meta-node (it logs DELETE-PACKAGE ... port content
changed CRC).

THE FLAVOR IS ALREADY KNOWN

Same job, one turn later:

  [tool:dsynth_log] origin=devel/llvm19@default lines=199 ok

dsynth_log is called WITH the flavor; dsynth_build is called without it.
dsynth addresses flavors fine -- the main build log has
"[003] FAILURE devel/llvm19@default". So this is a matter of passing
through what the bundle already knows, not new capability.

WHY IT MATTERS

The runner is serial. That one call blocked eight queued jobs for an
hour and a half. tier.max_iterations is 4, so a single port can spend
~6 hours on rebuilds, nearly all of it on flavors nobody is testing.

It also undercuts how poly-w3s was framed: lifting the token budget
left max_tool_turns and max_iterations as the bounds, which is true for
TOKENS and says nothing about wall clock. On a large multi-flavor port
the loop is dominated by rebuild time, not model time -- 14 minutes of
model against 92 of compiling here.

SCOPE

Pass the flavor to dsynth_build when the bundle has one, so the rebuild
verifies the thing being fixed.

Open question worth answering first: whether a flavored dsynth build
still rebuilds siblings because they share a work directory / meta-node.
If it does, the fix is not just the argument and this needs measuring
before it is written.

Worth considering separately, not necessarily here: a wall-clock guard
per attempt, so one port cannot monopolise a serial queue regardless of
the cause.

title: The agent never reads a sibling version's overlay before authoring one
description:
For a versioned port family the first thing a human does is read what
the previous version already carries and adapt it. The agent does not,
and nothing reliably tells it to.

MEASURED, devel/llvm19 patch attempt 1 (2026-08-30 18:18-20:07):

  llvm19@default fails at configure in 52 seconds:

    CMake Error at cmake/modules/AddLLVM.cmake:2041 (add_dependencies):
      The dependency target "asan" of target "check-sanmd" does not exist.
      The dependency target "ubsan" of target "check-sanmd" does not exist.

  i.e. the sanitizers are not built on DragonFly, so check-sanmd
  references targets that do not exist.

DeltaPorts carries llvm11, llvm12, llvm13, llvm14, llvm15, llvm16,
llvm17, llvm18, llvm19, llvm20 and llvm-morello -- eleven ports in the
same tree the agent can already list_dir and get_file. devel/llvm13
built clean in the very same run. Every one of them has had to deal
with this platform's toolchain.

The agent reached for dops_reference (generic .dops syntax docs) and
never looked at a sibling. It then spent 14 minutes of model time and
92 minutes of rebuild to arrive at rebuild_ok=False.

WHY IT DID NOT

There IS a line for this, but it is buried: playbooks/
error-freebsd-only-features.md, step 4 of a numbered list --
"Check if DeltaPorts already has a fix for similar ports". It is
inside one error-specific playbook, and this job logged

  [playbooks_selected] devel/llvm19: role=patch included=1 skipped=16

so it was almost certainly not among the ones loaded. Nothing in
flow-patch.md (the always-on flow playbook) mentions sibling ports.

SCOPE

A playbook that fires on the shape of the origin rather than on the
error text: when the port name ends in a version suffix (llvm19,
python311, gcc11, ruby33, php83 ...) and sibling versions exist under
the same category in DeltaPorts, read the nearest working sibling's
overlay.dops / diffs / dragonfly dir BEFORE authoring anything.

Nearest working matters: llvm20 may be as broken as llvm19; llvm13
built clean this run. The port_status / build_results tables already
know which siblings are green for the target, so "nearest sibling that
built" is answerable without guessing.

Consider whether this belongs in flow-patch.md instead of a new file,
since playbook selection is what suppressed the existing line. A hint
that only helps when it happens to be selected is not much of a hint.

RELATED, ALREADY WORKS

The operator CAN inject this by hand: the manual-requests page has a
context textarea posting to /api/manual-requests, stored with a
context_rev; the runner compares it to last_context_rev_handled and
re-enqueues triage carrying the text, and
_load_operator_context_history feeds every prior round into the
prompt. The guard is retriage_blocked -- it will not re-enqueue while a
job for that origin is active. So the channel exists; this bead is
about not needing it for the obvious case.

title: The target build page stops updating until a full reload
Bootstrap overlay stubs are left in the shared DeltaPorts checkout when the job does not land
description:
Three header-only overlay.dops files were found sitting untracked in the
env's shared DeltaPorts checkout (writable/work/ports-main), left behind
by jobs that did not land:

  ports/x11-toolkits/pango/overlay.dops        08-29 23:49
  ports/devel/json-glib/overlay.dops           08-29 23:49
  ports/shells/bash-completion/overlay.dops    08-30 01:10

All three are the Step 48 bootstrap stub -- a deterministic header with
no body:

  port x11-toolkits/pango
  type port
  reason "Step 48 bootstrap: deterministic header; patch authors the body"
  target @any

pango's bundle was REJECTED by the operator; json-glib's patch job died
on the token budget; bash-completion's died on a transient 404. Every
one of them left its stub behind.

WHERE IT COMES FROM

runner.py, the bootstrap branch:

  overlay_path = f"/work/DeltaPorts/ports/{origin}/overlay.dops"
  res = worker.put_file(env_name, overlay_path, header)

That path is hardcoded. The same function reads STATUS through
"$DELTAPORTS_ROOT/ports/$1/STATUS" and removes it through
"$DELTAPORTS_ROOT/..." -- two of the three filesystem operations respect
the indirection and one does not. worker.py documents
$DELTAPORTS_ROOT as "since B1 it can be a linked worktree".

TWO READINGS, NOT YET DISCRIMINATED

(a) A bug: the write should go through $DELTAPORTS_ROOT like its
    neighbours, and lands in the shared tree only because the path was
    hardcoded.
(b) Intended: the stub has to outlive the triage job that wrote it,
    because it is what makes the port dops-typed before a LATER patch
    job can author the body. A worktree would be torn down in between.

If (b), the defect is not the location but the absence of cleanup: no
code path removes the stub when the work it was preparing for is
rejected, dies, or never runs. Nothing found that unlinks overlay.dops
on abort.

EVIDENCE TO COLLECT

  * Whether a triage job has a worktree at all. If it does not,
    $DELTAPORTS_ROOT and /work/DeltaPorts are the same thing for this
    call and (a) is cosmetic.
  * Whether a stub is ever filled in by a patch job in a LATER runner
    invocation -- that is what (b) requires to be true.
  * Whether a stub left by a rejected bundle changes what compose
    produces on the next run. Today it does not: the stubs have no mk
    lines, and the composed pango Makefile carries no locale change.
    A stub that acquired a body would be a different matter.
  * Whether the count grows. Three so far, one per failed patch
    attempt on a non-dops port.

WHY IT IS NOT COSMETIC

dev-env update refuses to fast-forward while the checkout is dirty and
tells the operator to rerun with --force. With these stubs present that
is the normal state, so the documented recovery is a flag that discards
untracked files -- including any real agent output sitting beside them.
Found exactly this way while pulling the WRK_ENV locale fix.

title: The chat role never disables thinking, so fix-chat always pays for reasoning
description:
CORRECTED. This was filed as a hang. It is not one -- measured against
the live endpoint, nemotron answers fine with no chat_template_kwargs at
all:

  ultra-550b   no chat_template_kwargs  -> OK 29.5s  out=14
  ultra-550b   enable_thinking=False    -> OK 58.0s  out= 2
  super-120b   no chat_template_kwargs  -> OK  1.6s  out=21
  super-120b   enable_thinking=False    -> OK  0.6s  out= 2

The upstream report this was filed from (opencode 24264) is about
deepseek-v4 models on NIM, and specifically about STREAMING reasoning
tokens. We do not stream and we do not run deepseek on NIM, so it does
not apply to us. Two other claims in the original filing were also
wrong: the "300s timeout observed here" was a request that DID send
chat_template_kwargs (reasoning="none"), during the window when ultra
was returning 404s and 503s, so it was the outage rather than this; and
the poly-4av retry count cited as 3 shipped as 5.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY WRONG

Omitting chat_template_kwargs does not hang, it leaves THINKING ON.
That is the poly-r1g cost problem reintroduced through a role that
never opted out. On a one-word prompt it is 14-21 completion tokens
against 2; on real chat context it is the same multiple poly-r1g
measured, and output is billed at full rate and never cached at
generation.

Two ways in, both verified in the code:

1. The chat role never passes reasoning. There is no `reasoning`
   argument anywhere in the tracker's agentic_api module -- the
   llm.complete call passes model, api_base, api_key,
   custom_llm_provider and timeout only. _reasoning_kwargs returns {}
   for a falsy value, so nothing reaches extra_body and the model
   thinks by default.

2. `reasoning` set to the empty spelling. steps._reasoning_for returns
   None when DP_HARNESS_<ROLE>_REASONING is set but blank -- the
   documented way to ask for the provider default, with a test pinning
   it. On NVIDIA "provider default" means thinking on.

SCOPE

Give the chat role a reasoning setting of its own, defaulting to off.
It is the only role without one, and the fix-chat panel currently pays
for reasoning tokens nobody reads.

Decide what "provider default" should mean per provider. Leaving the
key off is a truthful rendering of "operator asked for the default";
it is just an expensive default on NVIDIA. Either is defensible --
what is not defensible is the current state, where the only role a
human interacts with is the one that always thinks.

NOT NEEDED: sending chat_template_kwargs unconditionally, and the
second key from the upstream report ("thinking: true" beside
"enable_thinking: true"). Neither is required for nemotron; a full run
of triage and patch worked with enable_thinking alone.

NO LONGER BLOCKS poly-4av. That dependency was predicated on the hang
-- a retry policy repeating a 600s hang five times. With no hang there
is nothing to repeat.

title: A resolved issue that fails again is not marked regressed
description:
x11-toolkits/pango was manually resolved at 22:37 with green_head_run_id=12. It then failed again in a later build (run 13, 23:18), raising a new bundle and incrementing times_seen to 2.

Observed state afterwards:

  origin            = x11-toolkits/pango
  stored state      = resolved
  effective_state() = resolved
  times_seen        = 2
  regressed_at      = (empty)
  green_head_run_id = 12

So a port that is demonstrably broken again reads as resolved in both the stored and the derived state, and the operator worklist will not surface it.

C3's regression derivation is supposed to place an occurrence against the fix's Green-Head watermark: an occurrence from a build run NEWER than green_head_run_id is a regression rather than a stale recurrence. Run 13 > run 12, so this is the case the mechanism exists for.

Not yet established: whether the derivation never ran, ran and declined, or requires a code path (page render, feed) that has not been hit. issue_state.effective_state() was called directly and still returned 'resolved', which suggests the input it keys on is not being set rather than the comparison being wrong.

Worth checking whether the occurrence carried build_run_id at all -- artifact_store._coerce_build_run_id notes it is 'absent whenever tracking is off, which the derivation handles by falling back to timestamps'. If the new occurrence has a NULL build_run_id the comparison degrades to wall clocks, which is exactly what C3 was built to avoid.

Reproduction is cheap: resolve an issue, rebuild the port while it still fails, inspect effective_state.

title: Delivery uses one body for both the git commit and the PR: unwrapped markdown in commits, thin PRs
description:
orchestrator.py:417 calls format_commit_message() once and github.py passes the SAME body string to git.commit_diff() (github.py:167) and to the GitHub PR API (github.py:142/208/237). The function docstring says it builds the body 'for the delivered PR' -- the commit reuse is incidental. Two media, one rendering, and it serves neither well.

PROBLEM 1 -- COMMITS CARRY UNWRAPPED MARKDOWN
No wrapping exists anywhere in dportsv3/delivery/*.py (no textwrap, no width constant). The only length control is md_section(max_chars=N), a total-character cap, not a line width -- which is why a 1106-char single line passes a 2000-char cap.

Measured on the merged commit dae2e1e5084 (devel/glib20):
  44 chars  subject (fine)
 148 chars  disclosure blockquote
 484 chars  Problem paragraph
 116 chars  an Evidence bullet
1106 chars  Fix paragraph, one line
Plus '##' headings, a '>' blockquote, '-' bullets and backticks -- markdown that has no business in a ports-tree commit.

PROBLEM 2 -- THE PR BODY IS THIN
It harvests only 4 of 7 triage.md sections and 1 of 5 patch.md sections, and ignores proposed_fix.md entirely (7 sections).

Not carried today: triage Platform, Suggested Fix, Notes; patch Patch Log, Rebuild Status, Patch Plan (JSON), Rebuild Proof (JSON); all of proposed_fix.md (Summary, Bundle, Cost, Files touched, Apply this fix, Verify independently, Audit trail).

Concrete loss: pango's triage Notes said 'this will recur in any dsynth environment without a valid default locale' -- the systemic-scope finding. It existed in the artifact and never reached the reviewer, who therefore saw a per-port fix with no hint the cause was tree-wide.

FIX -- TWO RENDERERS OVER THE SAME STRUCTURED INPUTS
format_commit_message already receives structured fields (origin, target, operator, model, attempts, tokens, verified_at, diff_text, patch_summary, root_cause, classification, confidence, evidence). Nothing is lost by rendering twice; the conflation is purely presentational.

  format_commit_message() -> plain text for git
  format_pr_body()        -> markdown for the forge

Commit renderer requirements:
- wrap prose at 72 columns
- no markdown: no '##' headings, no '>' blockquote, no '-' bullets, no backticks
- content limited to the change itself: what failed, why, what the fix does, which files. Provenance/cost/operator/agent stats belong in the PR.
- keep the Signed-off-by trailer and any other trailers, unwrapped
- the bot-disclosure line is arguably redundant in the commit: authorship is already recorded in the commit's author/committer fields (Fred [bot] <github@dragonflybsd.org>). Decide explicitly rather than by inheritance.

PR renderer requirements:
- keep today's markdown structure
- add the missing narrative: Platform, Notes, Rebuild Status/Proof, and the useful parts of proposed_fix.md (Files touched, Verify independently, Audit trail)
- deliberately consider EXCLUDING triage 'Suggested Fix': on pango it recommended LC_ALL=C.UTF-8, the exact value that causes the failure. Publishing a wrong suggestion beside the real fix invites a reviewer to 'correct' the fix toward it.

TRAP TO AVOID
The Evidence section is quoted build output. Running textwrap over it would silently alter recorded compiler/log lines and destroy their value as evidence. The commit renderer must wrap prose but pass verbatim blocks through unwrapped (indented if needed). This is a behavioural requirement, not formatting taste.

TESTS
tests/test_delivery_message_format.py currently pins the shared body (test_commit_message_body_full_narrative, test_commit_message_degrades_without_triage_or_patch_prose). Needs: a max-line-length assertion on the commit body; an assertion that no markdown syntax appears in it; an assertion that a verbatim evidence line survives byte-identical; and PR-body assertions for each newly carried section, including graceful degradation when an artifact is missing.
notes:
IMPLEMENTED in 65ce393. Two design points changed during implementation,
both against what this bead originally proposed:

1. NOTHING is lifted from proposed_fix.md. Reading it showed its
   "Apply this fix" section embeds a loopback tracker URL
   (curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/api/bundles/...), and "Verify
   independently" / "Audit trail" name in-bundle artifact paths that
   mean nothing outside the tracker. "Files touched" duplicates the
   diffstat. Lifting any of it would have leaked an internal address
   into a public pull request. The bead's suggestion was too generous.

2. NO bundle id in the PR body. An existing assertion
   (test_pr_body_full_narrative, formerly ..._commit_message_...)
   pinned "Bundle:" as absent under the comment "Provenance (no tracker
   URL)". A bundle id is meaningless to an upstream reviewer with no
   tracker access, so the prior decision stands.

Everything actually added comes from artifacts already plumbed into
deliver() -- triage Platform/Notes, patch Rebuild Status -- so no new
artifact wiring was needed.

Verified by rendering both bodies from the real pango bundle artifacts:
commit body max line 72, no markdown, no provenance; PR body carries
platform, the Notes scope paragraph, and Rebuild status, with no
loopback URL.

Suite 2717 -> 2724.

title: delivery preflight checks the retired token location
description:
preflight.py:124 builds the token path as Path(config_dir) / 'delivery.token' -- the pre-unification location. The live setting is delivery.token_file, defaulting to secrets/delivery.token and resolved by settings.secret_path().

Consequence: _check_token_mode() stats a file that no longer exists, returns [] and reports nothing, so a world-readable forge credential at the real path draws no warning. Confirmed on hardware: with a token in place at secrets/delivery.token, the preflight emitted no token line at all.

Fix: ask settings.secret_path('delivery.token_file') instead of rebuilding the path. Test should place a 0644 token at the settings-resolved path and assert the warning fires.
notes:
VERIFIED ON HARDWARE 2026-08-29, commit fb579e3.

The same tracker log holds the before and after. Previous startup, with a
0640 token already in place at secrets/delivery.token:

  delivery preflight: delivery provider is 'github'
  delivery preflight: clone_dir ... is a writable git tree
  delivery preflight: clone_dir is clean and on 'master'

No token line at all -- the check was stat'ing the retired location.

After the upgrade, same config, same token:

  delivery preflight: delivery provider is 'github'
  delivery preflight: /usr/local/etc/polytropos/secrets/delivery.token mode is 0640
  delivery preflight: clone_dir ... is a writable git tree
  delivery preflight: clone_dir is clean and on 'master'

The world-readable branch was not exercised on the live token (that would
mean chmod'ing a real forge credential); it is covered by
test_preflight_checks_the_token_the_settings_actually_name.

title: delivery.clone_dir has no default
description:
delivery.clone_dir is declared with default None (dportsv3/settings.py:344), so every operator has to invent a path. Every other path setting derives from a sensible root; this one does not.

/var/db/polytropos/DeltaPorts is the obvious default: /var/db/polytropos is already SERVICE_HOME (deploy.py:82) and polytropos_home in the rc config, it is created by deploy install, and it is already owned by the service account -- which is clone_dir's hard requirement, since the tracker delivers and is not root.

Open question the design has to answer: a default that points at a directory nobody created turns 'delivery is off' into 'delivery is misconfigured' the moment delivery.type is set. Either deploy install clones it, or the preflight has to distinguish 'default path, absent' from 'operator named a path, absent'.
notes:
VERIFIED ON HARDWARE 2026-08-29, commit e9a1dfd.

Throwaway config dir declaring only delivery type and repo, no clone_dir:

  config show ->  delivery.clone_dir  /var/db/polytropos/DeltaPorts  default
  preflight   ->  OK: clone_dir /var/db/polytropos/DeltaPorts is a writable git tree
                  OK: clone_dir is clean and on 'master'

So the default resolves to a real clone with no operator input.

The absent-default branch, run as the service account:

  ERROR: delivery.clone_dir is not set, so it defaults to
  /var/db/polytropos/DeltaPorts-absent, which does not exist -- nothing
  clones it for you. Either set delivery.clone_dir, or create it:
  git clone <repo url> ... && chown -R polytropos ...

deploy install still does not clone it; that was the deliberate call, a
400M fetch does not belong in a package install. The preflight carries
the instruction instead.

title: Unify config into one polytropos.toml, with env vars only where a value cannot be known in advance
description:
Phase 2 of poly-cu8, after poly-cu8.1. Collapse the six config mechanisms into
one TOML plus one file per secret, and cut the environment layer down to the
handful of variables that have a reason to exist.

The full inventory, the six mechanisms, the 39 read-but-unsettable variables,
and the test for which variables survive are in poly-cu8's description. The
target shape, the schema-table approach, the secret-file split, the
polytropos.conf shrink, the dev-env import-direction constraint and the
migration path are in poly-cu8's design.

Work, in the order the pieces depend on each other:

1. Decide where the shared loader lives. dportsv3 imports dports_dev_env
   (agent/health.py:88, agent/env_resolver.py:60-61) and nothing imports back,
   so a shared loader must live in dports_dev_env. The alternative is that
   dev-env keeps its own file and its own copy of the machinery. This is the
   one decision that is expensive to reverse — getting it backwards
   reintroduces the coupling paths.py exists to prevent.

2. Write the schema table: one entry per setting with TOML path, type,
   default and env= (or None). Generate the sample TOML from it. About 8
   entries carry env=; the rest are TOML-only.

3. Port the readers. 24 DP_HARNESS_*, 9 DPORTSV3_*, DP_ACTIVITY_LOG_MAX and
   the delivery/policy loaders. Note that agent/steps.py:618 builds its
   variable name with an f-string, so it will not be found by grepping for the
   name — it has to be ported by reading the code.

4. Fold delivery.toml and agentic-policy.json into sections of the one file,
   keeping their loaders' validation.

5. Split the secrets into one file per key, named from the TOML's *_file
   entries, with the modes following the two service identities rather than
   the two features.

6. Shrink polytropos.conf to rc's own knobs, stop sourcing the .env files,
   stop translating rc vars into env vars. Replace the prestart's dependence
   on queue_root/log_dir with `config get`.

7. `dportsv3 config show` and `config migrate`.
acceptance_criteria:
- One <prefix>/etc/polytropos.toml holds every non-secret setting; the two
  .env files and agentic-policy.json are gone, and delivery.toml is a section.
- Secrets are one value per file, named by the TOML, with modes that follow
  the runner/tracker identity split. A TOML syntax error cannot take out the
  credential set.
- A generated-from-schema sample lists every setting, so "read by code but
  settable nowhere" is zero rather than 39.
- `dportsv3 config show` prints each resolved value and its source.
- `dportsv3 config migrate` converts an existing install without hand-editing,
  and leaves the old files in place.
- The environment surface is the bootstrap variable, the five inter-process
  variables, DP_TEST_*, and about 8 declared per-run overrides. Nothing else.
- The rc scripts source no .env file and translate no rc var into an env var.
- The shared-loader import direction is dportsv3 -> dports_dev_env, or dev-env
  is self-contained. Never the reverse.
close_reason:
Landed across 423f832, 8bafb4e, aade04b, bf392e2, 10f41fe, 5837b94.

Six config mechanisms became one polytropos.toml plus one file per secret.
82 settings in two tables (61 polytropos, 21 dev-env) behind a shared
schema engine. The engine lives in dports_dev_env because the dependency
only points that way; each package owns its own table.

Environment surface: 69 -> 8 declared overrides, plus the bootstrap
variable, five inter-process arguments and DP_TEST_*. Each override was
argued individually against "is this knowable when the file is written".

Everything derives from the table: the value, the generated sample,
config show's provenance column, the unknown-key warning. config
show/get/check/sample/migrate. The rc scripts source nothing and
translate nothing; the runner prestart asks `config get paths.queue_root`
rather than holding a second copy.

Six variables the original audit missed, all found by the new structural
guard rather than by grep: DP_HARNESS_CONTEXT_FILE_CAP and
DPORTSV3_STALE_QUEUED_MAX_AGE_SECONDS split the call and the name across
lines; the four DP_CONFIRM_* knobs passed the name to a helper. The guard
now scans for the name itself, however it is reached, and fails the suite
on an undeclared one.

Four defects found by hardware validation, each fixed:
- deploy install migrated all four credentials at 0640, handing the
  runner's patch key to the unprivileged tracker. Modes now follow the
  reader, from one table the installer, migrate and check all read.
- install told the operator to run `config migrate`, which then refused
  because install had just written a settings file. migrate merges now;
  the installer carries the values across itself. Without that the host
  had keys but no llm.triage.model and would refuse every job.
- the tracker exited with "unable to open database file": a default
  paths.state_db was treated as "unset" and fell back to $PWD/state.db,
  and a service's cwd is /.
- retiring an operator file broke `deploy install` for anyone upgrading,
  because the installed planner demands a sample the new checkout no
  longer ships.

Validated on hardware 2026-08-29: both services restarted on the new
configuration and are serving; models resolve from the settings file;
config check passes as root and as the service account; the tracker
cannot read the runner's patch key; the startup preflight reports
delivery correctly. harness.env and chat.env are left in place, untouched.

Suite: 2704 passed.

title: litellm only imports because dportsv3 is imported first
description:
Found probing reasoning controls on hardware 2026-08-29.

On the deployed host, litellm cannot be imported at all:

  $ /usr/local/lib/polytropos/bin/python -c "import litellm"
  ImportError: /usr/local/lib/python3.11/site-packages/tokenizers/
  tokenizers.abi3.so: Undefined symbol "esaxx_int32"

Same failure from the checkout venv and from the bare system python, as
root and as the operator. Yet the runner makes real LLM calls, because
this works:

  import dportsv3.agent.llm   # pulls in tokenizers first
  import litellm              # now fine
