The system tokenizers .so is missing a symbol it only resolves once
something else has loaded the library providing it. The runner survives
purely because of the order its own imports happen to run in.

Why it matters: nothing pins that order. Any refactor that moves the
litellm import earlier, or drops whatever currently pulls tokenizers in
first, turns every LLM call into an ImportError at runtime -- on a host
where the test suite still passes, because the suite does not import
litellm this way.

Options worth weighing:
  - fix the broken tokenizers package on the host (it is a DragonFly
    binary-package problem, not ours) and stop depending on order
  - pin the working order explicitly with a comment saying why, so a
    tidy-up does not silently remove it
  - vendor a litellm import shim that does the preload deliberately

Related: poly-170 (extras cannot install on DragonFly), poly-lx9 (the
deployed venv is not self-contained).
notes:
INVALID -- closing. I misread this.

dportsv3/agent/__init__.py already handles it deliberately, with the
reason recorded: _ensure_tokenizers_importable() injects a no-op
tokenizers stub when DragonFly's py311-tokenizers .so fails to load
(missing DT_NEEDED entries for libonig and esaxx). litellm only imports
tokenizers for local cost calculation, which the harness does not use --
usage comes from response.usage.

So 'import dportsv3 first, then litellm works' is not luck and nothing
is unpinned. It is the shim working exactly as designed, and the module
docstring says so. My probe failed only because it imported litellm
without importing the package that installs the stub.

title: get_file returns unnumbered text, so the model renumbers it by hand in reasoning
description:
From the session dump, devel/glib20, 2026-08-29 13:19 run (the one with
all three efficiency fixes deployed).

WHERE THE BUDGET ACTUALLY GOES. Of the assistant's output:

  reasoning_content  199,450 chars   93.8%
  tool_calls          13,108 chars    6.2%
  content                  0 chars    0.0%

Model output is ~51% of billable spend and did not move at all when
tool-result spend dropped 37% -- 60,341 before, 60,762 after. It is the
dominant cost and nothing so far has touched it.

THE CHEAPEST SLICE TO RECOVER. get_file returns a window with
first_line=166 in the metadata and then unnumbered text. To reason
about hunk positions the model has to attach the numbers itself, and it
does so by transcribing the file line by line inside its reasoning:

  - Line 166: `   * always returns 'undefined symbol'. Only if RTLD_DEFAULT or `
  - 167: `   * NULL is given, dlsym returns an appropriate pointer.`
  - 168: `   */`
  - 169: `  lock_dlerror ();`

Measured across the attempt: 9 of 21 assistant turns do this, ~20,951
chars of reasoning, ~10.5% of all reasoning. That is a lower bound --
the regex only catches lines that begin with the number.

PROPOSED FIX. Have get_file prefix each line with its 1-indexed number
(the tool already computes first_line/last_line, so this is free). Cost
is roughly 7 chars per line of INPUT, which is cached from the next turn
on; the saving is OUTPUT, which is never cached and is billed every
time. For a 200-line window: ~1.4K input once against ~21K output.

Worth checking at the same time whether the patch playbook asks the
model to reason in line numbers more than it needs to.

RELATED, same run, smaller:
  - overlapping windows are not deduped. Turn 18 read lines 166-195,
    turn 19 read 1-212 of the same file, so 30 lines came back twice.
    poly-47d only elides an identical window.
  - two turns still spent probing paths the chroot does not usefully
    expose: list_dir /lib FAIL, grep /usr/include matches=0 FAIL. Same
    shape as the /usr/lib probe in the previous run, so it is habitual
    rather than incidental.
notes:
SHOULD THERE BE A sed TOOL? Considered and rejected, with the reason.

The observation behind it is sound: LLMs are fluent in sed -n 'N,Yp'
and reach for it naturally. But measured across both session dumps, the
model almost never fumbles our parameterisation --

  thinking-on run   2 of 21 turns mention offset/index mechanics, 7 refs
  patch-low run     2 of 30 turns,                                3 refs

What it does constantly instead is map CONTENT to line numbers:

  'And first_line=201, last_line=212. So line 201 = ,
   line 202 = blank, etc.'

A sed tool returns unnumbered text exactly as get_file does, so the
model would still count by hand. It does not touch the expensive
behaviour. Numbered output does.

Also against a shell sed tool: it duplicates grep and get_file, and a
general sed-expression executor is a far wider surface (arbitrary
expressions, unbounded output) than a fixed line-range read.

WORTH TAKING FROM THE IDEA, folded in here rather than filed separately:
accept a 1-indexed inclusive range alongside the existing 0-indexed
offset+count, because 'lines 201-212' is how the model already thinks
and says it. Small win -- 3 to 7 references per run -- next to the
numbering, which is a 53,124-char turn.

NEW EVIDENCE FOR THIS BEAD, from the patch-low run: the single largest
reasoning turn of the whole attempt was 53,124 chars and opens

  Line 975: (blank)
  Line 976: 
  Line 977: 

-- transcribing the file to attach numbers, then hand-writing a patch
from it. Lowering reasoning_effort did NOT cap this: max output per turn
rose from 8,221 to 16,248 even as the median fell 87%. reasoning_effort
moves the average; numbering removes the cause.
CORRECTION to the note above: three quoted code lines came out empty.
They were backtick-quoted and my shell ate them as command
substitution. The intended quotes were:

  What the model reasons, mapping content to line numbers:
    'And first_line=201, last_line=212. So line 201 = const gchar *msg;,
     line 202 = blank, etc.'

  The opening of the 53,124-char turn:
    Line 975: (blank)
    Line 976: # Dependencies used by executables below
    Line 977: have_libelf = false

The argument is unchanged; only those three samples were lost.
IS LINE-NUMBERED OUTPUT ACTUALLY STANDARD? Checked, because the fix
rested on an assumption I had not verified. Three independent harnesses:

  Claude Code   'Results are returned using cat -n format, with line
                numbers starting at 1' -- from its own Read tool
                description.
  Roo Code      documented output format is '1 | This is the first
                line.' -- number, pipe, content, on every read.
  Zed           PR 56779 'Prefix read_file tool output with line
                numbers', merged 2026-05-22. cat -n style, right-aligned
                in a 6-char field then a tab.

The Zed PR is the useful one, because it is a project that ADDED this
and recorded why. Two points from it land directly on us:

  1. 'Numbering reflects the actual file lines, so a ranged read
     starting at line 42 emits 42 for its first line, not 1.' That is
     exactly our case -- we return first_line=166 as metadata and then
     unnumbered text, and the model reconstructs the mapping by hand.

  2. The reviewer approved rollout without a feature flag because
     'models are all passing -n to every tool already, and evals looked
     good.' Independent confirmation of the behaviour measured here: if
     the tool does not number the lines, the model will do it itself.

So this is not a speculative optimisation. It is the established
convention, we are the outlier, and our session dumps show the exact
cost of being the outlier.

Sources:
  https://github.com/zed-industries/zed/pull/56779
  https://docs.roocode.com/advanced-usage/available-tools/read-file
close_reason:
Landed in 6fc5b5a. get_file returns cat -n numbered content
(content_is_line_numbered=true), a window carries the file's own numbers, and
start_line/end_line take an inclusive 1-indexed range. put_file refuses
content that still carries the numbers (_reject_line_numbered_content), keyed
on three consecutive matches so real number-tab content is not blocked.
Covered by tests/test_get_file_line_numbers.py.

title: An attempt starts with a budget it cannot possibly finish in
description:
Measured on hardware 2026-08-29, devel/glib20:

  [attempt_start] attempt 2/4 for devel/glib20 (tokens used 111554/120000)
  ... 5 turns ...
  tool_loop: token budget exhausted after turn 5 (12018 >= 8446 billable)
  attempt_loop: budget exhausted after attempt 2 (123572 >= 120000 billable)

Attempt 2 began with 8,446 billable tokens left. Its own first five
turns cost 12,018 -- it overran on the turn it was always going to
overrun on. The spend was not merely wasted, it was predictably wasted:
attempt 1's cold start alone was 30,216 billable, so no attempt has ever
completed in under ~30K.

Worse, attempts do not inherit anything. Attempt 2 spent its whole
budget re-deriving state attempt 1 already had -- get_file on
patch-gmodule_gmodule-dl.c and patch-gio_meson.build (both read in
attempt 1), materialize_dports (run three times in attempt 1),
env_verify (already ready). 71% of attempt 2's spend was model output
re-reasoning from scratch.

Two candidate fixes, not exclusive:
  1. refuse to start an attempt when remaining budget is below the
     observed cost of a cold start, and report budget-exhausted from
     the last attempt that could actually run
  2. carry a short findings summary across attempts so a retry starts
     from what the previous one established

Related: poly-7eh (tool results), poly-x9c (budget on an
unreproducible report).
notes:
FIXED (candidate 1) 2026-08-29.

attempt_loop.run now refuses to start attempt N>1 when the remaining
billable budget is under MIN_ATTEMPT_BUDGET_FRACTION of the whole
budget (default 0.25, DP_HARNESS_MIN_ATTEMPT_BUDGET_FRACTION). The old
gate was 'remaining <= 0', which only refuses an attempt with literally
nothing left. Attempt 1 is never gated -- it is what the budget was
granted for.

The floor is a fraction, not an absolute, because the budget is
per-tier: a larger allowance implies larger attempts. Grounded on the
measured run -- the cheapest path to the first real tool call
(make_extract, turn 4) had already cost 37,227 billable of 120,000,
about 31%, so a retry that cannot reach that far only re-establishes
context before dying.

CORRECTION to this bead's description: 'attempts do not inherit
anything' was too strong. _failure_context_message carries the last
2000 chars of the previous attempt's final RESPONSE into the retry.
What is discarded is the tool history -- every file read, every grep,
every build result. That is precisely why attempt 2 re-read both patch
files and re-ran materialize_dports: it inherited what it said, not
what it learned.

So candidate 2 (carry a findings summary across attempts) is still
open and is the more valuable half. The gate only stops the waste; it
does not make a retry cheaper.

title: dsynth_log returns lines=0 for a log that exists
description:
Measured on hardware 2026-08-29, devel/glib20, the first patch run that
got past extract.

  [tool:dsynth_log] origin=devel/glib20 lines=0 FAIL

The log was there the whole time. The agent recovered by hand:

  T13 list_dir /work/dsynth/logs                     ok
  T14 get_file /work/dsynth/logs/devel___glib20@bootstrap.log  ok

So the tool cannot find a file the very next list_dir enumerates. Cost
was ~4 turns and roughly 5K billable tokens to route around a tool that
should have answered in one.

Note the name shape: devel___glib20@bootstrap.log -- category and port
joined by THREE underscores, plus a @flavor suffix. Worth checking
whether dsynth_log builds the name without the flavor, or looks in the
profile log dir rather than /work/dsynth/logs.

Aggravating factor: it FAILs silently enough that the agent treats it
as "try something else" rather than "this tool is broken", so the cost
is paid on every run rather than reported once.

title: Shipped harness/chat samples name a model the API rejects
description:
deploy/harness.env.sample and deploy/chat.env.sample default to
"deepseek/deepseek-v4", which is not a valid model name:

  litellm.BadRequestError: DeepseekException - The supported API model
  names are deepseek-v4-pro, deepseek-v4-flash, and
  deepseek-v4-flash-vision-exp, but you passed deepseek-v4.

The failure mode is bad: triage names deepseek-v4-flash, which IS valid,
so an operator following the setup gets a runner that starts clean,
triages correctly, decides a tier, enqueues the patch job -- and only
then dies. It reads as a patch-loop bug rather than a config typo.

tests/test_proposed_fix.py already uses deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro, so the
correct name was known.
notes:
Still live, and now visible in the new layout. deploy/harness.env.sample was
corrected but chat.env.sample was not, so a deployed host carried
DP_HARNESS_CHAT_MODEL="deepseek/deepseek-v4" — the invalid name. poly-cu8.2's
migration carried that value into llm.chat.model faithfully, which is correct
behaviour for a migration but means the bad value survives.

Both .env samples are gone now; the shipped defaults for llm.*.model are empty,
so the class of bug is narrower. What remains is any host whose migrated
llm.chat.model still says deepseek-v4. Check with `dportsv3 config show`.
VERIFIED ON HARDWARE 2026-08-29, commit 5e31590.

Caught against the host's real migrated value, not a fixture. The host
carried llm.chat.model = deepseek/deepseek-v4 from the chat.env migration:

  warning: llm.chat.model is 'deepseek/deepseek-v4', which the provider
  rejects; use deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro, or deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash
  for triage

Exit 1, identical as root and as the unprivileged tracker account.

It also reaches the boot path: restarting the tracker printed

  /usr/local/etc/rc.d/polytropos_tracker: WARNING: settings in
  /usr/local/etc/polytropos did not validate; run: dportsv3 config check

which is the point of the bead -- the report moved from mid-job to start.

The host's value is unchanged; correcting it is the operator's call.

title: make_extract runs outside dsynth's context, and dev-env has no override channel for base-owned config
description:
Two problems that look like one. Today (poly-cx6) proved they are
separable, and that fixing the second does not fix the first.

PROBLEM 1 - TWO PACKAGE UNIVERSES

dsynth builds inside its own builders against packages it built itself.
worker.py:1905 make_extract runs a bare `make ... extract` in the
chroot proper, against packages pkg-installed from the official
DragonFly mirror. Only one of those matches the ports tree.

  dsynth build      : glib20's deps Already-Built, reached patch phase
  agent make_extract: rc=1, wrksrc="", never unpacked anything

It is not only perl. With PERL5_DEFAULT forced to 5.42 the extract got
one layer further and died on the same skew:

  gobject-introspection -> bison -> m4 -> texinfo -> help2man
  -> p5-Locale-gettext -> gettext-runtime>=0.26
  "An older version of gettext-runtime is already installed (0.23.1)"

extract-depends must pass before do-extract runs, so no config override
of any kind reaches this. The agent is asking a package set that tracks
DragonFly releases to satisfy a ports tree on 2026Q3.

PROBLEM 2 - NO PER-ENV OVERRIDE CHANNEL

The base is null-mounted read-only and shared across envs
(bases/p/<id>/root), so nothing can write into it per-env. Writable
overlays are declared in runtime.py:14 WRITABLE_DIRS and today cover
work, root, tmp, var/tmp, etc/dsynth, construction.

/etc/make.conf and /usr/local/etc are both read-only with no override
path. That is a real gap independent of problem 1 - make.conf is the
sanctioned place for exactly the kind of env-wide ports setting we
wanted, and it is the one file we cannot write.
design:
Undesigned on purpose. Recording the constraints and the shape of a
good answer so nobody reaches for a hack.

HARD CONSTRAINT: nullfs mounts a sub-tree, not a file (mount_null(8)).
So "just null-mount /etc/make.conf" is not available. The choices are
overlay a whole directory, or use the tool's own config-path variable.

PROPOSED PRINCIPLE for problem 2:

  Overlay a directory only when the env owns ALL of it. Otherwise use
  the tool's own config-path variable.

/etc/dsynth works precisely because dsynth's config is entirely
env-owned - there is no base content to shadow. /etc and
/usr/local/etc fail that test badly: overlaying them shadows passwd,
group, and pkg's own repo config, and any seeded copy drifts from the
base it was copied from. Do not extend WRITABLE_DIRS to either.

For make specifically, the variable exists and is verified working:

  make __MAKE_CONF=/work/make.conf ... -V PERL5_DEFAULT  ->  5.42

So the clean shape is a dev-env-managed config dir under an
already-writable root (e.g. /work/env-config/), with build_env_dict
exporting __MAKE_CONF at it, and the same treatment for other tools
that accept a config path. That gives a real override channel with no
new mounts and nothing shadowed. Worth doing on its own merits.

BUT IT DOES NOT FIX PROBLEM 1. Measured today: with __MAKE_CONF
honoured, extract still failed on extract-depends. Anyone picking this
up should not expect the config channel to unblock the patch flow.

OPTIONS FOR PROBLEM 1, none chosen:

  a. Drive extract through dsynth, so the agent and the build share one
     package universe. Most correct, least clear how it fits the tool
     loop - dsynth is a whole-build orchestrator, not an extract
     primitive.
  b. Give the chroot a package set built from the same tree (dsynth
     builds them already; the packages exist). Closest to "make the two
     universes one".
  c. Have the agent operate on the distfile directly rather than via
     the ports extract machinery, sidestepping extract-depends.
     Cheapest, and gives up make_patch's post-files/* baseline - which
     flow-patch.md says the hunk context depends on.

WHATEVER IS CHOSEN, a failed make_extract must abort the attempt rather
than let the agent improvise - that half is poly-n78.
notes:
REVIEWED 2026-08-28. Problem 1 and Problem 2 are not independent, and
option (b) is far cheaper than the bead assumed. Measured, not argued.

THE ENV ALREADY HAS THE PACKAGES. dsynth builds into
/work/dsynth/packages and writes a real pkg repository there - meta.conf,
packagesite.pkg, data.pkg, 156 packages including perl5-5.42.3, the
exact version the tree wants and the one the official mirror does not
ship. Every extract-depend the chain died on is present: bison, m4,
texinfo, help2man, gettext-runtime.

So "give the chroot a package set built from the same tree" needs no
building. The packages exist; nothing points pkg at them.

PROVEN CONSUMABLE. With a repo conf naming file:///work/dsynth/packages
and a writable PKG_DBDIR:

  dsynth repository update completed. 156 packages processed.
  perl5 -> perl5-5.42.3   bison -> bison-3.8.2_2,1   m4 -> m4-1.4.21,1
  texinfo -> 7.3_1,1      help2man -> 1.49.3_1       gettext-runtime -> 1.0_1

TWO THINGS NEEDED, AND BOTH ARE PROBLEM 2:

  1. a repo conf pkg can read  -> REPOS_DIR
  2. a writable package db     -> PKG_DBDIR
     (/var/db/pkg is in the read-only base; without this pkg refuses
      with "Insufficient privileges to update the repository catalogue",
      which reads like a permissions bug and is not one)

Both are config-path variables, not mounts. That is exactly the
principle already written here - "overlay a directory only when the env
owns all of it, otherwise use the tool's own config-path variable" -
and it now has a second consumer besides __MAKE_CONF.

SO THE SHAPE COLLAPSES to one piece of work: a dev-env-managed config
directory under an already-writable root, with build_env_dict exporting
the paths tools read. __MAKE_CONF, REPOS_DIR and PKG_DBDIR are the three
known consumers. Problem 1 then falls out of it rather than needing its
own design.

Options (a) drive extract through dsynth and (c) operate on the distfile
are both heavier and neither is needed. Recommend (b), delivered as
Problem 2.

NOT YET ESTABLISHED: whether pointing the chroot at the dsynth repo
should replace the official mirror or merely outrank it. Replacing
means a package the env has not built is simply unavailable; outranking
risks mixing two universes again, which is the bug. Leaning replace,
but it wants a deliberate decision.

CORRECTION 2026-08-28. The review above overstated option (b). "Proven
consumable" proved the catalogue is READABLE, not that packages are
INSTALLABLE. `dsynth repository update` fetches and parses; it installs
nothing. extract-depends needs packages installed, and that step was
never reached.

WHY IT CANNOT WORK AS WRITTEN. The base is shared and quarter-agnostic
by design: base.py:70 provisioned_base_id hashes the world archive plus
the tooling package lists (bootstrap_pkgs, tool_pkgs_required,
tool_pkgs_optional, python_pkgs). The ports tree and the target quarter
are not inputs. One base serves every env. runtime.py:78 mounts it
read-only and /usr/local is not in WRITABLE_DIRS, so no env can install
into it. REPOS_DIR + PKG_DBDIR make the dsynth repo visible; they do not
make it installable.

So Problem 1 does NOT fall out of Problem 2. The config channel is still
worth building on its own merits (__MAKE_CONF is real), but it is a
smaller thing than the review claimed.

THE DEEPER PROBLEM. dsynth builders always hold tree-matched versions
because dsynth built them. The dev-env holds whatever the official
mirror shipped when the base was provisioned. Incremental work on a
quarter needs the tree's versions in the dev-env, and there is no path
to put them there. On top of that /work/dsynth/packages holds only what
this env has already built - zero on a fresh env, and otherwise whatever
the last bulk run happened to cover.

SHAPES THAT SURVIVE:

1. Per-env writable /usr/local + /var/db/pkg, so the env installs its
own set. Breaks the overlay principle badly - /usr/local is where the
base's own dsynth/python/git live. Wants copy-on-write, which nullfs
does not give.
2. Do not make the dev-env chroot match the tree. Run extract where the
matched universe already exists (option a), and treat the dev-env as an
editing/orchestration host rather than a build chroot.

UNMEASURED AND CHEAP - TEST BEFORE DESIGNING EITHER. Does the patch flow
need extract-depends at all? make_extract only unpacks the distfile and
leaves WRKSRC pristine (worker.py:1885). extract-depends is a gate on
that target, not something the unpack consumes. If NO_DEPENDS=yes (or
DEPENDS_TARGET) lets the unpack through, Problem 1 stops mattering for
patching without touching the package universe. This is not option (c):
the ports extract machinery and the post-files/* baseline are kept, only
the dependency gate is skipped. Caveat: ports whose extract genuinely
needs a tool from a package still fail, correctly.

Blocked on a live env - x6's envs and provisioned bases are both empty.

DSYNTH SOURCE INVESTIGATION 2026-08-28. Read /usr/src/usr.bin/dsynth on
x6 (mount.c, build.c, config.c, dsynth.c, mktemplate.sh).

CONFIRMED: A DSYNTH BUILDER DOES NOT HAVE THE AGENT'S TOOLS, BY DESIGN.

mount.c DoWorkerMounts is the whole builder topology:
  NULLFS_RO from the host world: /bin /sbin /lib /libexec /usr/bin
    /usr/include /usr/lib /usr/libdata /usr/libexec /usr/sbin
    /usr/share /usr/games (+/usr/src if UseUsrSrc)
  TMPFS_RW_MED  -> /usr/local        <-- EMPTY, every builder
  TMPFS_RW_BIG  -> /construction
  NULLFS_RO     -> /xports (DPortsPath)
  NULLFS_RW     -> /packages /distfiles /options (+/ccache)
  DEVFS /dev, PROCFS_RO /proc, TMPFS /boot and /

mktemplate.sh creates only EMPTY /usr/local/{bin,sbin,lib,etc,etc/pkg}.
Two things ever populate /usr/local in a builder:
  1. pkg/pkg-static - dsynth untars the pkg package into the Template
     (build.c ~270) and mount.c cp -Rp's Template/. over the builder
     after mounting.
  2. the port's own dependencies, build.c ~1840:
     pkg install -q -U -y /packages/All/<pkgfile>

Measured on x6 where our required commands actually live:
  base       patch=/usr/bin/patch  make=/usr/bin/make        SURVIVE
  /usr/local bash curl git jq python3 genpatch dupe pkg      GONE

config.py wants tool_cmds_required = pkg indexinfo bash curl git patch
jq python3, plus genpatch/dupe from tool_pkgs_optional. Six of eight are
absent from a builder. Impact by primitive:
  make_extract / make_patch / install_patches  -> make+patch only, fine
  genpatch, dupe                               -> ABSENT (the core of
                                                  the patch flow)
  emit_diff, commit_port_changes,
  create_job_worktree, _git_diff_*             -> git, ABSENT

BUT DSYNTH LEAVES A DOOR OPEN: `dsynth debug <port>`.
  dsynth.c:358   debug -> ParsePackageList(..., debugstop=1)
  build.c:1516   PKGF_DEBUGSTOP -> WORKER_PROC_DEBUGSTOP
  build.c:2328   if ((WorkerProcFlags & WORKER_PROC_DEBUGSTOP) == 0)
                     DoWorkerUnmounts(work);
  build.c:2341   FREEZEWORKER holds the slot

The unmount skip is after the phase loop and does not test success, so a
FAILED build freezes too - exactly our case. The builder stays at
${BuildBase}/SL%02d (= /work/dsynth/build/SL00 in our config) with the
tree-matched /usr/local populated and WRKSRC under
${basedir}/construction/<origin>/.

DSYNTH ALSO SETTLES THE make.conf QUESTION.
  build.c:2164  writes ${basedir}/etc/make.conf fresh per builder from
                BuildEnv entries of type BENV_MAKECONF
  config.c:551  which are parsed from <configbase>/<profile>-make.conf
/etc in a builder is a COPY (mktemplate.sh cp -Rp $sysbase/etc/.), not a
mount. That is why dsynth can just write the file and the dev-env cannot.

NO_DEPENDS IS REAL AND PROVEN. bsd.port.mk ~4004:
  .for deptype in PKG EXTRACT PATCH FETCH BUILD LIB RUN TEST
  ${deptype:tl}-depends:
  .  if defined(${deptype}_DEPENDS) && !defined(NO_DEPENDS)
Dry-run on x6, devel/git-merge-changelog (real EXTRACT_DEPENDS):
  plain            -> do-depends.sh with dp_DEPENDS_TARGET="install"
                      (the recursive install that dies on the skew)
  NO_DEPENDS=yes   -> zero commands
Caveat: a port whose extract genuinely needs an unarchiver package will
now fail at do-extract instead. Base bsdtar covers gz/bz2/xz/zst.

RANKED SOLUTIONS:

1. NO_DEPENDS=yes in make_extract. One flag, no new machinery, unblocks
the patch flow without touching the package universe. Do this first.

2. Run the agent's tools FROM the dev-env against the frozen builder's
filesystem rather than inside it. The builder is just a path
(/work/dsynth/build/SL00/construction/<origin>/...) visible from the
dev-env, where git/genpatch/dupe already exist. No mounts, no dsynth
patch, no effect on normal builds. genpatch needs $WORKTREE repointed at
the builder's construction dir - a config change, not a redesign.
UNTESTED; validate before committing to it.

3. Toolchain injection into the builder, if 2 proves insufficient.
Nullfs a self-contained toolchain dir into the FROZEN builder after
dsynth releases it. Do NOT seed dsynth's Template: it applies to every
builder, changes what real builds can detect at configure time, and is
regenerated whenever /bin/ls mtime changes or pkg is rebuilt.

Note for whoever implements 2 or 3: runtime.py's 79-char
MAX_STATFS_MOUNT_TARGET_LEN guard is likely to bite, since builder paths
nest under the env's already-long writable root.

VALIDATION 2026-08-28: SOLUTION 2 WORKS, PROVEN END-TO-END ON x6.

(Correcting the previous note: "x6's envs and provisioned bases are both
empty" was wrong - a csh glob failure on an unquoted path, not an empty
directory. The 2026Q3-editors_vim env and its base were there all along.)

THE PREMISE, NOW A FILESYSTEM FACT. The builder Template's entire
/usr/local is 23 files, all of them pkg and libpkg. /usr/local/bin is an
empty directory. git, python3, genpatch, dupe, bash: all absent, before
and after a build.

genpatch AND dupe TURN OUT TO BE PURE BASE-TOOL SHELL SCRIPTS. Read them
on x6: between them they invoke only sh, diff, sed, cp, realpath, wc,
expr, cut, dirname, echo - every one in base. They ship in /usr/local/bin
via the genpatch package, but they have no /usr/local dependency at all.
That makes solution 3 far cheaper than estimated too: injecting them into
a builder is copying two shell scripts, not mounting a toolchain.

FROZEN BUILDER, MEASURED. `dsynth -y -S debug print/indexinfo` inside
the env:
  [000] SUCCESS print/indexinfo   00:00:02
  [000] FROZEN(DEBUG) print/indexinfo
22 mounts left live. WRKSRC at
/work/dsynth/build/SL00/construction/<origin>/<distname>/, reachable
from inside the dev-env at a plain path.

THE ACTUAL TEST, RUN FROM THE DEV-ENV AGAINST THE FROZEN BUILDER:
  dupe indexinfo.c                       -> indexinfo.c.orig
  WORKTREE=$CONS genpatch indexinfo.c    -> generated patch-indexinfo.c
Output is canonical dports format - correct relative paths, stripped
date, function context in the @@ line. The agent's patch primitives run
from the dev-env against a builder that contains none of them.

BLOCKER FOR IMPLEMENTATION - HOST-SIDE PATHS DO NOT REACH THE BUILDER.
dsynth mounts onto the env's MOUNTED VIEW (<env>/root/work/dsynth/build/
SL00/...), not its backing store (<env>/writable/work/...). Confirmed
both ways: a host-side find under writable/ says "No such file or
directory" while the same path inside the chroot shows the full tree.

worker.py:_resolve_chroot_path maps /work/... to paths.writable/work/...
So every host-side primitive - get_file, put_file, list_dir - would see
an EMPTY builder. put_file is the dangerous one: it would write into the
backing store underneath the tmpfs, where nothing can read it, and report
success. Silent, not a visible failure.

Fix shape: builder paths must resolve through env_dir/root/work/... (the
view), or those primitives must exec into the chroot instead of going
host-side. Decide this before writing any of solution 2.

79-CHAR TRUNCATION IS REAL. `mount` output showed SL00/boo, SL00/pro,
SL00/sbi, and libexec truncated to lib. Display artifact at these
lengths, but it is exactly what runtime.py's MAX_STATFS_MOUNT_TARGET_LEN
guards, and any NEW mount added under a builder (solution 3) will be
past the limit.

Env left as found: dsynth cleanup run, 0 mounts remaining, repo back at
156 packages with indexinfo rebuilt.
BLOCKED IN PRACTICE BY poly-cx6, established on hardware 2026-08-29.

NO_DEPENDS (f3f937c) is shipped and correct, but has still never run
inside an agent attempt. A full loop on glib20 reached make_extract on
turn 4 and stopped on the perl IGNORE before dependency resolution was
attempted. The flag guards a code path the framework refuses to enter.

So the validation this bead wants needs poly-cx6 first. Everything else
on the path is now proven working on hardware: dsynth hooks -> bundle ->
job -> triage -> patch enqueue -> bundle branch -> tool loop.

title: Nothing warns when the evidence root is on a volatile filesystem
description:
x6 was running with polytropos.conf:46 setting

  : ${polytropos_logs_root:="/tmp/polyverify/logs"}

and /tmp is tmpfs. So state.db, the blobstore and the job queue all
lived on a filesystem that empties on reboot. It had emptied: the
tracker was down and 78 blobs of build evidence were gone.

Nothing anywhere said so. The visible symptom was the tracker failing
with "attempt to write a readonly database" (poly-cka), which points at
permissions and says nothing about the data having evaporated. Working
back from that error to "the evidence root is on tmpfs" took a while
and was mostly luck.

How it got there: a verification run pointed the config at a scratch
root and it was never pointed back. The .bak file beside it has the
same value, so even the backup was taken after the change. Both the
tracker and the runner honour the setting silently.
design:
Two cheap guards; the first is the one that matters.

1. WARN AT STARTUP when the resolved evidence root sits on a volatile
filesystem. Both services already resolve it; a statfs check for tmpfs
/ mfs and a loud log line ("evidence root /tmp/... is on tmpfs and will
not survive a reboot") turns a confusing permissions error into a
statement of the actual problem. Warn, do not refuse — a scratch root
on tmpfs is legitimate for exactly the verification runs that created
this, and refusing would break them.

2. Have deploy install note the configured root when it differs from
the default, so an operator reading the install output sees where the
data is actually going.

Not in scope: choosing the root, or preventing the verification flow
from writing to /tmp. The defect is silence, not the value.

Related: poly-cka is the crash this presents as. Fixing cka's ownership
race would have made the tracker start cleanly on tmpfs and lose every
build on the next reboot with no error at all — quieter, and worse. The
two want fixing together.

title: Tool results accumulate untruncated, so prompt cost grows quadratically and the budget dies before the fix
description:
tool_loop.py:247 appends every tool result whole:

    messages.append({"role": "tool", "tool_call_id": call.id,
                     "name": call.name, "content": json.dumps(result)})

Nothing truncates, summarizes or evicts. The list is resent in full on
every turn, so N turns cost O(N^2) in prompt tokens. Individual read
tools have caps (limit_lines, 32KB base64) but the transcript has none,
and a build's stdout_tail or a grep across freebsd-ports/Mk lands whole
and stays forever.

MEASURED, x6 2026-07-31, both from analysis/patch_audit.json:

  graphics/jpeg-turbo  SUCCESS  1 attempt
    prompt 297,365  completion 3,276     91:1
  devel/glib20         FAILED   4 attempts, budget-exhausted
    prompt 4,510,102 completion 35,708  126:1
    per attempt: 1,386,097 / 1,505,820 / 1,314,543 / 339,350

Triage on the same failure cost 22,814 prompt / 1,348 completion. So
the blowup is specific to the patch flow's tool loop, not the model or
the payload.

For scale: jpeg-turbo's answer was one line —
"mk remove CFLAGS -ffp-model=strict" — and cost 297K prompt tokens.

CONSEQUENCE, and why this is not merely expensive. Budget exhaustion is
what strands the patch flow mid-sequence. glib20 died with the fix's
materialize line already deleted and no replacement written (poly-28j),
and wrote analysis/patch.md as 2 bytes. Cheaper turns are not a cost
optimization here; they are what lets an attempt reach a safe state.
design:
Undesigned. Options, cheapest first — measure before picking:

- Cap each tool result before it enters history (head/tail with an
  explicit "[N bytes elided]" marker). The model can re-read with a
  narrower range if it needs more. Biggest win for the least risk.
- Evict or collapse older tool results once superseded: a second
  get_file on the same path makes the first one dead weight.
- Cap total transcript bytes and drop oldest-first, keeping the system
  prompt, the playbooks and the last K turns.

Worth measuring first: which tools actually produce the bulk. The audit
records per-attempt totals but not per-tool, so add that to the
tool_call event before optimizing blind — the fix should follow the
measurement, not the guess.

Also check whether the same unbounded growth affects the triage flow.
Triage measured cheap (22K), but that may be because it makes few tool
calls rather than because it is bounded.
notes:
MEASURED AGAIN 2026-08-28, devel/glib20, after poly-2xd landed.

  prompt 2,093,676  completion 66,908  total 2,160,584
  attempt 1: 1,817,137   attempt 2: 343,447   budget-exhausted

Down from 4.5M but still fatal, and the 2026-07-31 run had 4 attempts
against this one's 2 - so per-attempt cost went UP.

NEW: the volume is not mostly transcript decay. The 49-call tool trace
is 15 list_dir calls plus repeated grep/get_file between call 8 and
call 36 - the agent hunting for a file it could not locate. Untruncated
accumulation is what makes that hunting quadratic, but the hunting is
what generates the calls.

So two levers, and capping results only addresses the second:
  1. Stop the agent needing 15 list_dir calls to find WRKSRC. That is
     a navigation problem (see poly-n78 - it never ran make_extract's
     result through dupe/genpatch, which is what knows the path).
  2. Cap what each result contributes to history.

The per-tool token attribution this bead already asks for would have
shown this immediately. Worth doing before either lever.
Cause of the 15 list_dir calls: make_extract failed (poly-cx6), so the
agent had no wrksrc and spent 30 calls hunting for an extracted tree
that was never unpacked. The hunting is not a navigation weakness in
general - it is what this agent does when step 1 silently fails.

Does not retire this bead. Untruncated accumulation is what turns 30
wasted calls into 1.8M prompt tokens, and any failure mode that
produces a long tool loop will hit it. But it does mean the 2026-08-28
and 2026-07-31 numbers are both measurements of a BROKEN env, not of
the flow working normally. Re-measure on a healthy env before sizing
the fix.
PAYLOAD COMPOSITION, from the first session dump (x6 2026-08-28,
bundle devel_glib20@bootstrap-20260828-120749Z, triage attempt 1).
The triage user message is 67,127 chars:

  Agent Playbooks          7.4KB   11%
  Build Errors             6.9KB   10%
  Makefile                 4.5KB    7%
  pkg-plist               32.9KB   49%   <--
  distinfo + patches       ~6KB     9%

Half the triage prompt is a package file list. It is inert for every
classification except plist-error, and it is the single biggest input
on the largest ports - the same pkg-plist that dominates the blobstore
(473KB stored; poly-ir3).

Gating pkg-plist on classification (or dropping it from triage, which
cannot know the classification yet) roughly halves the triage payload
for no loss. Cheapest concrete win found so far and independent of the
transcript-accumulation work.

ALSO: the runner logs per-turn accounting the audit does not surface -

  [llm_turn] A1.T6 in=42561 (cached=42240) out=1726 billable=2047

so prompt caching is active and billable is far below raw. Check
whether patch_audit.json reports raw or billable before sizing
anything: the 4.5M and 2.16M figures may overstate real cost by an
order of magnitude. This is the per-tool/per-turn attribution this bead
already asked for, and it partly exists in the log already.
THIS BEAD'S CORE CLAIM IS WRONG. Correcting it rather than quietly
re-scoping, because two other beads cite it.

The title says prompt cost grows quadratically and the budget dies. The
growth is real; it is not what kills the run, and the numbers I used
were the wrong metric by ~18x.

  llm.py:30   billable_tokens = (prompt - cached) + completion
  tool_loop.py:107  the budget gates on billable_tokens
  attempt_loop.py:239  the AUDIT records attempt_usage.total_tokens

So patch_audit.json reports raw, cache-inclusive totals - it counts the
re-sent cached prefix on every turn - while the budget counts only new
work. From the live run:

  attempt_loop: budget exhausted after attempt 2 (120064 >= 120000 billable)
  patch_audit.json tokens_total: 2,160,584

Cap is 120K billable. The audit number is 18x that. Every conclusion I
drew from "4.5M prompt tokens" was measuring re-sent cache.

Prompt caching already solves the re-billing problem and was designed
to - llm.py:31 says so explicitly: "the per-attempt budget gates on
this so re-sending a cached prefix every turn doesn't exhaust the
budget for no real work". Per-turn from the log:

  A1.T10 in=51903 (cached=51712) out=5867 billable=6058

99.6% cache hit. Truncating history would save almost nothing billable.

WHAT ACTUALLY SPENDS THE 120K, and the rewritten scope of this bead:
  - each large tool result costs its full size ONCE, as uncached prefix
    delta. The greps in this run returned 7745, 5303, 5239 and 3432
    matches. That is where a capped-result fix still pays - but the
    mechanism is "expensive once", not "quadratic".
  - completions: out=5867 on a single turn, and they are never cached.
  - there is also a smaller per-attempt sub-cap:
    "tool_loop: token budget exhausted after turn 8 (15639 >= 11535)"

SEPARATE DEFECT worth splitting out: the audit reports a number that is
not the number the budget uses, with no cache column. It is the figure
an operator reads to decide whether a run was expensive, and it is
misleading by an order of magnitude. It misled me for a full session.
SHAPE CONFIRMED ON HARDWARE 2026-08-29, and the arithmetic is now
measured rather than inferred. One 30-turn attempt on devel/glib20,
123,572 billable across two attempts:

  model output                60,341   49%
  cold start (turn 1)         30,216   25%
  tool results (turns 2+)     33,015   26%

So prompt caching IS working -- by the last turn 113,664 of 113,852
input tokens were cached, and re-sending context is nearly free. The
budget goes on OUTPUT first, cold start second, tool results third.

That reorders this bead's premise. Untruncated tool results are real,
but they are a quarter of the spend, not the dominant term. The two
biggest single turns were output, not input: A1.T8 out=10,919 and
A1.T24 out=8,800 -- together 33% of attempt 1's entire output.

Still worth fixing here: greps that return enormous match sets are
reported ok rather than as the truncation events they are --

  grep 'FAILED:|error:|Error:|undefined reference' matches=8192  ok
  grep 'ninja: build stopped|...'                  matches=2179  ok

A match set that size is not an answer the model can use; it is a
signal the query was too broad. Returning it as ok teaches nothing.

See also poly-5e1 (an attempt starting on a budget it cannot finish in),
which is where the cold-start term does the most damage.

title: The build page's logfile links are dead, and only failures can be fixed by pointing at the tracker
description:
Two separate things, both visible on the build page (/builds/{run_id},
which renders progress.html client-side from /api/progress/).

WHY ONLY THE FAILED PORTS SHOW A LINK

They are not the only ones meant to. progress.js infoHTML() emits a
"logfile" link for result 'built' as well as 'failed'; 'skipped' and
'ignored' get prose and no link, correctly — those ports never ran, so
there is no log to point at.

What made it look failures-only is the run itself. summary.json for
build 1 on x6:

    built: 0, failed: 3, skipped: 25, queued: 188

Everything else was already packaged from the earlier build, so nothing
had result 'built'. On a from-scratch run every successful port shows a
"logfile" link too — and every one of those is broken as well.

WHY THE LINK IS BROKEN

    function logfile(origin) {
        var p = origin.split('/');
        return '../' + p[0] + '___' + (p[1] || '') + '.log';
    }

A relative path inherited verbatim from dsynth's own static HTML report,
where the report file sits in a directory beside the .log files. The
tracker serves the page at /builds/1, so '../graphics___jpeg-turbo.log'
resolves to /graphics___jpeg-turbo.log. Verified on x6: 404. The tracker
has never served that path; this has been dead since the progress UI was
adopted.

WHAT CHANGED, AND THE ASYMMETRY IT LEAVES

Since poly-g19 / poly-b2r the compressed full log is a blob in the
tracker, not a path on the builder. For a FAILED port the link is now
fixable — verified on x6, same port, same run:

    /api/bundles/graphics_jpeg-turbo-20260827-193938Z/artifacts/logs/full.log.gz  ->  200

For a BUILT port it is not. Success uploads nothing at all —
hook_pkg_success is 12 lines and never calls artifact_store — so there
is no bundle, no blob, and nothing for a link to resolve to. That is the
storage model working as intended (only failures produce evidence), not
an oversight.

So the fix is not one URL rewrite:

- failed  -> point at the bundle's logs/full.log.gz. Needs the progress
  payload to carry the bundle_id, which it does not today.
- built   -> either drop the link, or start uploading success logs,
  which is a storage-policy decision (188 logs per run instead of 3)
  and should not be made incidentally.
- skipped/ignored -> unchanged, no link.

Dropping the link for 'built' and wiring the failed one through the
bundle is the cheap correct move; uploading success logs is a separate
question worth asking on its own terms.
notes:
FIXED AND VERIFIED ON x6 2026-08-28.

Decision: failures only. Successes lose the link rather than gain a
working one — hook_pkg_success uploads nothing, so there is no log in the
tracker to point at. Uploading success logs stays an open question, not
something settled sideways to fix a 404.

CORRECTION to the description above. It said the dead link resolved to
/graphics___jpeg-turbo.log. Wrong: progress.html sets
<base href="{{ progress_base }}">, so '../x.log' resolved against
/api/progress/build/1/ and gave /api/progress/build/x.log. Confirmed 404
either way, and 404 on /api/progress/x.log for the /target/ variant too.
It changes the fix: the new link is root-relative precisely so <base>
cannot rewrite it.

Also fixed in the same cell: the failed branch rendered
'Failed ' + info.split(':')[0] + ' phase', but info is
build_results.version, so real rows read "Failed 3.1.4.1 phase". Both
failed and built now show the version.

The history payload carries bundle_id, resolved with a correlated
subquery through runs.build_run_id -> bundles.run_id + origin, newest
bundle first so a retried port links to its latest evidence.

Verified against the live tracker on the clean-slate run:

  rows: 28
  failed  graphics/jpeg-turbo  bundle_id=graphics_jpeg-turbo-20260827-193938Z
  failed  devel/glib20         bundle_id=devel_glib20@bootstrap-20260827-193939Z
  failed  lang/rust            bundle_id=lang_rust-20260827-193944Z

  /api/bundles/<id>/artifacts/logs/full.log.gz -> 200 1728B
                                               -> 200 1448B
                                               -> 200 1181B

  served progress.js: 1 occurrence of /api/bundles/, 0 of the old form

The glib20 id carries an '@', so both the raw and the percent-encoded
form were checked — the JS uses encodeURIComponent and the browser will
send %40. Both 200.

8 unit tests: bundle_id present for a failure with evidence, absent for a
success, absent for a failure whose upload never landed, entry shape
otherwise unchanged, the constructed URL serving the real bytes, and
guards against the relative form coming back.
FOLLOW-UP 2026-08-28: the link resolved, but it downloaded a .gz.

Pointing at /api/bundles/.../artifacts/logs/full.log.gz was right about
the bytes and wrong about the destination. The stored log is gzip, so
that endpoint correctly answers application/gzip and the browser saves a
file nobody opens.

The tracker already had an artifact viewer with log highlighting; it just
refused gzip. artifact_media_type returns ("application/gzip", False) for
kind=gzip, and it has to — the raw endpoint streams the real compressed
bytes and anything scripting against them depends on that. So the
unpacking went into artifact_view_data instead, deciding by the name
INSIDE the .gz: logs/full.log.gz renders as the highlighted log it is, a
gzipped binary still gets a download card. Bounded at 4MB decompressed,
since gzip expands ~10-20x on log text.

The build row now links to the viewer, not the raw endpoint.

Bonus: the bundle reader's artifact fragment shares the same renderer, so
full logs stopped being a download there too — that path had a test
pinning the download card, which was the old behaviour being asserted as
correct.

VERIFIED ON x6, live tracker, after redeploy:

  viewer   http=200  text/html  12576B
           "shown decompressed" present, "raw download" absent
           rendered: "===>  License BSD3CLAUSE IJG ZLIB accepted by the user"
                     "===>   jpeg-turbo-3.1.4.1 depends on file: ..."
  raw      http=200  application/gzip  1728B, gzip -t passes
  served progress.js -> '/agentic/bundles/', 0 hits for the raw path
  all three failures render decompressed

Test fixture note: the seeded full.log.gz was b"\x1f\x8bcompressed",
not a valid gzip, so it could only ever have exercised the error path.
It is a real gzip now, and a genuinely binary artifact was added to keep
covering the download fallback. Plus a corrupt-gzip case — a truncated
upload reports rather than 500ing the page.

title: A wiped evidence tree lets the runner create a state.db the tracker cannot write
description:
Hit on x6 2026-08-27 doing a clean-slate redeploy: wipe the evidence
tree, start the stack, and the tracker refuses to start.

  sqlite3.OperationalError: attempt to write a readonly database
    dportsv3/tracker/server.py:98  _startup -> init_db

Cause is a race over who creates state.db. The runner runs as root and
the tracker as polytropos. Whichever starts first creates the file, and
when the runner wins it lands root-owned:

  -rw-r--r--  1 root  polytropos  state.db
  -rw-r--r--  1 root  polytropos  state.db-shm
  -rw-r--r--  1 root  polytropos  state.db-wal

Group is right — BSD takes it from the parent directory — but the mode
is 644, so the tracker cannot write it. polytropos_runner sets umask 002
for exactly this reason and it did not help: SQLite creates the database
0644 regardless of umask.

Only bites on a fresh or wiped evidence tree, which is why it has not
shown up before. It is silent in the wrong direction too: the runner
comes up fine and starts claiming work, so the stack looks half-alive
with no tracker.

Workaround used: stop the runner, chown -R polytropos:polytropos plus
chmod -R g+w on the logs root, start the tracker first.

Fix options: have deploy create state.db owned by the service account
before either service starts; or have the runner chmod g+w after
init_db; or run both as the same account, which is a bigger question
since the runner needs root for dev-envs.

Related to poly-af7 only in that both are upgrade/first-boot ordering
problems, not the same bug.
notes:
REPRODUCED 2026-08-28 on x6, and the "only on a fresh or wiped tree"
qualifier in the description is too narrow.

No clean-slate redeploy was involved. The host rebooted, and the
deployed polytropos.conf had polytropos_logs_root pointing into /tmp,
which is tmpfs. So the reboot wiped the evidence tree, the runner (root)
recreated state.db as root:wheel 0644 at 11:50, and the tracker refused
to start with the same traceback:

  sqlite3.OperationalError: attempt to write a readonly database
  dportsv3/tracker/server.py:98  _startup -> init_db

The half-alive shape the description predicts is exactly what was
found: runner up and claiming, no tracker, nothing on :8080.

So the trigger is not "an operator wipes the tree" but "the tree is
absent at boot for any reason", which includes every reboot of a
deployment whose evidence root is volatile. That is a routine event,
not a rare one. See poly-vqp for the volatile-root half.

Same workaround as before: stop the runner, restore a writable tree,
start the tracker first. Ordering-only is not a fix — it just loses the
race less often.
Correction: the volatile-root half is poly-cl3, not the ID written in the note above.

title: blob_objects has no refcount: nothing can safely delete an artifact
description:
blob_objects is (sha256, size, created_at). There is no refcount and no
maintained reverse index, so nothing in the system can answer "is this
blob still referenced?" without a full scan of artifact_refs.

Consequence: no artifact can be safely deleted. Dropping a bundle cannot
know whether its blobs are shared with other bundles, and deduplication
makes that worse rather than better — the blob referenced by the most
bundles is exactly the one that must not be dropped. So today the only
safe retention policy is "keep everything forever", by omission rather
than by decision.

Currently harmless: 49 blobs, 655.6 KB, zero dedup, measured on x6
2026-08-27 across three failures from unrelated ports. It stops being
harmless well before disk does — the constraint is that the system has
no delete operation at all, not that it runs out of space.

Independent of where artifacts live. Centralizing (the decision taken in
poly-g19) does not create this and distributing would not fix it; an
object-store backend would offer age-based lifecycle rules that still
cannot answer the reachability question.
design:
Undesigned. This bead is to decide the policy first, then the mechanism.

POLICY, which has to come first:
- Does anything expire at all? Bundles for resolved issues, bundles from
  targets no longer built, superseded agent iterations?
- Is evidence for a closed issue still wanted, and for how long?
- Are agent session dumps (the largest blobs) treated differently from
  port evidence?

MECHANISM, once the policy exists:
- Refcount column on blob_objects, maintained in the same transaction
  as every artifact_refs insert/update/delete. Cheap reads, but every
  writer must be correct forever and a missed decrement leaks silently.
- Mark-and-sweep over artifact_refs. No writer discipline required and
  self-correcting, but a full scan; fine at this size.
- Neither, until the policy question is answered.

Sweep-based is probably right at this scale, and it stays correct even
if a writer is wrong. Worth confirming against blob count after a real
full run rather than against the current 49.
notes:
2026-08-28, x6: the "zero dedup" figure in the description is stale.
104 refs over 78 blobs, 1,354,418 logical vs 830,784 physical — 39%
saved, 1.63x. Measurement recorded in poly-ir3.

This sharpens the bead rather than softening it: a shared blob is now
the common case, not a hypothetical, and the most-referenced object is
the one a bundle-scoped delete would wrongly drop. Dedup is all
port-tree snapshots (one pkg-plist stored twice is ~90% of the saving);
logs never dedup.
MEASUREMENT REFRESH, 2026-09-02 (2026Q3 builder)

The figures in the description are from 2026-08-27 and are now off by more than
an order of magnitude:

                     2026-08-27      2026-09-02
  blob_objects       49              1,816
  bytes              655.6 KB        22.5 MiB
  dedup              zero            41%

Six days, ~37x the objects and ~35x the bytes. Disk is still nothing --
53.5 MiB on a filesystem at 29% of 101 GB -- so the description's conclusion
holds unchanged: the constraint is that there is no delete operation at all,
not that space runs out.

THE DEDUP PREDICTION HAS COME TRUE

The description argues that deduplication makes the deletion problem worse
rather than better, because the blob referenced by the most bundles is exactly
the one that must not be dropped. That was written when dedup was zero and the
concern was theoretical. It is not any more: 2,968 artifact_refs resolve to
1,757 distinct blobs, so 1,211 references (41%) are shared. Any delete path
built from here has to answer the sharing question first.

Concentration is worth knowing for the same reason: port/pkg-plist is 10.7 MiB
across 148 refs -- 47% of all artifact bytes from 5% of the refs. The bytes a
retention policy would want back are the ones most likely to be shared.

INSTANCE COUNT FOR THIS BEAD'S EXACT CASE

The same scan found 59 blob_objects rows referenced by no artifact_refs. Those
are the rows this bead is about, and nothing can currently prove they are safe
to remove.

Separately, 3,120 files exist in the store with no blob_objects row at all --
the opposite direction, filed as poly-87g. Between the two, reachability is
unanswerable both ways, and a fix for either alone still leaves the store
unable to say what it holds.

title: Builder-side ingest relay: hooks post to loopback, one credential per host
description:
Remote builders reach the tracker; the tracker never reaches them, and
there is no VPN. So the tracker's machine surface is internet-facing and
a per-host runner token is the entire boundary.

If the dsynth hooks talked to the tracker directly, every env's hooks
conf would have to carry the tracker URL and a credential. That puts a
token in a file inside the build sandbox — the one place on the host
where arbitrary port build scripts run. Worst possible location for it.

The current arrangement already avoids this by accident. hook_common.sh
posts to ARTIFACT_STORE_URL, which inside a chroot is 127.0.0.1 because
the chroot shares the host's network namespace. It works and costs
nothing. Keep it.

WHAT THE RELAY CENTRALIZES PER HOST

- Auth. One credential, held by one process, never inside a sandbox.
  N dev-envs on a host share it instead of each carrying a copy.
- The tracker URL. One place per host instead of every env's conf. A
  dev-env's hooks conf becomes independent of deployment topology:
  `dev-env hooks-install` writes the same loopback URL whether the host
  is local or remote, so going remote changes nothing inside any env.
- TLS, and later any transport concern.
- Durability. artifact_store_put currently catches every exception and
  returns False, and nothing spools or retries, so a tracker restart or
  a network blip silently loses evidence with no record it existed.
  Under a pull model the bytes stayed on the producer until asked; push
  trades that away and the relay is where it has to be bought back.
  Content-addressing makes retry free: put_blob already skips the write
  when the object exists, so re-sending is idempotent.
design:
A loopback listener on each builder that accepts the same /v1/ calls the
hooks already make and forwards them to the tracker. It stores nothing.

This is not a new service. poly-g19 folds ArtifactStore into the tracker
and would otherwise delete ArtifactStoreServer and the Handler class
outright; instead they are reduced to a forwarder. The
artifact-store-client is unchanged and still points at 127.0.0.1.

- Forward, do not interpret. The relay should not need to understand
  payloads; adding an endpoint to the tracker must not require touching
  it.
- Spool on failure, to disk, surviving a restart, retrying until the
  tracker acks. Bounded, and loud when the bound is hit — a full spool
  must not fail silently the way the current swallow-and-return-False
  does.
- Hold one token for the host (poly-fij.4) under this host's runner
  identity (poly-fij.3).

OPEN: whether the relay is a thread inside the runner process or its own
service. The runner already runs continuously on the builder, but a
relay that dies with a crashing runner loses the spool guarantee for
builds still in flight.
notes:
2026-08-28: internet exposure deferred by the operator, so this bead's
two rationales have come apart and should be scheduled separately.

EXPOSURE-DRIVEN (deferred with poly-fij.4): keeping the credential out
of the build sandbox, TLS, one tracker URL per host. All of it presumes
a credential and a remote tracker; neither exists yet.

LIVE TODAY, INDEPENDENT OF EXPOSURE: durability. artifact_store_put
catches every exception and returns False, and nothing spools or
retries, so a tracker restart or a blip silently loses evidence with no
record it existed. That is a real defect on a single LAN host right now
— it is not waiting on auth, identity, or a relay process.

Splitting the durability half out as its own bead would let it land now.
Content-addressing already makes retry free: put_blob skips the write
when the object exists, so re-sending is idempotent.

title: The patch agent proposed deleting a failing patch instead of repairing it
description:
First real patch attempt on a reproducible failure, and the fix it
proposed would have removed the thing that was broken rather than
repairing it.

devel/glib20@bootstrap failed because the DragonFly overlay patch
dragonfly/patch-gio_meson.build no longer applies to glib 2.86.4 —
upstream moved the libelf detection block, so its single hunk hit
drifted context.

Triage diagnosed this correctly and prescribed the fix:

  "Re-cut dragonfly/patch-gio_meson.build against the glib 2.86.4
   source while keeping the static patch form. [...] Use make_extract
   to get the correct WRKSRC, edit the file, then genpatch to refresh
   the patch. Do not convert this to an overlay.dops text
   substitution: meson.build is a hand-written, not generated, file,
   and a REINPLACE-style op would silently no-op on the next upstream
   drift instead of failing loudly."

The patch agent's changes.diff (790 bytes) instead edits overlay.dops:

  +mk add DEFAULT_VERSIONS "perl5=5.42"
  -file materialize dragonfly/patch-gio_meson.build -> dragonfly/...

Two problems in three lines.

1. DELETING THE MATERIALIZE LINE DROPS THE FIX. The patch stops being
   copied into the composed port, so glib builds with FreeBSD's
   cc.find_library('elf', ...) instead of DragonFly's
   declare_dependency(link_args: '/lib/libelf.so.2'). The build goes
   green and the platform-specific fix is silently gone. That is the
   worst possible shape for this system: a change that looks like a
   pass and is a regression.

2. THE perl5 PIN IS UNRELATED. Nothing in the failure touches
   DEFAULT_VERSIONS or perl. It came from a thread the agent chased
   through freebsd-ports/Mk during attempt 1.

It also did the exact thing triage told it not to do — reach for
overlay.dops. So triage's prescription is not binding the patch agent
in any way; it is apparently context, not instruction.

Nothing was applied: rebuild_ok=false, status=budget-exhausted, and
rebuild_proof.json is synthetic:true — no rebuild ever ran. The overlay
was reset afterwards. The proposal was stopped by the budget running
out, NOT by anything recognising it as destructive.

Cost: 127,758 billable tokens across 2 attempts (2,339,598 total
including cached prompt reads).
design:
Two separable pieces.

GUARD (the safety half). Removing a 'file materialize' line for a patch that exists, or otherwise dropping a platform fix, should not be a silent option. The verify/apply path already knows the overlay's before and after; a diff that deletes a materialize entry without adding a replacement is a distinct, recognisable shape. Either refuse it, or require it to be justified as an explicit removal intent rather than arriving as an incidental line in a fix diff. Note the danger only appears when the rebuild PASSES — here the budget hid it.

BINDING (the quality half). Triage produced a correct, specific, actionable fix and the patch agent ignored it, including its explicit warning against the route it took. Worth establishing whether triage.md's Suggested Fix reaches the patch prompt at all, and if it does, why it carries no weight. A prescription that is cheaper and more accurate than the patch agent's own exploration is being discarded.

Related but distinct from poly-x9c, which is the same budget exhaustion for a different reason — there the report was unreproducible, here it is reproducible with a known fix and the agent still wandered (attempt 1 alone spent 1.64M total tokens on a DEFAULT_VERSIONS thread).
acceptance_criteria: 1. A diff that drops a materialize entry for an existing patch is refused or flagged, not applied silently. 2. Triage's prescribed fix demonstrably shapes the patch attempt. 3. A rebuild that passes because a platform fix was removed is not reported as success.
notes:
2026-08-28 root cause: the agent followed a playbook. Two of the three
playbooks attached to a patch-error payload say to remove the
materialize line first, and one of them says it for a "drifted" patch
specifically. See poly-2xd. The budget exhaustion that stranded it
mid-sequence is poly-7eh.

So this is reachable again by any agent reading the same corpus. Fixing
judgment without fixing the corpus will not hold.
CORRECTION 2026-08-28. This bead says of the perl5 pin:

  "THE perl5 PIN IS UNRELATED. Nothing in the failure touches
   DEFAULT_VERSIONS or perl. It came from a thread the agent chased
   through freebsd-ports/Mk during attempt 1."

That is wrong, and the tool trace from the 2026-08-28 rerun shows why.
make_extract fails with "Invalid perl5 version 5.36" before the agent
does anything else, and the greps through freebsd-ports/Mk are it
diagnosing that failure. `mk add DEFAULT_VERSIONS "perl5=5.42"` was a
correct fix for a real blocker sitting in front of its own tooling -
not a rabbit hole. See poly-cx6.

What remains true, and is still the bug this bead is about: it also
deleted the file materialize line, and shipped the perl5 pin as part of
a patch proposal for an unrelated failure rather than reporting the
environment as broken. Diagnosing correctly and then silently folding
the fix into someone else's changeset is its own defect.

title: A packaged install has no 'dportsv3 dev-env', but the docs tell operators to use it
description:
docs/OPERATOR_SETUP.md instructs 'bin/dportsv3 dev-env hooks-install myenv' and 'bin/dportsv3 dev-env shell'. That works from a checkout, because the repo's bin/dportsv3 shell wrapper routes dev-env by exec'ing dports-dev-env (worker.py documents the same three-way resolution).

The installed /usr/local/bin/dportsv3 is a venv console script for dportsv3.cli:main, which has no such subcommand:

  dportsv3: error: argument COMMAND: invalid choice: 'dev-env'
  (choose from 'compose', 'compose-report', 'dsl', 'migrate', 'tracker',
   'artifact-store', 'agent-queue-runner', 'deploy', 'verify-fix',
   'env-health')

So on a deployed host every dev-env instruction in the operator docs fails, and the operator has to discover that the command is actually dports-dev-env. Confusingly the dev-env CLI still prints its usage as 'dportsv3 dev-env create', which reinforces the wrong invocation.
design:
Either route dev-env from dportsv3.cli the way the checkout wrapper does — exec the dports-dev-env entry point, which deploy already links into the prefix — or change the docs and the dev-env CLI's own prog name to say dports-dev-env consistently.

Routing is preferable: one command name for operators, and it matches what the docs, the wrapper and the CLI's usage string all already claim.
acceptance_criteria: 1. The invocation in OPERATOR_SETUP.md works on a packaged install. 2. The usage string and the working command agree.
notes: Same class, another instance: env_health_status.operator_action tells the operator to 'run `dportsv3 dev-env health <env>`'. There is no such command — dev-env has no health action, and the probe is `dportsv3 env-health <env>`. So the guidance printed when an env is broken names a command that does not exist, in a tool where the same string is stored in the DB and shown in the UI.

title: A stale active build_runs row silently disables tracking for every later build
description:
hook_run_start calls 'dportsv3 tracker start-build'. If a previous run left a build_runs row with finished_at NULL, the tracker returns 409 and the hook responds by setting TRACKING_DISABLED=1 for the whole run.

Observed on x6 2026-08-27: a run started 2026-08-26T23:22:35 never got its hook_run_end, so the row stayed active. Every subsequent in-env build gets:

  tracking disabled for profile=2026Q3-editors_vim: start-build failed:
  Tracker API error (409) for POST /api/builds: Active build already
  exists for @2026Q3 test: run 2

Consequence: no build_runs ordinal is minted, so occurrences arrive with build_run_id NULL and the C3 regression derivation silently falls back to wall-clock timestamps — the exact comparison C3 exists to avoid. Nothing surfaces in the UI; the only trace is a line in the hook log.

runner.py's dsynth_active already documents the same class of staleness: 'build_runs.finished_at can be stale (operator ^C'd dsynth, hook_run_end never ran, row left at NULL forever)' — and deliberately refuses to use it as a gate for that reason. start-build has no such defence.
design:
Options, cheapest first.

1. Let start-build adopt or supersede a stale active run past some age, rather than 409ing. An active run older than any plausible build is not active.
2. Have hook_run_start retry once after asking the tracker to close a stale run, so an interrupted build self-heals on the next attempt.
3. Surface it: an active run with no heartbeat should show as stale in the UI instead of being invisible until it blocks something.

Whatever the mechanism, the failure mode to remove is that tracking silently degrades to timestamps. If tracking cannot start, that should be visible where someone looks, not only in the hook log.
acceptance_criteria: 1. An interrupted build does not disable tracking for every subsequent build. 2. When tracking does get disabled, it is visible outside the hook log. 3. C3's ordinal comparison is not silently downgraded to wall clocks.
notes:
RECURRED 2026-08-31, and the cost is larger than the original note suggests.

A build was killed by hand at 08:47 (operator stopping a batch that had
pulled a heavy dependency). Its build_runs row id=20 stayed active. Over the
next 2.5 hours, on the same host:

  builds run                    9 batches, 137 ports built, 30 failures
  build_results recorded        0    (last row 08:47:01)
  runs rows created            14
  runs with a build_run_id      2
  build_runs still open         1    <- id 20, started 08:43:47

All 137 builds and 30 failures are permanently unrecorded. The packages
exist; the tracker has no rows for them. The failures never became agent
work either, so the loop was fed nothing for that whole window.

HOW IT WAS NOTICED — worth noting, because nothing surfaced it

Not by an alert. By an operator saying "in the last build in the tracker I
see no gcc12" about a port that had in fact been built and failed twice.

The 409 IS logged, 12 times, but only in the builder-local hook log:

  /work/dsynth/logs/dportsv3-hooks.log   12 occurrences
  tracker.log                             0
  dsynth stdout                           nothing; the build looks normal
  tracker UI                              no banner, no stale-build warning

That path is inside the chroot. Nothing an operator watches ever mentions it.

RECOVERY, confirmed working

  dportsv3 tracker finish-build --run 20 --finished-at <ts>

The very next build recorded end to end (run 21: started, marked building,
recorded result, finished). No restart or repair beyond that was needed.

SUGGESTED SCOPE, in order of what would actually have helped

- Surface an open build run: the tracker already has the row and its
  started_at, so a stale one is detectable by age. A banner and a line in
  `tracker status` would have turned 2.5 hours into 2 minutes.
- Log the 409 on the TRACKER side. It is the process that knows the
  conflict exists, and its log is the one an operator reads.
- `finish-build --stale`, or auto-close past a bound, so recovery does not
  require knowing the numeric run id.
- Reconsider TRACKING_DISABLED=1 as the response. Degrading to "collect
  nothing, quietly, indefinitely" is the wrong default for a data-collection
  tool; recording against a fresh run would lose far less.

Severity looks higher than P2 on this evidence — it is silent, unbounded,
and destroys data that cannot be recovered without rebuilding.

Related: poly-fij.8 records that the same (target, build_type) active-unique
constraint is the multi-builder attribution problem; this bug is that
constraint biting with a single builder.

title: The log distiller has no patterns for ports/bmake failures
description:
distill_log's "First error candidates" section came back empty for all
three real DragonFly ports failures captured on x6 — a patch-phase
failure (devel/glib20@bootstrap), a fetch failure (lang/rust), and one
line for a configure failure (graphics/jpeg-turbo).

The pattern list is compiler and build-system vocabulary: fatal error:,
undefined reference, ld: error:, collect2: error, CMake Error,
configure: error, meson.build:.*ERROR, ninja: build stopped, error:
failed to run custom build command for, "ERROR: ", No such file or
directory.

None of the ports vocabulary is there:

    *** Error code N        the bmake marker on EVERY ports failure
    Stop.                   bmake, immediately after
    ===>  FAILED ...        the patch phase
    FAILED to apply cleanly the patch phase
    N out of M hunks failed patch(1) reject
    FAILED 00:00:01         dsynth's own phase marker

So for the two most ports-specific failure classes the section is
completely empty, and errors.txt carries the failure only inside its
"Tail (last 200 lines)" block.

WHY THAT IS NOT GOOD ENOUGH

It worked here by luck of shape: a patch failure, a fetch failure and a
configure failure all stop the build immediately, so the error IS the
tail. A compile failure does not — bmake keeps other jobs running and
prints their output after the first error. With Max_jobs_per_builder
raised (2 -> 4 on x6 today) that window widens, and the first error can
fall outside a 200-line tail. errors.txt is what triage reads first, so
the failure would simply not be in the evidence.

Verified against the bundle the store actually holds, not by reading the
script: devel_glib20@bootstrap-20260827-105701Z, logs/errors.txt, 188
lines, failure text at lines 178-182.
design:
Add the ports vocabulary to both grep -nE lists in distill_log (candidates and error blocks). At minimum: '\*\*\* Error code', 'FAILED to apply', 'hunks failed', '===>  FAILED'. Keep them anchored where possible so a port that merely prints the phrase does not flood the section.

Worth pairing with a test that runs distill_log over a captured real ports log and asserts the failure line appears in the CANDIDATES section, not just the tail — the tail masks this bug, so a test that only greps the whole file would pass today.
acceptance_criteria: 1. A patch-phase failure and a bmake 'Error code' failure both appear in First error candidates. 2. A failure occurring more than 200 lines before the end of the log still reaches errors.txt.
notes: RECONFIRMED 2026-08-27 on the clean stack, devel_glib20@bootstrap-20260827-120810Z: errors.txt is 188 lines, the 'First error candidates' section has ZERO non-blank lines, and the failure appears only at lines 178/181 inside the 200-line tail. Same for the other two failures of the run.

title: The deployed venv is not self-contained, so it half-works when bind-mounted
description:
deploy install builds the venv with --system-site-packages, deliberately:
DragonFly pkgs supply modules pip cannot build there (see poly-170). The
venv therefore imports part of its dependency set from
/usr/local/lib/python3.11/site-packages on the HOST.

That breaks the moment the venv is bind-mounted into a dev-env chroot.
The venv's own lib travels with the mount; what it inherited from the
host's system site-packages does not, and the chroot's
/usr/local/lib/python3.11/site-packages is a different, emptier
directory.

Observed on x6 after mounting the venv at /work/polytropos: python
resolves correctly (sys.prefix=/work/polytropos, 3.11.12, matching the
host) and artifact-store-client works, because it is stdlib-only.
dportsv3 dies at import with ModuleNotFoundError: No module named
'tomli_w'. Full gap was tomli_w, tomli, requests, packaging — all
pure-Python, all present on the host only via system site-packages.

Consequence: the artifact-store half of the hooks works in-chroot and the
tracker half does not, which reads as a tracker outage rather than a
packaging problem.

Worked around by hand on x6:

    pip install --ignore-installed tomli_w tomli requests packaging

into the venv. Note that plain "pip install" is a no-op here — with
--system-site-packages pip sees the host copies and reports them already
satisfied, exits 0, and installs nothing. That workaround is operator
improvisation and is lost on the next deploy install.
design:
Two candidate fixes.

1. Make the venv self-contained for anything pure-Python. deploy install already knows the distribution set; have it force pure-Python deps into the venv (--ignore-installed) so nothing it needs is inherited. Keeps --system-site-packages for the compiled modules that genuinely need to come from pkg, which are the reason it exists.

2. Install the same pkgs inside the env base. Loses on version skew and repeats per env.

(1) is preferred: one venv, self-contained, mountable anywhere. It also makes the relocation property explicit rather than accidental — the venv is a deployment artifact that gets bind-mounted, so depending on the host's site-packages is a bug by construction.

Worth a test that imports every top-level dependency with the system site-packages hidden (PYTHONNOUSERSITE + a stripped sys.path), so the gap is caught in CI rather than on a chroot.
acceptance_criteria: 1. dportsv3 runs inside a dev-env chroot straight after deploy install, with no manual pip step. 2. The check is automated, not a runbook note. 3. --system-site-packages still covers the compiled modules that need it.
notes: OBSOLETE — superseded by poly-svh. The premise was 'the venv breaks when bind-mounted into a chroot', and 6e9c7c5 removes the bind-mount. Envs reach the tool through the checkout at TOOL_DIR, which builds its own venv inside the chroot from the chroot's python, so nothing is inherited from the host's system site-packages. The four modules that had to be force-installed on x6 were only needed to prop up the mount.

title: Step 31 — fold the artifact-store into the tracker (single service)
description:
The central side runs two HTTP services on one host:

- tracker (:8080, FastAPI) — reads state.db, serves bundle artifacts from
  a local artifact_root, and writes state.db directly.
- artifact-store (:8788, stdlib BaseHTTPRequestHandler) — the nominal
  "single writer", serving /v1/artifacts/{get,put,put-fs},
  /v1/bundles/upsert, /v1/jobs/transition, /v1/user-context.

They share one filesystem and one state.db file — the tracker reads
exactly what the artifact-store writes — so they already MUST co-locate.
Running them as two processes buys nothing and costs an extra port, an
extra thing to supervise, and a second network + auth surface the moment
a builder goes remote (poly-fij).

THE SINGLE-WRITER INVARIANT IS FICTION THREE WAYS OVER

Not two, as the backlog doc had it. Three processes write state.db:

- artifact-store, the nominal one;
- the tracker — 24 write statements across 14 tables: activity_log,
  build_results, build_runs, bundle_review_requests, bundles, events,
  issues, origin_skip_flags, port_status, tracker_active_env,
  user_context, user_context_history, user_context_requests,
  verify_requests. The doc called this "operator actions"; it is most of
  the tracker.
- the runner — 57 execute/commit sites across 9 tables (poly-fij).

Folding 31 makes the tracker the single central service and the single
writer PROCESS. The runner is then the only remaining direct-sqlite
writer, which poly-fij converts to HTTP.

THE SPLIT IS ALREADY COSTING US SOMETHING CONCRETE

The runner has two ways to fetch the same bytes and tries them in order:

    data = artifact_store_get(bundle_id, rel)      # :8788 /v1/artifacts/get
    if data is None:
        data = tracker_artifact_get(bundle_id, rel) # :8080 /api/bundles/.../artifacts/...

Two ports, two URL shapes, two accessors (_artifact_store_url and
_tracker_url), and a fallback chain that exists for no reason other than
there being two services. At two call sites. The fold deletes the
fallback, one accessor and one config knob.

And the on-disk layout is encoded twice. artifact_store.blob_path(root,
sha) builds it from blob_root (evidence/blobstore); the tracker's
render.resolve_artifact_path(artifact_root, ref) rebuilds the same path
from artifact_root (evidence) with 'blobstore' spelled inline. Two
modules, two differently-rooted inputs, one layout. Changing the layout
silently breaks whichever copy is not edited. Reads and writes must go
through one function after the fold.

STALE DOCSTRINGS FIXED SEPARATELY
