Tests: tests/test_env_gate_unresolved.py (12). Mutation-tested with
__pycache__ cleared between steps — removing the PermissionError branch,
the refusal-reason branch, the startup refusal, or the gate's `return True`
each fails a test. Suite 2162 passed.

Docs: docs/AGENTIC_BUILDS.md "No env, no jobs".

KNOWN BEHAVIOUR CHANGE, not verified on hardware yet: on a host with
several envs and no tracker selection, hook-driven jobs that carry their
own dev_env used to run (ungated); they now hold. Gating per-job on the
job's own env is poly-s9m.1, which is the real fix for that shape.

## Verified on x6 2026-08-24 (commit f47aeed)

T1 non-root, real store: rc=4. Message named the store path, the errno and
the fix ('run the runner as root'). No runner.lock created — the refusal
lands before the lock, as designed. Confirms the original x6 observation
came from list_infos() RAISING PermissionError, not from a silent empty,
which is the reading the dead fallback probe was removed for.

T2 root, empty env store (DPORTS_DEV_ENVS_DIR at an empty tmp dir):
  WARN  no dev-env resolved at runner start; the runner will hold ...
  INFO  runner paused: no dev-envs exist; create one with ...
  INFO  [no_env] no dev-env resolved; holding jobs (dsynth-busy gate unavailable)
  INFO  skipping --once: no_dev_env: no dev-envs exist; ...
rc=0, no job claimed. runner_status.current_stage kept the no_dev_env
reason through shutdown, so the last state is legible after the fact.

T3 root, real store: (('2026Q3-editors_vim',), None) — no false refusal
for the operator's actual setup, and the single env still auto-picks.

Follow-up found and fixed while verifying: the message logged twice,
because stub_unprobed_envs() enumerated before the check. Refusal moved
directly after init_state_db (commit 61d5467). Not re-run on x6; the
ordering does not affect T1-T3 outcomes, only the duplicate line.

title: Cross-env dependency hazard: divergent ports trees produce conflicting fixes
description:
REGISTERED AND DEFERRED — genuinely complicated, needs its own design pass. Blocks the epic; do not build multi-env scheduling without an answer here, even if the answer is 'serialize dependent origins'.

THE HAZARD: each env has its own DeltaPorts checkout, so the trees diverge. If A depends on B and you fix B in env2, that fix is invisible to env1. A then rebuilds against unfixed B, fails for a reason that is already solved, and the agent in env1 tries to fix B itself. Two agents then edit the same port in two divergent trees and someone reconciles the conflicting patches later.

WHY NOTHING CATCHES IT TODAY: there is no dependency awareness anywhere in dportsv3 — no BUILD_DEPENDS/RUN_DEPENDS parsing, no dep graph, nothing (grepped). _has_active_same_origin_job (runner.py:1418) guards a single origin, not a dependency cone, so it does not help.

WHERE THE DATA COULD COME FROM: dsynth already computes the graph to order its own builds. We just never capture it. Also available from make -V BUILD_DEPENDS per port. Cheap sources exist; the hard part is the scheduling policy, not the data.

SKETCH OF OPTIONS, none chosen: partition work by dependency cone so one env owns a whole cone; or give each env an exclusive origin set (lanes); or allow overlap and detect collisions after the fact at merge.
acceptance_criteria: 1. A design exists for how concurrent envs avoid working inside one dependency cone. 2. The chosen policy is implemented or explicitly deferred with the hazard documented where a scheduler author will see it.
notes:
AUDIT 2026-08-23. VERIFIED: there is no dependency awareness in dportsv3 — no BUILD_DEPENDS/RUN_DEPENDS parsing, no dep graph (grepped); _has_active_same_origin_job guards a single origin, not a cone; each env holds its own ports checkout so the trees genuinely diverge.

INFERRED, NOT VERIFIED: 'dsynth already computes the graph to order its own builds, we just never capture it.' That is about dsynth's internals, which I did not read. It is very likely true — dsynth must order builds somehow — but whether that ordering is extractable, and in what form, is an open question, not an established fact. Anyone picking this up should treat 'where the data comes from' as unsolved.

title: Scope the dsynth busy-gate to an env instead of the whole host
description:
dsynth_active (runner.py:2169) pgreps -x dsynth host-wide and returns busy if ANY dsynth exists. Called from _gate_blocked (runner.py:4525) it pauses the entire runner loop, so one build anywhere blocks every env. Needed for multi-env; also correct single-env.

REJECTED APPROACH — matching the dsynth profile on argv. Looks attractive because DPORTS_DSYNTH_PROFILE is per-env (dsynth.py:11) and appears as -p on every invocation from worker.py:2143 and the dev-env helpers. Two reasons it does not hold:

  * sanitize_name is not injective. It maps / : @ and space all to _ and deletes anything else, so envs 'foo/bar', 'foo:bar', 'foo\@bar', 'foo bar' and 'foo_bar' share ONE profile name. Attribution would point at the wrong env.
  * dsynth.ini sets profile_selected=, so an operator typing 'dsynth build x11/foo' inside the chroot passes no -p at all. argv shows nothing and the env reads free while a build runs — exactly the operator-initiated case the host-wide pgrep exists to catch.

CANDIDATE APPROACH — attribute by filesystem, not by process. dsynth's buildbase is per-env (/work/dsynth/build) and mounts_under() already exists (dev-env/dports_dev_env/mounts.py:58), reading the host mount table by path. Builder mounts under an env's buildbase are ground truth regardless of who started dsynth. MUST VERIFY ON A REAL HOST FIRST: that dsynth actually mounts under buildbase, and how wide the window is between process start and first mount. Not asserted.

DESIGN RULE: failure to attribute must mean BUSY, not free. Keep the host-wide pgrep as the floor and let attribution only ever narrow it.

RELATED WART: dsynth_active currently fails OPEN when pgrep is missing (runner.py:2199 returns False), which is the wrong direction under that rule.
acceptance_criteria: 1. A dsynth running in env A does not gate env B. 2. An operator-started dsynth (no -p on argv) still gates its own env. 3. Unattributable dsynth gates everything. 4. Missing pgrep fails closed, not open.
notes:
AUDIT 2026-08-23. Confidence labels for this bead's claims.

VERIFIED: sanitize_name is not injective (demonstrated — 'foo/bar', 'foo:bar', 'foo@bar', 'foo bar', 'foo_bar' all yield 'foo_bar'); dsynth.ini sets profile_selected so a bare in-chroot 'dsynth build' carries no -p; mounts_under exists and reads the host mount table by path; dsynth_active fails open when pgrep is missing.

STILL UNVERIFIED, as the bead already says: that dsynth mounts under buildbase at all, and the size of the window between process start and first mount. The whole candidate approach rests on that and it has not been checked on a real host. Do not treat it as the answer until it is.

Line numbers stale after c67416a — dsynth_active is now ~2271, was cited as 2169.

poly-i7y made this sharper: the runner now HOLDS when no runner-level env
resolves, so a multi-env host with hook-driven jobs (which carry their own
dev_env) stops processing them entirely rather than processing them
ungated. Gating on the job's env instead of the runner's env is what
unblocks that shape.

title: (EPIC) Multi-env concurrent building
description:
Run builds in more than one dev-env at once. The chroot layer is already close: each env root is a read-only nullfs of a shared provisioned base plus per-env writable dirs (runtime.py:76), and every dsynth path is inside the env — Directory_packages, buildbase, logs, options all under /work/dsynth (dsynth.py:44-52). env_health_status is already keyed by env and resolve_env_for_job already takes env per job.

The blockers are all in the runner's scheduling layer:

1. dsynth_active pgreps host-wide and gates the WHOLE loop from _gate_blocked (runner.py:4525), not per job. Any dsynth anywhere pauses everything.
2. The runner loop is serial: one claim -> process_job at a time, no pool.
3. Env resolution is a preference, not a scheduler. Precedence is job.dev_env > tracker_active_env (singleton) > --env > auto-pick-if-exactly-one > refuse. With >1 env and no operator selection it REFUSES (env_resolver.py:127), so a second env degrades the system rather than scaling it.
4. jobs has no env column; the env lives only in the .job payload.

THE FORK IN THE ROAD: in-process worker pool vs multiple runner processes. A pool sidesteps the lease/liveness problem entirely — one process owning N envs needs no cross-process ownership protocol. Multiple runners needs the full runner-identity + lease machinery (poly-bg1). Decide this before building anything under this epic.

Not a blocker, checked and dismissed: /usr/distfiles is bind-mounted RW into every env (runtime.py:94), but ports checksum distfiles, so a raced or partial fetch fails its checksum rather than being silently consumed.
acceptance_criteria: 1. The pool-vs-multiple-runners decision is made and recorded. 2. Two envs can build concurrently without either corrupting the other or falsely gating each other. 3. The cross-env dependency hazard has an explicit answer (see child bead), even if that answer is 'serialize dependent origins'.
notes:
AUDIT 2026-08-23. Separating what I verified from what I inferred.

VERIFIED by reading the code: env roots are a read-only nullfs of a shared provisioned base plus per-env writable dirs (mount_env_root); every dsynth directory is inside the env (write_dsynth_config); dsynth_active pgreps host-wide and gates the whole loop from _gate_blocked; the runner loop is serial; resolve_env_for_job refuses when >1 env exists with no selection; jobs has no env column.

INFERRED, NOT VERIFIED: the dismissal of /usr/distfiles as a shared write surface. The argument — ports checksum distfiles, so a raced or partial fetch fails its checksum rather than being silently consumed — is general ports behaviour I did not check in this codebase or in dsynth. It is probably right and it matches what you said, but it is reasoning, not a verified finding. If multi-env ever runs for real, watch for distfile checksum failures before assuming this was settled.

Line numbers in the description are stale after c67416a; cite the function names.
RELATION TO poly-fij (Step 17), noted 2026-08-27. The two are orthogonal axes of the same matrix: M hosts x N envs. Step 17 is scheduling ACROSS builders (a claim endpoint replacing the pending/ sweep); this epic is scheduling WITHIN one (pool, host-wide dsynth gate, env resolution). Neither replaces the other, and a builder running N envs needs both.

What that does change: blockers 1 and 3 here are not on Step 17's critical path. dsynth_active pgrepping host-wide and env resolution refusing with >1 env are both CORRECT behaviour when a host has exactly one env, so one-env-per-builder does not hit them. The two epics can land in either order.

It also informs THE FORK IN THE ROAD. If Step 17 lands first, cross-process ownership already exists as jobs.owner_id plus a lease, so 'multiple runner processes' stops needing bespoke lease machinery and the in-process pool loses its main advantage.

title: Document the stack bring-up as a unit (runbook)
description:
The tracker, artifact-store and agent-queue-runner have no documented,
repeatable way to be brought up. The operator runs them from an ad-hoc local
script that is not in the repo, so nobody else can start the stack and nothing
that depends on it can be exercised or tested.

Surfaced while scoping X5's criterion 5: "a real agent job runs end to end"
could not be attempted, and the reason turned out to be this, not anything
about the chroot layout. Criterion 5 was narrowed to what X5 owns and this was
split out.

TODO before picking this up: capture what the operator's script actually
starts, in what order, with what environment (litellm provider config —
DeepSeek, not Claude — ports, queue/log roots, tracker DB). Ask rather than
reconstruct; guessing produces a runbook that does not match the working setup.

docs/OPERATOR_SETUP.md covers per-command invocation but not bringing the stack
up as a unit.
notes:
Reparented under poly-abr 2026-08-24 as its documentation child, and
retitled: 'no supported way to run the services' is now the epic's
scope, and this bead is specifically the runbook half.

Sequencing that follows from the epic: this bead stays workable right
now — capturing what the operator's ad-hoc script actually starts needs
nothing but the operator. It is marked as blocking poly-abr.1 for that
reason: encoding a bring-up in rc.d before knowing what the working one
does would reconstruct rather than capture, which the original
description warns against.

The finished runbook should document the rc.d path once it exists, not
the three-shells path, so expect a second pass after poly-abr.1 and
poly-abr.2 land.

## Recon on x6, 2026-08-25 (read-only)

Looked for the operator's ad-hoc script before asking, and it is not on
that host: nothing in ~/bin, no shell script anywhere under $HOME
referencing agent-queue-runner / artifact-store / 'tracker serve', and
no history hits. None of the three services is running. So the script
is somewhere else and still has to come from the operator.

What the host does show, and it changes the picture:

  * /build/synth/logs/evidence exists with the documented shape —
    blobstore/, full-logs/, state.db — so the stack HAS run here.
    Everything is root-owned. state.db is dated 2026-08-01 and was left
    with a 4 MB -wal and a -shm beside it, i.e. not cleanly shut down.
  * There is NO queue root. $LOGS_ROOT/evidence/queue, which
    OPERATOR_SETUP.md names as where the hooks write .job files, does
    not exist. The only queue dirs on the box are my own test leftovers
    under /tmp.
  * The dsynth hooks are NOT installed in the live env
    (2026Q3-editors_vim has no dportsv3-hooks.conf).

So the hook -> queue -> runner path has never been wired on this host,
and 'cold start on x6' (poly-abr.5) is a genuine from-scratch exercise
that has to include dev-env hooks-install. The runbook needs to say so.

## Premise corrected by the operator, 2026-08-25

There is no ad-hoc script. The operator runs the three documented
commands by hand. The original description's claim — 'the operator runs
them from an ad-hoc local script that is not in the repo' — was wrong,
which also explains why searching x6 for it found nothing.

Consequences:

  * Nothing is being reconstructed if the rc.d scripts are written from
    OPERATOR_SETUP.md section 6 and the code's own flags and defaults,
    because that documentation IS the procedure. The blocking edge
    poly-abr.1 -> poly-4kr is therefore removed.
  * This bead inverts: rather than feeding the rc.d work, it documents
    the result of it. It now depends on poly-abr.1/.2/.3 and should be
    written once there is an rc.d path worth documenting.
  * The remaining gap is unchanged and still real: there is no unit
    bring-up. Three commands in three shells is what exists.

## Implemented 2026-08-25

docs/OPERATOR_SETUP.md section 6 now leads with the supported path —
`deploy install`, rc.conf knobs, `service ... start` — and keeps the
three-shells version below it, labelled as the development one. The
original gap is closed: there is a way to bring the stack up as a unit.

Added 'Running it day to day': a table of the entire operational surface
(where the UI is, how to stop/start/restart, which log is which, how to
check an env), a note that restarting the runner is safe by design and
why, and what to do when a service will not run.

Reconciled the two troubleshooting tables rather than leaving both. The
new one is about services that will not run; the pre-existing 'Common
stumbles' is about a stack that is up but misbehaving, and each now says
which is which. The old 'Upgrading' section overlapped too — it is now
the env half (hooks do not move when you pull) and points at the runbook
for the service half.

Also documented the checkout case explicitly, since it is the one that
will bite: installing from a checkout does not put console scripts in
/usr/local/bin, so polytropos.conf has to name the wrapper. deploy
install prints those exact lines when it detects the commands are
missing.

Note the premise correction earlier in this bead: there was never an
ad-hoc script to capture. This documents what exists.

title: sudo dev-env runs leave root-owned files in the user's venv
description:
dev-env commands need root, and bin/dportsv3 reinstalls dev-env into the venv
whenever its sources change. So `sudo bin/dportsv3 dev-env ...` after any
dev-env edit writes root-owned files into the developer's checkout — seen on
x6: 10 root-owned files under dev-env/.venv/lib/python3.11/site-packages after
one `sudo dev-env list`.

The next unprivileged run then fails to reinstall, and the usual reflex (run it
under sudo again) entrenches it.

Known workaround is "bootstrap unprivileged first", but that only covers venv
creation, not the reinstall-on-source-change path, which recurs every edit.

Options: have the wrapper drop privileges for the pip step, keep the dev-env
venv outside the checkout, or refuse to bootstrap as root with a clear message.
notes:
Observed on x6 2026-08-24: ~/s/polytropos-test carries 787 root-owned
.pyc files (sampled: dev-env/dports_dev_env/__pycache__/*.pyc, 2026-08-23
18:59). Left by earlier sudo dev-env runs, so this reproduces outside the
venv too — the working tree itself accumulates them. PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1
on the sudo invocation prevents new ones; verified it added none.

title: polytropos has no CI at all
description:
Neither repository runs CI against this tool. Found while verifying X6: the
Jenkinsfile its criterion 1 was written against was never tracked in git — an
uncommitted local draft in the DeltaPorts working copy, since deleted at the
operator's instruction. Polytropos has no Jenkinsfile and no .github/workflows.
DeltaPorts' .github/workflows/github-actions-pullrequests.yml shells
/root/bin/*.sh on a self-hosted runner and does not touch dportsv3, so it is a
consumer of ports/ only and is unaffected either way.

The suite is 2089 tests and runs green on macOS (3.11.14) and DragonFly
(3.11.12), so there is something worth gating on. Nothing gates on it.

Worth deciding before this is picked up:
- what runs it — GitHub Actions on the polytropos repo is the obvious default,
  but the tool's real target is DragonFly, which needs a self-hosted runner
- whether a macOS/Linux run of the pure-Python suite is enough for PR gating,
  with DragonFly reserved for the chroot/dev-env paths that cannot run
  anywhere else
- poly-170 blocks installing the [dev] extra on DragonFly (maturin needs
  rustc >= 1.89, pkg ships 1.85.1), so a DragonFly job cannot install pytest
  the normal way today

title: sync-dirty does not propagate host tool-repo edits into an env
description:
After X5 a chroot holds two checkouts: the ports tree at /work/DeltaPorts and
the tool at /work/polytropos. `dev-env sync-dirty` (sync.py DirtySyncer) only
resets and patches the ports checkout, so uncommitted TOOL edits on the host
never reach a running env — you have to destroy and recreate to test a tool
change, which is the workflow dev-env exists to avoid.

Deliberately left out of X5: resetting the tool checkout invalidates the cached
generator venv (venv.py keys on pyproject hashes), so this needs a
rebuild-or-revalidate path rather than a straight `git reset --hard` + patch.

Was flagged during the X5 review and confirmed as a real gap, not dismissed.

title: [dev] and [tracker] extras cannot install on DragonFly: maturin needs rustc >= 1.89, base has 1.85.1
description: The documented build recipe in CLAUDE.md ('uv pip install --python .venv -e ".[tracker,agent,dev]"') cannot complete on DragonFly, for two independent reasons. (1) uv is not present on the DragonFly host (x6, DragonFly 6.5-DEVELOPMENT) and is not in pkg; bin/dportsv3 does not need it - the wrapper bootstraps with stock 'python3 -m venv' + 'pip install -e' (bin/dportsv3:167,170) - but the documented dev recipe assumes uv. (2) DragonFly is not a wheel platform, so pip builds sdists from source. mypy 2.3.1 now depends on librt>=0.13.0 and ast-serialize>=0.6.0, whose build backend is maturin; maturin 1.14.1 requires rustc 1.89 while pkg rust is 1.85.1, so the build dies with 'rustc 1.85.1 is not supported by the following packages' (also cargo-platform 1.88, icu_* 1.86, time 1.88, zip 1.88). [tracker] fails the same way via fastapi -> pydantic-core. Observed effect: 'pip install -e ".[dev]"' and '".[tracker,agent,dev]"' both fail. Workaround used to run the suite on x6: 'pip install pytest' alone (pure Python). The suite still collected all 2085 tests ONLY because fastapi 0.115.12 and litellm 1.65.0 happen to be installed system-wide in /usr/local/lib/python3.11/site-packages and are visible to the venv - on a clean DragonFly box collection would fail. mypy is therefore not installable on the target platform at all, so type-checking cannot run there.
acceptance_criteria: 1) A documented dev setup that completes on a clean DragonFly host - e.g. pin mypy<2.3 (last release before the Rust-backed librt/ast-serialize deps), or split type-checking into an extra that is not required to run tests. 2) The suite installs and runs without relying on packages that happen to be present system-wide. 3) CLAUDE.md build instructions work on DragonFly as written, or state the platform caveat and the supported alternative explicitly.

title: compose needs three roots; --lock-root degrades silently and only --delta-root is documented
description: Running compose from outside the ports repo needs THREE input trees, but the docs name one. Verified on x6: --target and --output and --freebsd-root are mandatory, --delta-root defaults to $DPORTS_DELTA_ROOT else cwd, and --lock-root falls back to delta_root/'locked' (compose.py:98). DeltaPorts has no locked/ directory, so the fallback silently mis-resolves and yields 5x E_COMPOSE_LOCK_SOURCE_MISSING instead of naming the missing input. Passing --lock-root ~/s/dports (the DPorts checkout, per worker.py:304 'lock root (/work/DPorts/)') dropped errors 150 -> 134 and RAISED applied ops 9531 -> 9544, so the fallback was also losing real work. CLAUDE.md documents only --delta-root / $DPORTS_DELTA_ROOT. Silent degradation on a missing input is exactly what the paths.py invariant forbids - missing inputs must raise, not degrade.
acceptance_criteria: 1) A missing/unresolvable lock source raises a clear error naming the input instead of falling back to a path that does not exist. 2) Docs state the full three-root invocation (--delta-root, --freebsd-root, --lock-root) as the supported way to run outside the ports repo, satisfying X3 criterion 4. 3) Env-var equivalents documented alongside $DPORTS_DELTA_ROOT if they exist.
notes: Hash correction: the fix commit is 82329b8 (referenced as d1344fc before the attribution trailer was stripped and the unpushed commits rewritten).
close_reason: Fixed in d1344fc. A missing lock root is now reported once as E_COMPOSE_LOCK_ROOT_MISSING naming the path tried, and surfaced as a hint so it reaches plain compose output rather than only the JSON report. Gated on a type lock overlay actually needing the tree, preserving the documented 'only needed if' contract. Three-root invocation documented in CLAUDE.md and docs/dportsv3-user-guide.md, including that only --delta-root has an env var. Verified against the real DeltaPorts tree on x6. Satisfies X3 criterion 4.

title: X8 Cut over: delete moved files from the ports repo
description: The irreversible step, deliberately last and deliberately separate. Until this runs, both repos have the tool and the ports repo keeps working exactly as today, so every earlier phase is reversible. Remove scripts/generator, scripts/tools/dev-env, scripts/dsynth-hooks, scripts/snippet-extractor, the shims, the root ./dportsv3 wrapper, config/*.sample and the tool docs from the ports repo; leave ports/, special/, the ports-infra scripts and the legacy workflow. Keep a short pointer in the ports README saying where the tooling now lives and how to get it. Requires X1-X7 done and a green CI run against the split.
acceptance_criteria: 1) Ports repo builds ports with no tool code present. 2) A pointer to the tool repo exists where contributors will look. 3) CI green from a clean checkout of both repos. 4) Tagged commit on both sides marking the split, so the boundary is findable later.
notes:
Re-reviewed 2026-08-21.
- Criterion 1 met: DeltaPorts builds ports with no tool code.
- Criterion 2 met: README.md, CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md all name Polytropos. No
  URL in the pointer; not worth a bead.
- Criterion 3 has no subject: there is no CI on either side. See poly-1h4.
- Criterion 4: polytropos has no tag and does not need one — its root commit
  3414779 IS the split boundary, since the repo starts at the extraction.
  DeltaPorts' side is 75dee579255. Considered satisfied by construction.
close_reason: Cut-over done: 442 files / ~107.5k lines removed from DeltaPorts on branch dportsv3-removal, single squashed commit fcc0be9f842. Every removed file verified present in polytropos first. ports/ and special/ untouched (0 changed). Old tip tagged pre-removal-squash.

title: X7 Move the beads issue history to the tool repo
description:
The issue tracker for the TOOLING lives in the ports repo: .beads/config.yaml pins sync.remote to git+https://github.com/dragonflybsd/deltaports.git, and the Dolt DB (.beads/embeddeddolt) plus interactions.jsonl sit under the ports checkout. Every open issue there — this epic included, plus the whole build-confirmed resolution programme (Blocks A-D) and the review findings — is tool work, not ports work. Also .beads/hooks/ installs post-checkout/post-merge/pre-commit/pre-push/prepare-commit-msg git hooks into whichever repo hosts it.

Decide and execute: move the Dolt DB to the tool repo and repoint sync.remote, versus leaving history behind and starting clean. Moving keeps the audit trail of why the design is what it is, which is the main asset here. Sequence this LAST — the beads DB is how the rest of this plan is tracked, so moving it mid-flight would be self-defeating.
close_reason: Beads moved to polytropos: .beads/ + .agents/ + .codex/ carried over, prefix renamed DeltaPorts- -> poly- via bd rename-prefix, all 45 issues intact (31 open / 14 closed) with hierarchy. sync.remote cleared (it pointed at the DeltaPorts GitHub remote). Removed from DeltaPorts along with the managed CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md blocks. Commits 35539ae (poly) / fcc0be9f842 (DeltaPorts).

title: X6 Update the consumers: CI, hooks, docs, agent configs
description:
Consumers of the tool outside the tool itself. Re-verified 2026-08-20 from the
polytropos side; the original notes were written from the DeltaPorts side
before the cutover and three of the four criteria turned out to have no
subject at all.

CRITERION 1 (CI): NO SUBJECT. The Jenkinsfile that DEV_ENV_RUNNER='./dportsv3'
came from was never tracked in git — no history in either repository, in any
branch. It was an uncommitted local draft in the DeltaPorts working copy.
Deleted at the operator's instruction. Neither repo has any other CI: no
Jenkinsfile, no .github/workflows in polytropos. Filed separately as the
absence of CI is a real gap, just not this one.

CRITERION 2 (hooks reach the tool through a documented, configurable binary
path): ALREADY MET. hook_common.sh takes DPORTSV3_BIN from dportsv3-hooks.conf
and soft-fails when it is unset or not executable (lines 381-385), so the path
was never hardcoded. Only the example value and the docs were stale; both
corrected. The bead's path reference was also stale — the hooks moved to
dev-env/dports_dev_env/dsynth-hooks/ as package data in X1.

CRITERION 3 (operator docs): DONE, and the scope needed splitting first.
16 files carried stale references, but they are two different things:
- HISTORICAL RECORD, deliberately left alone (~296 refs): v3-refactor.md,
  implementation-plan-v3.md, dev-env-python-migration-plan.md,
  BUNDLE_LLM_ANALYSIS.md, the agentic-* set, dsl-v0.md, dsl-engine-review.md,
  build-tracker-plan.md. These correctly describe a layout that existed at the
  time. Rewriting them would falsify the record.
- LIVING DOCS, rewritten (58 refs): dportsv3-user-guide.md, OPERATOR_SETUP.md,
  dev-chroot-environment.md, TESTING_E2E.md, AGENTIC_BUILDS.md, plus the
  dsynth-hooks README.
Corrections made: ./dportsv3 -> bin/dportsv3 (the repo root `dportsv3` is the
Python package here, not the wrapper); scripts/generator/{.venv,tests,pyproject}
-> repo root; --delta-root . -> ../DeltaPorts and --root . likewise, since cwd
is the tool checkout now; overlay.dops example paths rebased onto the ports
tree; --lock-root added to three compose examples that omitted it while the
same document warned about the fallback; `dev-env create myenv` -> `--name
myenv`, which was wrong independently of the split. dev-chroot-environment.md

CRITERION 4 (.claude configs and permissions): NO SUBJECT. There is no
.claude/ directory in either repository. Polytropos has .agents/, .codex/,
AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md; DeltaPorts has .crush/. Grepped all of them for
DeltaPorts/scripts/generator and s/DeltaPorts: zero hits. settings.local.json
is gitignored, so it only ever existed in a working copy.
acceptance_criteria: 1) CI green with the two-repo layout, tool version pinned explicitly rather than implied by the checkout. 2) dsynth hooks reach the tool through a documented, configurable binary path. 3) Operator docs describe the split setup and live with the thing they document. 4) .claude configs and permissions updated in the repo they belong to; none dangle.

title: X4 Extract with history (git filter-repo)
description:
Carve the 677 tool commits out of 398,819 into a new repo, preserving blame. Neither git-filter-repo nor git subtree is installed on this machine — filter-repo is the right tool and needs installing first. Paths to keep: scripts/generator, scripts/tools/dev-env, scripts/dsynth-hooks, scripts/snippet-extractor, scripts/agent-queue-runner, scripts/artifact-store, the root dportsv3 wrapper, config/*.sample, docs/agent-playbooks and the tool docs. Then restructure to a sane top level (the tool should not live under scripts/generator/ in its own repo) — do the path rewrite as part of the filter so history follows the files. Reproduce the tool-specific .gitignore rules (venv, config local copies, *.db). Decide the uv.lock question (it was git rm --cached'd; lock state is currently ambiguous).

DECISION NEEDED: preserve history (this task) vs clean-slate squash. Preserving keeps blame across 677 commits for ~78k LOC and is the default assumption here.
acceptance_criteria: 1) New repo contains the tool with its 677 commits and working blame. 2) Top-level layout is idiomatic for a Python project, not scripts/generator/. 3) Paths rewritten inside history so blame survives the restructure. 4) Ports repo history is untouched. 5) Fresh clone + install + full suite green.
notes:
Re-reviewed 2026-08-21. Criteria 1 and 3 were not met and will not be:
extraction was a squashed "Initial import" (3414779), not filter-repo, so the

title: EPIC: Extract dportsv3 tooling into its own repository
description:
The tooling has outgrown the ports repo. Evidence: the tool is 415 real files / ~78k LOC (42k source + 36k tests) and 677 commits, inside a repo of 38,855 ports files and 397,224 ports commits — 0.17% of history, buried in a 469MB .git. Anyone cloning to work on the tracker drags 400k commits of port updates.

In its favour: the package is already properly formed (pyproject/hatchling, name dports-dragonfly, console script dportsv3, extras tracker/agent/dev), and scripts/ splits cleanly into tool (generator, tools/dev-env, dsynth-hooks = 677 commits) vs ports infrastructure (portsnap, share-mk, builderhooks, new-generator = 6 commits, stays).

MOVES: scripts/generator (dportsv3 + 138 test files), scripts/tools/dev-env, scripts/dsynth-hooks, scripts/snippet-extractor, the scripts/agent-queue-runner + artifact-store shims, the repo-root ./dportsv3 wrapper, config/*.sample, docs/agent-playbooks (18 files, runtime input), and the tool docs.
STAYS: ports/, special/, Makefiles, the ports-infra scripts, the legacy .github workflow.

The move itself is easy. The work is DE-COUPLING: the tool currently discovers everything by walking Path(__file__).parents[N] out into the ports repo, and the dev-env assumes it is installed inside the very checkout it mirrors into the chroot.

KEY DE-RISKING DECISION (verified): do NOT change /work/DeltaPorts inside the chroot. That path is the agent's only legal edit surface — it is baked into LLM prompt text (prompts.py, tools.py) AND actively enforced by the worker guardrails (worker.py rejects other prefixes). Moving it would invalidate prompt behaviour and guardrail logic simultaneously. The ports tree keeps its chroot path; the TOOL gets a new second path.
acceptance_criteria: 1) The tool builds, tests and runs from its own repo with the ports repo as an explicit input path. 2) The ports repo contains no tool code and still builds ports. 3) dev-env provisions a chroot from two repos with /work/DeltaPorts unchanged. 4) CI, dsynth hooks and operator docs work against the split. 5) Tool issue history (beads) lives with the tool. 6) No silent degradation: every formerly-implicit path either resolves or fails loudly.

title: Operator build controls: trigger / retry / cancel a confirm build
description:
The 'operable builds' requirement: an operator looking at an issue awaiting build confirmation has NO action available. The occurrence card offers only Reopen (correct for an accepted bundle) and the issue offers Resolve/Reopen — nothing to run, retry, or stop the confirm build itself.

The plumbing already exists and is currently DEAD CODE: issue_actions.request_confirm_build() bumps requested_build_generation as a standalone operator-facing entry point, and the C2 reconcile loop already picks up anything where requested > confirmed. What is missing is the HTTP endpoint and the UI control.

Note the C2 feed only surfaces issues in state='resolving', so a manual build on an issue in another state needs either a state precondition (gate the action to resolving) or a broadened predicate. Gating is the smaller, safer choice and matches the current model: a confirm build confirms an accepted fix, and 'accepted fix' IS resolving.

Cancel is the counterpart to the yt7 bound: an operator who knows a build will never succeed should be able to stop it without waiting for the retry budget to burn.
acceptance_criteria: 1) POST /api/issues/{key}/build requests a confirm build via request_confirm_build (gated: 409 when the issue is not in a state where a confirm build is meaningful; 404 unknown issue). 2) Requesting while a build is already in flight is a no-op or explicitly supersedes it — never double-enqueues (respects the single-flight claim). 3) POST /api/issues/{key}/build/cancel clears the pending request (and the in-flight marker) so the loop stops re-deriving it, leaving the issue in a coherent state. 4) Both actions are exposed on the issue page and gated through issue_state so the UI only shows what is legal. 5) Both emit an event so the audit log shows who asked for the build. 6) Tests cover: request bumps and the loop enqueues; request while in flight does not duplicate; cancel stops re-derivation; gate rejects an ineligible state.
close_reason: Implemented: POST /api/issues/{key}/build and /build/cancel, gated to resolving, event-emitting, wired to Build now / Cancel build buttons. Verified live. Surfacing build STATE remains chf.

title: Runner startup sweeps assume a single runner (no identity/leases)
description: Surfaced while fixing DeltaPorts-i8n. Every startup sweep is GLOBAL and unqualified: reap_orphans transitions all _INFLIGHT_STATES jobs to DEAD, and _reset_building_markers clears all building_generation markers + discards all queued confirm jobs. If a second runner starts while one is live, it kills the first runner's in-flight work. This is pre-existing and system-wide (reap_orphans predates the confirm loop), not specific to build-confirmed resolution — claim_next_job_batch is explicitly written to tolerate a competing runner, so the system half-assumes multi-runner while the startup path assumes single-runner. Fixing it properly needs runner identity + leases (claim rows tagged with a runner id + heartbeat, sweeps scoped to jobs whose owner is demonstrably dead).
acceptance_criteria: 1) A runner's startup sweep only reaps work owned by a runner that is demonstrably not alive. 2) Jobs/markers carry an owning runner identity. 3) Starting a second runner does not disturb a live runner's in-flight jobs or confirm-build markers. 4) Decide explicitly whether multi-runner is supported; if not, make starting a second runner refuse loudly instead of silently corrupting the first.
notes:
CODE PATHS RE-REVIEWED 2026-08-23. The description overstates the damage; the
mechanism is different from what it says and the severity is lower, with one
behavioural edge.

"If a second runner starts while one is live, it kills the first runner's
in-flight work" — IT DOES NOT. _apply_transition (runner.py:458-463) states the
model: "The filesystem queue is the source of truth for what processes next;
the typed jobs table is the UI's read model." Both halves verified:
  - nothing in the processing path reads jobs.state — no `SELECT state FROM
    jobs`, no `== JobState.DEAD` guard anywhere in runner.py;
  - DEAD has NO outgoing transitions, so when the live runner later applies its
    real terminal event it raises IllegalTransition, which _apply_transition
    catches, warns about, and swallows. Work continues to completion.

ACTUAL DAMAGE FROM A SECOND RUNNER'S STARTUP:
  1. Read-model corruption: a live job shows `dead` in the tracker and keeps
     showing it after it completes, because the terminal transition is refused.
     Only the tracker read queries consume DEAD (agentic_queries/jobs.py:34,38,
     overview.py:45) — no behavioural consumer there.
  2. BEHAVIOURAL: _has_active_same_origin_job (runner.py:1418) treats DEAD as
     not-active, so the duplicate-enqueue guard opens and a second triage can
     be enqueued for a port another runner is currently working.
  3. _reset_building_markers deletes queued confirm .job files and clears
     markers. Real deletion, but the intent is level-triggered so the feed
     re-derives; recoverable by design.

CORRECTION TO AN EARLIER CLAIM OF MINE: I said concurrent dsynth in one env was
an unguarded physical-corruption risk. Wrong. dsynth_active (runner.py:2106)
pgreps HOST-WIDE and deliberately so — "Process existence is the only state
that actually matters for 'would a second dsynth invocation collide'". A second
runner's dsynth is gated. There is a check-then-act race, but it is not
unguarded.

WHY THIS BLOCKS B3 ANYWAY: every sweep today touches DB rows and queue files —
cosmetic or recoverable. B3's sweep would be the first to `rm -rf` a directory
a live process is building in. Different class of damage, and the reason B3
must not land on unqualified sweeps.

WHAT MAKES CRITERIA 1-3 EXPENSIVE:
  - jobs has no owner column (schema.py:135-151).
  - runner_status is a hard singleton: `id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT 1
    CHECK (id = 1)` (schema.py:180). The 5s heartbeat (runner.py:1611) writes
    that one row, so two runners overwrite each other. "Is the owner alive?" is
    unrepresentable until that table stops being a singleton or a runners table
    exists.
Criterion 4 (decide multi-runner; if not, refuse loudly) is by far the cheapest
and would make B3 safe on its own: one runner means every job-* worktree is
demonstrably ours.

SEPARATE GAP FOUND, NOT IN THIS BEAD: nothing sweeps the inflight/ DIRECTORY at
startup. reap_orphans only touches DB rows, so after a crash the .job files sit
in inflight/ forever while their rows go DEAD. Belongs with B3's crash-safety
theme.

EVIDENCE FOR THE CONTRADICTION THE BEAD NAMES: claim_next_job_batch really is
written for concurrency — atomic rename with the comment "Move lead first; if
that races, try the next pending job" (runner.py:2186-2190).
---

CRITERION 2 DONE 2026-08-23: runner identity is now RECORDED, not enforced.
Multi-runner stays parked; this is only the substrate.

 - jobs.owner_id (schema.py, + a MIGRATIONS ALTER so an existing state.db
   keeps its rows).
 - runners table: runner_id, hostname, pid, started_at, last_heartbeat_at,
   stopped_at. Separate from runner_status, which stays a singleton because
   it is the UI's "what is the runner doing" panel — de-singletoning it would
   have meant touching overview.py:78, agentic_api.py:102, pages.py:632 and
   two tests for no gain here.
 - lifecycle.apply(owner=...) stamps it, COALESCE so an ownerless hook-side
   event does not blank the claiming runner. _apply_transition passes
   runner_id(); the 5s heartbeat refreshes runners.last_heartbeat_at; clean
   shutdown stamps stopped_at, a crash leaves it NULL with a stale heartbeat.

THE TRAP, for whoever does criteria 1 and 3: reap_orphans must stay UNSCOPED
until liveness is queryable. Scoping it to the current runner skips the
previous process's rows — which are exactly the orphans — leaving them
inflight forever and jamming _has_active_same_origin_job, the same jam
reap_stale_queued exists to unstick. Verified by mutation: adding
"AND (owner_id IS NULL OR owner_id = ?)" to the sweep fails
test_reap_orphans_ignores_owner. That test and a comment on reap_orphans are
the guard.

test_job_ownership.py also asserts nothing outside lifecycle.py reads
owner_id, so enforcement cannot arrive by accident without the liveness
machinery.

STILL OPEN: criterion 4. An exclusive startup lock is the cheap answer and
unblocks B3 on its own; criteria 1 and 3 remain the expensive lease work.
IMPLEMENTED 2026-08-23 as an exclusive startup lock. Multi-runner is refused, not supported.

THE FACT THAT COLLAPSED THIS BEAD: state.db is a plain local sqlite file (get_state_db_path, runner.py:364) opened WAL, and WAL needs shared memory, so it cannot live on a network filesystem. Two runners sharing a state.db are therefore two processes on the SAME host, and os.kill(pid, 0) settles liveness exactly. No heartbeat-staleness heuristics needed.

HOW THE FOUR CRITERIA RESOLVED:
  1. Sweep only reaps demonstrably-dead work — satisfied BY CONSTRUCTION, not by scoping. Holding the lock means no other runner exists, so every inflight row is genuinely an orphan. It must be done this way: scoping reap_orphans by owner_id was mutation-tested and BREAKS single-runner restart recovery (test_reap_orphans_ignores_owner).
  2. Identity — done earlier, 7d4b337.
  3. Second runner does not disturb the first — it never reaches the sweeps.
  4. Decide + refuse loudly — done. This was the only real work.

The bead's original premise, 'fixing it properly needs runner identity + leases', is wrong for a parked-multi-runner world. Leases are only needed if concurrent runners are WANTED.

PRIMITIVE CHOICE: fcntl.flock(LOCK_EX|LOCK_NB), NOT dev-env's CacheLock. CacheLock is mkdir-based and does not release on death — its own error text says to remove it by hand — so a SIGKILLed runner would block every later restart, which is exactly the crash this lock exists to recover from. Verified empirically with two real processes rather than trusting the man page: second acquirer got EWOULDBLOCK while held, and acquired cleanly after the holder was kill -9'd.

The runners table is the diagnostic (describe_lock_holder names pid + started_at + heartbeat age); the flock is the mechanism. The table alone has a check-then-act race between two simultaneous starts.

SEPARATE FINDING, now fixed by the same change: the sweeps run BEFORE main() branches on --once, so running 'agent-queue-runner --once' by hand while the service was up would reap the service's in-flight jobs. --once is gated too, and the test says so.

Exit code 3 (EXIT_RUNNER_LOCKED), distinct from 1 so a supervisor can tell 'already running' from a broken start. Documented in docs/AGENTIC_BUILDS.md.

SCOPE LIMIT, deliberate: the lock is per queue_root. Two runners with different queue roots but the same DPORTSV3_STATE_DB would both start and fight over the read model. Not this lock's job.

STILL OPEN ELSEWHERE: stranded inflight/*.job files after a crash (poly-tr8). Compatible with poly-s9m — a worker pool inside one process is unaffected by a per-process lock.

NOT VERIFIED IN A REAL DEPLOYMENT — poly-4kr still blocks running the services.
AUDIT 2026-08-23. Went back over this bead's claims against the code rather than against my own earlier prose.

CLAIM REFINED — 'nothing in the processing path reads jobs.state'. Too broad, and I had not checked decision.py when I wrote it. decision.py DOES query the jobs table for a real decision: it counts failed patch attempts filtered on retire_reason IN ('patch_gave_up','patch_budget_exhausted'). A startup reap writes retire_reason='runner_restart' (_TERMINAL_REASONS[REAP_ORPHAN], checked programmatically), which that filter excludes, so the conclusion survives — but the accurate statement is 'no consumer branches on jobs.state, and the one consumer that reads the jobs table filters on retire_reason values a reap does not produce', not the blanket version.

CLAIM VERIFIED — DEAD has no outgoing transitions. Checked programmatically against TRANSITIONS, not by eye.

LINE NUMBERS IN THIS BEAD ARE STALE. The runner lock added ~113 lines to runner.py, so every runner.py:NNNN citation written before c67416a is wrong (_gate_blocked 4525->4602, dsynth_active 2169->2271, _has_active_same_origin_job 1418->1460). Read the function names, not the numbers. Going forward these beads cite functions.
VERIFIED ON x6 2026-08-23 (DragonFly 6.5, real flock, real processes).

  * --once on an empty queue: rc 0.
  * Second runner while one holds the lock: rc 3 (EXIT_RUNNER_LOCKED) and the refusal named the holder from the runners table — 'runner x6.sector.int-10444-d50cdd7a (pid 10444, started ..., last heartbeat ...)'. So describe_lock_holder works against a live row, not just a synthetic one.
  * kill -9 the holder, start again: acquires cleanly. The property that ruled out CacheLock, confirmed on the target OS.
  * --once is gated by the same lock, as intended.

title: Confirm builds skip the muted-issue guard
description: The confirm dispatch runs a full build unconditionally. The muted-issue short-circuit (_maybe_skip_muted_issue) is only on the triage path, so an issue muted after its fix was accepted still burns full dsynth builds — and with A4 that is 2 builds per confirmation. The verdict's terminal transition is correctly guarded (a muted issue is not resolved), so this is wasted budget rather than wrong state, but it contradicts the documented invariant that muting suppresses BOTH surfacing and auto-work.
acceptance_criteria: 1) process_build_requests (or the confirm dispatch) skips muted issues, matching the muted-issue invariant. 2) An issue muted mid-flight does not get its follow-up A4 build requested. 3) Test covers mute-after-accept.

title: Confirm loop: apply/reapply failures conflated with a red build
description: The dispatch treats any result.ok==False as a RED verdict, including failure_stage()=='apply'/'reapply' (verify_fix.py:112-115) — i.e. the accepted diff no longer applies to base, which is drift/rebase, NOT 'the accepted fix did not hold'. That path reopens the issue and NULLS delivery_bundle_id, losing the pointer to the accepted (possibly already-merged) fix. Combined with the worklist-band bug it silently loses both its delivery pointer and its visibility. Also (minor, same area): the red handoff PUTs analysis/manual_handoff.md into the accepted delivery bundle, clobbering any handoff that bundle already carried from its own triage/patch history, with no generation in the path to distinguish repeats.
acceptance_criteria: 1) apply/reapply failure is distinguished from a genuine red build and does not destroy delivery_bundle_id. 2) Drift gets its own operator signal (re-base/re-verify), not 'the fix did not hold'. 3) The confirm handoff does not silently overwrite a pre-existing bundle handoff.

title: Tests for the build-confirmed resolution path (C1/C2/A1-A4)
description: The confirm loop shipped with NO dedicated tests. All verification during implementation was ad-hoc scratch scripts against a temp state.db, which are not committed and do not protect against regression. The 2006 passing tests cover pre-existing behaviour only; the sole test touched was test_lifecycle.py (added the CONFIRMING walk-path).
acceptance_criteria: 1) issues_needing_build feed predicate (resolving + requested>confirmed + not in-flight). 2) process_build_requests: enqueues once, single-flight on 2nd pass, skips no-delivery-bundle, re-enqueues after _reset_building_markers. 3) _record_confirm_verdict: green->resolved+green_head, red->reopened+cleared, guards reject muted/unresolved, rollback leaves no partial write. 4) A4: green,green->resolved on 2nd; green,red->reopen+tally reset; threshold=1 resolves on first. 5) Merge no longer resolves a resolving issue.
close_reason: 35 tests committed covering C1/C2/A1-A4 plus a regression test per review defect; mutation-checked (removing each fix fails its test). Suite 2045 green.

title: Surface build-confirmation state in the tracker UI
description: A1-A4 added issues.requested_build_generation / last_confirmed_build_generation / building_generation / green_head_run_id / confirm_green_count, but NOTHING surfaces them. Two concrete gaps: (1) the 'resolving' badge still reads 'Awaiting delivery' (issue_state.py:102/124) which is now wrong-ish — it means 'awaiting build confirmation'; (2) an operator cannot see WHY an issue sits in resolving: is a confirm build in flight, provisional-green 1/2, or stalled with building_generation set after a gave-up? Without this the loop is opaque.
acceptance_criteria: 1) resolving badge/label distinguishes awaiting-build-confirmation from awaiting-delivery. 2) Issue detail shows confirm build state: in-flight (building_generation), provisional green count N/threshold, green head ordinal when resolved. 3) A stalled confirm (building_generation set, no live job) is visibly distinguishable from one in flight.

title: D1 Direct vs transitive failures
description: D1 Direct vs transitive failures. Mark an issue whose failure is only a failed build-dep as blocked/transitive; surface the root issue first. Prior art: Hydra red-cross vs greyed; pbulk direct vs indirect.

title: D6 Drop dead runs.build_run_id column
description: D6 Drop dead runs.build_run_id column. The sole INSERT INTO runs (artifact_store.py:131) never populates it; always NULL. The confirm-reader joins on (target,origin); no consumer needs build-run provenance. Hard cutover.
close_reason: Obsolete: the premise no longer holds. C3 needs an occurrence's build ordinal to place it against a fix's Green-Head watermark, so runs.build_run_id is now written (hook_pkg_failure sends the tracker run ordinal with the bundle) and read (the occurrence join in agentic_queries.issues). Dropping it would put the regression derivation back on wall clocks.

title: Block B — Stability & atomization: isolate per build, destroy after
description: Move the build path from 'mutate the shared checkout -> reset it' to 'isolate per build -> destroy it'. Warranted on its own merit (deletes verified-gnarly code), NOT a feature prerequisite. dsynth already isolates its own build slots; the shared git checkout is the real contamination point.
design:
Block B — Stability & atomization: DESIGN OF RECORD
(grounded in a read of the real apply/reset/attempt flow; file:line refs inline)

== D1. Granularity = PER-JOB worktree (settled) ==
The codebase already has a per-job git *branch* abstraction; B evolves it into a
per-job *worktree*. Current flow:
- Patch job runs on branch `bundle/<id>`, REUSED across the bundle's job chain
  (triage->patch); created-from-base once, edits left UNCOMMITTED in the shared
  working tree; branch dropped at patch-job end.
  create: checkout_bundle_branch (worker.py:1505) via runner.py:3231
  drop:   drop_bundle_branch/_drop_branch (worker.py:1604) via runner.py:3394
- Verify runs on a THROWAWAY `bundle/<id>-verify`, force-recut with `-B`
  (worker.py:1709/1754), dropped after the verdict (worker.py:1773, runner.py:3574).
- Attempts within a job SHARE the working tree (attempt_loop.py is only the LLM
  conversation; it does not reset between attempts).

B: replace "checkout branch on the ONE shared tree" with "git worktree add a
per-job working dir on that branch". Create at job start (replaces
checkout_bundle_branch / checkout_verify_branch); DESTROY at job end (replaces
drop_bundle_branch / drop_verify_branch and apply_and_build's _post_build_cleanup).
All attempts in a job share that one worktree, exactly as today.

== D2. THE ONE REAL BLOCKER — gitdir prefix split (load-bearing) ==
Git runs on the SAME physical dir through TWO path prefixes:
- IN-CHROOT `/work/DeltaPorts` (via _exec / ChrootRunner): branch ops, reset_port,
  reapply/materialize, apply_and_build. (worker.py:794; chroot.py:29)
- ON THE HOST `<writable>/work/DeltaPorts` (via `git -C`): ONLY the changes.diff
  capture — _git_diff_against_base (worker.py:654) and emit_diff (worker.py:676).
A linked worktree's `.git` file stores an ABSOLUTE `gitdir:` pointer that resolves
under exactly one prefix. So a naive per-job worktree breaks one side.

FIX (default, no version dependency): move the two host-side diff-capture helpers
to run IN-CHROOT via _exec, unifying all git on the `/work/...` prefix. Then a
worktree created in-chroot is self-consistent. (put_file needs NO gitdir — it is a
plain file write; just retarget its write path into the worktree dir.)
ALT: relative-path worktrees (`git worktree add --relative-paths`, git >= 2.48) —
resolves under both prefixes because the worktree->main relative path is identical
in both views. Requires verifying the dev-env git version; prefer the in-chroot fix
to avoid that dependency.

== D3. Scope: serial (B1-B3) isolates the SOURCE only; the rest stays shared ==
Only the DeltaPorts checkout needs per-job isolation for the stability win. These
are per-ENV (shared), NOT under the checkout, and are FINE shared under the single
serial runner — they'd need per-job partition ONLY for concurrency (that is B4):
  - compose tree /work/artifacts/compose/<target>  (dsynth Directory_portsdir)
  - WRKDIR /work/obj  (make_extract, worker.py:927)
  - genpatch staging /work/genpatch-out
  - module dicts _MATERIALIZE_STATE / _WRKSRC_CACHE / _TARGET_CACHE (worker.py:819,940,948)
So B1-B3 = worktree the source overlay ONLY. Do not touch the compose/obj/dsynth
dirs for the serial feature.

== D4. reset_port's fate ==
reset_port's WHOLE-TREE hammer (`git checkout HEAD -- . && git clean -fd`,
worker.py:1331) exists to stop writes that escaped ports/<origin> from poisoning
the NEXT JOB (worker.py:1325-1330). A per-job DISPOSABLE worktree removes that
rationale entirely — destroy, don't reset. The per-ATTEMPT "start clean" reset
(each attempt from branch HEAD) may be kept, but becomes a SAFE, SCOPED op inside
the disposable worktree (no cross-job blast radius). Net: delete the whole-tree /
cross-job cleanup; keep at most a scoped per-attempt reset inside the worktree.

== Task designs ==
B1 (per-job worktree): new worker.create_job_worktree(env, bundle_id, kind) doing
   in-chroot `git worktree add <wt_path> <branch>` (reuse branch for patch; `-B`
   recut for verify). Retarget the job's paths.deltaports to <wt_path>. Move
   diff-capture in-chroot (D2). Replaces checkout_bundle_branch (runner.py:3231)
   and checkout_verify_branch (runner.py:3462).
B2 (delete cleanup): new worker.destroy_job_worktree -> in-chroot
   `git worktree remove --force <wt_path>` (+ optional branch -D). Replaces
   _drop_branch (worker.py:1604), drop_verify_branch (worker.py:1773), and
   apply_and_build._post_build_cleanup (cli.py:383). Delete reset_port's whole-tree
   reset (steps.py:1083 call becomes a no-op or a scoped in-worktree reset only).
B3 (stale sweep): on runner startup, in-chroot `git worktree prune` + remove
   orphaned worktree dirs whose owning job is not live. Name worktrees `wt/<id>`
   and either pidfile them or diff against active jobs. Replaces "SIGKILL ->
   dirty env -> manual reset-port" recovery.

== Open verifications BEFORE coding ==
- git in the dev-env chroot: version (for the --relative-paths option) + confirm
  `git worktree` is available.
- apply_and_build refactor: today it applies --3way into /work/DeltaPorts then
  _post_build_cleanup; confirm it can instead build inside a per-verify worktree.
- product call: keep the per-attempt "clean start" reset, or let attempts build on
  prior state? (Affects whether B2 keeps a scoped in-worktree reset.)

title: A4 Flaky-aware confirmation
description: A4 Flaky-aware confirmation. A single green is provisional; the next scheduled / 2nd independent green confirms. Guards transient build flakiness (network/toolchain). Prior art: ClusterFuzz 2-bot, >=5/10 reproductions.
design:
## Design

Guard against transient build flakiness (network / toolchain): a SINGLE green is
provisional; require N independent greens before resolving. Prior art: ClusterFuzz
2-bot reproduction, >=5/10 threshold.

**Config:** `confirm_green_threshold` (default 2) in config/agentic-policy.json.

**State:** add `confirm_green_count INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0` to `issues`.

**Modifies A2's green handling — first green is NOT terminal:**
- green verdict, `confirm_green_count + 1 < threshold`: stay in `resolving` (the
  "confirming" band — no new state value needed), record the provisional green +
  candidate green-head, and REQUEST ANOTHER build by bumping
  `requested_build_generation` again — so C2 naturally schedules a 2nd INDEPENDENT
  confirm build (reuses the spine; no separate scheduler).
- green verdict, count reaches `threshold`: hand to A2 -> `resolved`; green-head =
  the confirming (last) build.
- 'Independent' = a DISTINCT `build_run_id` / generation, not a re-read of the same
  build result.

**Any red before threshold:** A3 reopen path; reset `confirm_green_count = 0`.

**Depends on A1 + A2** (verdict + resolve path). Optional-ish hardening; the MVP
resolves on a single green until this lands.
acceptance_criteria: 1) confirm_green_threshold config (default 2). 2) issues gains confirm_green_count. 3) First green: issue stays resolving, count=1, requested_build_generation bumped so C2 runs a 2nd INDEPENDENT build (distinct build_run_id/generation). 4) Count reaches threshold -> A2 resolves; green-head = confirming build. 5) Any red before threshold -> A3 reopen + count reset. 6) Test: green,green -> resolved on 2nd; green,red -> reopened + count reset.
close_reason: Implemented + reviewed + committed. Threshold via DP_CONFIRM_GREEN_THRESHOLD env knob (codebase convention) rather than agentic-policy.json.

title: D3 Timestamp skew at source
description: D3 Timestamp skew at the source. Hooks write compact YYYYmmdd-HHMMSSZ; regression checks are naked lexicographic compares that only work because _normalize_ts canonicalizes at the single writer. Emit ISO at the hook source; keep _normalize_ts as a guarded fallback that asserts. (ts_utc is bundle/agentic data, not dsynth build_*.)

title: A3 Red -> auto-reopen + handoff
description: A3 Red -> auto-reopen + manual handoff. On a red confirm build, reopen the issue out of resolving and write analysis/manual_handoff.md instead of leaving a falsely-resolved issue. Prior art: Google TAP auto-rollback (tracker-side).
design:
## Design

On a RED confirm-build verdict (from A1's report-back), do NOT leave a falsely
"resolving" issue — reopen it and hand off to a human. Prior art: Google TAP
auto-rollback.

**Transition (red branch of the confirm-build report-back handler):**
- `state: resolving -> unresolved` — reuse `reopen_issue` (issue_actions.py:127),
  which clears `resolved_at` / `regressed_at` / `delivery_bundle_id`.
- GUARD: only from `state='resolving'` (a muted / already-resolved issue untouched).
- advance `last_confirmed_build_generation = generation`, clear
  `building_generation` — so the C2 loop does NOT re-enqueue this generation and
  spin on a persistently-red fix.

**Manual handoff (not auto-triage):** write `analysis/manual_handoff.md` via the
existing escalation writer (agent/manual_handoff.py) with: which accepted fix
(`delivery_bundle_id`) was built, the red verdict, `build_run_id`, and the log
pointer. A red confirm goes to a HUMAN — it does NOT re-trigger the agent loop.

**Event:** emit `issue_reopened` (or `issue_confirm_failed`) with
`source='build-confirmed'`, `verdict='red'`, `build_run_id`.

**Depends on A1** (verdict + report-back endpoint). Pairs with A2 (green branch).
acceptance_criteria: 1) Red verdict for a resolving issue -> state resolving->unresolved via reopen_issue (resolved_at/regressed_at/delivery_bundle_id cleared); guard only from resolving. 2) analysis/manual_handoff.md written via manual_handoff.py with the failed delivery_bundle_id, red verdict, build_run_id, log pointer. 3) last_confirmed_build_generation advanced + building_generation cleared -> C2 does NOT re-enqueue the persistently-red fix. 4) Does NOT auto-retrigger the agent (manual handoff, not auto-triage). 5) Event emitted. 6) Test: resolving+red -> reopened + handoff file; second C2 pass -> no re-enqueue.
close_reason: Implemented + reviewed + committed 4th A task. Handoff carries generation+log instead of build_run_id (dev-env hooks disabled -> no build_runs row).

title: C3 Two-axis status (regressed derived)
description: C3 Two-axis status. Split resolution axis (unresolved->resolving->resolved->muted) from build-observation axis (green/red at ordinal). `regressed` becomes DERIVED (resolved AND newer build re-emits fingerprint >= boundary), not a stored mode. Prior art: ArgoCD sync-vs-health; Sentry release boundary.
design:
## Design

Split the two axes that are currently conflated in `issues.state`, and make
`regressed` a DERIVED read, not a stored mode. Prior art: ArgoCD sync-vs-health;
Sentry release boundary.

**Two axes:**
- RESOLUTION axis (operator/build intent) — `issues.state` constrained to
  {unresolved, resolving, resolved, muted}. `regressed` is REMOVED as a stored value.
- BUILD-OBSERVATION axis (facts) — `port_status` / `build_results` / the A2
  green-head ordinal (`green_head_run_id`).

**Derive `regressed` in the projection layer (tracker/issue_state.py, which already
layers on fix_state):**
`regressed  ==  state == resolved  AND  a build at ordinal > green_head_run_id
re-emits the same fingerprint` (i.e. resolved on the resolution axis but red past the
known-good boundary on the observation axis). `regressed_at` becomes the
boundary-crossing build's timestamp, also derived.

**Writer change:** the artifact-store path that currently sets `state='regressed'`
on a new occurrence after resolve instead LEAVES `state='resolved'` and lets the
projection derive the regressed badge. One-time migration: existing `regressed` rows
-> `resolved` (the derivation reproduces the badge from the observation axis).

**Depends on A2** (green-head boundary) **and A3**. Touches issue_state.py badge +
worklist bucketing; keep fix_state.py's `merged` dominance intact.
acceptance_criteria: 1) issues.state constrained to {unresolved,resolving,resolved,muted}; 'regressed' no longer a stored value. 2) issue_state.py derives regressed = state==resolved AND a build at ordinal > green_head_run_id re-emits the fingerprint; regressed_at derived from that build. 3) Badge + worklist reflect derived regressed with no stored column; fix_state 'merged' dominance intact. 4) Writer stops setting state='regressed'; existing regressed rows migrated to resolved (derivation reproduces the badge). 5) Test: resolved + newer failing build past green-head -> derived regressed; newer build without re-emit -> stays resolved.
close_reason: Implemented + reviewed. regressed is derived from the Green-Head watermark in issue_state.derived_regression; issues.state is CHECKed to {unresolved,resolving,resolved,muted} and legacy regressed rows migrate on open. effective_state folds the two axes so the badge, action gate and worklist keep their existing shape. An occurrence arriving on a resolving issue no longer reopens it — the confirm verdict owns that exit.

title: C4 Workqueue hygiene
description: C4 Workqueue pacing. The confirm-build feed retries on two paths with no delay between attempts: the bounded machinery-failure path (spends its whole retry budget at loop speed) and the enqueue-failure path (retries forever, uncounted). Add a persisted per-key next_eligible_at with exponential backoff and honour it in the reconcile SELECT. Keying and single-flight already landed with C1/C2. Prior art: controller-runtime workqueue.
design:
## Design

Rewritten against the code after C1/C2/yt7 landed; the original scope was
written before them and three of its four asks no longer describe reality.

**Already delivered, not part of this:**

- Keying by (target, origin, fingerprint) — that triple IS issue_key
  (fingerprint.py:80), and every marker and counter is keyed on it.
- Single-flight per key — _claim_issue_build (runner.py:1046) is a
  conditional UPDATE taken BEFORE the enqueue, so a failed claim cannot
  leave a duplicate.
- 'env busy' requeue-without-penalty — moot rather than done. _gate_blocked()
  returns True on dsynth-busy and the loop continues BEFORE
  process_build_requests runs, so nothing is enqueued and there is nothing to
  forgive.

**Explicitly NOT in scope:** backing off A4 re-requests. A green below the
consecutive-green threshold bumps requested_build_generation inline in the
verdict transaction (runner.py:1388) to schedule an independent build. Those
are successes being repeated on purpose; pacing them only slows confirmation.

**What is actually missing — pacing, on two paths that retry without it.**

1. The bounded path. A confirm build that could not RUN increments
   confirm_failure_count and clears the in-flight marker
   (_record_confirm_failure, runner.py:1246), so the feed retries on the very
   next pass. The bound (DP_CONFIRM_MAX_FAILURES, default 3) is therefore
   spent at loop speed for a fast failure — 'no dev-env', 'could not
   establish fresh confirm/verify branch' raise in seconds, so three tries
   burn in seconds and the issue is reopened with a manual handoff for
   something transient. For a slow failure — 'confirm verdict could not be
   recorded' (runner.py:4412), i.e. the write lost the SQLite lock race after
   the build ran — each retry costs a full dsynth run, so the same three
   tries waste three builds. runner.py:4458 already names this as C4's.

2. The unbounded path. An enqueue failure in process_build_requests
   (runner.py:1502) logs a WARN, releases the claim and continues; the
   level-triggered feed re-derives the same work next pass, roughly every 5s,
   forever, with no counter and no escalation. confirm_failure_count never
   sees it — that counter lives on the job-execution path. The sibling loop
   the docstring claims to mirror does not do this: process_verify_requests
   marks its request 'failed' (runner.py:993) and stops.

**Shape.** A per-key next_eligible_at alongside confirm_failure_count on
issues, and one AND (next_eligible_at IS NULL OR next_eligible_at <= now)
clause on the issues_needing_build SELECT. Backoff is exponential in the
existing failure count, so no second counter is needed for path 1; path 2
starts using the same counter and bound, which also gives it the escalation
it lacks. State is a column, so it survives a runner restart — the startup
sweep clears building_generation only (runner.py:1185), never the tally.

A produced verdict already resets confirm_failure_count (runner.py:1363);
it must reset next_eligible_at with it, or a recovered issue stays parked.
acceptance_criteria: 1) A per-key next_eligible_at persists on issues and is honoured by issues_needing_build, so backoff survives a runner restart. 2) A confirm build that could not RUN backs off exponentially in confirm_failure_count before the feed re-derives it; the bound (DP_CONFIRM_MAX_FAILURES) still reopens the issue with a manual handoff. 3) An enqueue failure in process_build_requests counts against the same budget and backs off the same way, so a persistently unwritable queue escalates to a human instead of logging every 5s forever. 4) A produced verdict clears next_eligible_at along with confirm_failure_count. 5) env busy is untouched: the gate stops the loop before the feed runs, so no penalty is possible. 6) A4 re-requests are not paced. 7) Tests: repeated machinery failures show growing gaps and terminate at the bound; a job becomes eligible once the delay elapses; a green verdict clears the delay.
close_reason: Implemented + reviewed. Per-key next_eligible_at on issues, exponential in the existing confirm_failure_count, honoured by issues_needing_build. Enqueue failures now go through the same budget instead of releasing the claim silently and retrying uncounted forever. Verdicts and give-up both clear the delay. Scope was cut to pacing after re-reading the code: keying and single-flight came with C1/C2, env-busy is handled by the gate stopping the loop, and A4 re-requests are successes that must not be paced.

title: B1 Per-job git worktree for overlay source
description: B1 Per-job git worktree for the overlay source. Each build applies its diff into its own `git worktree add --detach` of /work/DeltaPorts (shared object store, no clone-per-build). Eliminates the shared-checkout collision.
design:
## Design

Replace "checkout branch on the ONE shared /work/DeltaPorts tree" with "git
worktree add a per-job working dir on that branch". Evolves the existing per-job
git *branch* abstraction into a per-job *worktree*. All attempts in a job share the
one worktree, exactly as they share the tree today (attempt_loop.py is only the LLM
conversation; it does not reset between attempts).

**New op:** `worker.create_job_worktree(env, bundle_id, kind)` doing in-chroot
`git worktree add <wt_path> <branch>` — reuse `bundle/<id>` for patch; `-B` recut
for verify. Retarget the job's `paths.deltaports` to `<wt_path>`. Replaces
`checkout_bundle_branch` (runner.py:3231) and `checkout_verify_branch`
(runner.py:3462).

**THE ONE REAL BLOCKER — gitdir prefix split (load-bearing, fold the fix in here):**
git touches the same physical dir through TWO path prefixes — IN-CHROOT
`/work/DeltaPorts` (via _exec/ChrootRunner: branch ops, reset, reapply,
apply_and_build) and ON THE HOST `<writable>/work/DeltaPorts` (via `git -C`: ONLY
the changes.diff capture — `_git_diff_against_base` worker.py:654, `emit_diff`
worker.py:676). A linked worktree's `.git` file stores an ABSOLUTE `gitdir:` pointer
that resolves under exactly one prefix, so a naive worktree breaks one side.
FIX (default, no version dependency): move those two diff-capture helpers IN-CHROOT
via _exec, unifying all git on the `/work/...` prefix. (`put_file` needs no gitdir —
just retarget its write path into the worktree.)
ALT: `git worktree add --relative-paths` (git >= 2.48) — needs a version check;
prefer the in-chroot fix to avoid that dependency.

**Open verifications before coding:** git version + `git worktree` availability in
the chroot; confirm `apply_and_build` can build inside a per-verify worktree.
acceptance_criteria: 1) worker.create_job_worktree does in-chroot 'git worktree add <wt> <branch>' (reuse bundle/<id> for patch, -B recut for verify); job paths.deltaports retargeted to <wt>. 2) Replaces checkout_bundle_branch (runner.py:3231) + checkout_verify_branch (runner.py:3462). 3) Diff-capture (_git_diff_against_base, emit_diff) moved in-chroot so all git shares the /work/... prefix; changes.diff still captured correctly. 4) All attempts in a job share the one worktree. 5) Verified pre-code: git worktree available in chroot; apply_and_build builds inside a per-verify worktree.
notes:
IMPLEMENTED in 5cc4931. Acceptance criteria:

1. create_job_worktree does in-chroot `git worktree add` (reuse bundle/<id>
   for patch, -B recut for verify) and repoints the job's tree — MET, though
   by symlink rather than by retargeting paths.deltaports. See the placement
   note: EnvPaths needs no change under B.
2. Replaces checkout_bundle_branch + checkout_verify_branch — MET at the call
   sites (runner.py:2682, 2762, plus both drop wrappers). The four worker
   functions now have NO production callers but are still defined and still
   have tests. B2 owns deleting them.
3. Diff-capture moved in-chroot — MET, and wider than the design said. It was
   not only _git_diff_against_base + emit_diff: dev-env's _port_dirty_paths
   (cli.py) was a third host-side git consumer the design missed, used by
   apply_and_build's pre-replay check. It also swallowed git failures and
   returned [] — i.e. "clean" — which would have inverted the refusal its
   caller exists to make. Now raises.
4. All attempts in a job share the one worktree — MET by construction: the
   worktree is created at job start and destroyed at job end, attempts do not
   touch it.
5. Pre-code verifications — git worktree in chroot: DONE (2.49.0).
   apply_and_build inside a per-verify worktree: STILL NOT DONE. It needs a
   real dsynth build. Everything around it is verified, but that specific
   claim is not, and B2/B4 lean on it.

VERIFIED ON X6, end to end, five runs covering both the branch-creation and
branch-reuse paths: create -> host-side write through the symlink -> in-chroot
diff helper sees it -> in-chroot dirty check sees it -> destroy -> main
checkout still CLEAN. That last part is the point of B1.

UNEXPLAINED: the very first e2e create returned ok=False and I could not
reproduce it in five subsequent runs, including after deleting the branch to
force the creation path. Cause unknown; recorded rather than guessed at.

Suite 2121 passed. New tests in tests/test_dev_env_job_worktree.py; several
existing tests updated where B1 changed a contract (the diff helpers take an
env, the pre-replay dirty check is now a chroot call, the verify wrapper
returns no ref to restore).

title: B2 Delete whole-tree reset_port + cleanup dance
description: B2 Delete the whole-tree reset_port (worker.py:1331 `git checkout HEAD -- . && git clean -fd`) and the fragile _post_build_cleanup git-reset dance (cli.py:383); replace with 'destroy the worktree'. reset_port comment itself admits escaped writes poison the next job classify/compose.
design:
## Design

With a per-job DISPOSABLE worktree (B1), the whole rationale for the fragile
cleanup dances evaporates — you destroy the worktree instead of scrubbing a shared
tree. reset_port's whole-tree hammer (`git checkout HEAD -- . && git clean -fd`,
worker.py:1331) exists ONLY to stop writes that escaped ports/<origin> from
poisoning the NEXT job's shared checkout (worker.py:1325-1330); a disposable
worktree removes that cross-job blast radius entirely.

**New op:** `worker.destroy_job_worktree(env, bundle_id, kind)` -> in-chroot
`git worktree remove --force <wt_path>` (+ optional branch `-D`). Called at job end.

**Delete / replace:**
- `_drop_branch` (worker.py:1604) and `drop_verify_branch` (worker.py:1773) ->
  replaced by destroy_job_worktree.
- `apply_and_build._post_build_cleanup` (dev-env cli.py:383) — the 3-step git-reset
  dance a SIGKILL skips -> deleted; the worktree is thrown away instead.
- reset_port's whole-tree reset (called at steps.py:1083) -> becomes a no-op, OR at
  most a SCOPED per-attempt reset INSIDE the disposable worktree (safe, no cross-job
  blast radius).

**Orthogonality note (verified):** this does NOT touch dsynth's own ephemeral build
dirs. dsynth self-isolates the compile (Directory_buildbase=/work/dsynth/build +
Number_of_builders -> per-port tmpfs builder slots); the real build never dirties
the base /var /tmp or the checkout. The cleanup we delete was only ever about
source-checkout dirtiness, which the worktree now owns. Two ephemerality layers,
separate: source checkout = our worktree; build sandbox = dsynth's, untouched.

**Product call (open):** keep the per-attempt "clean start" reset (now scoped inside
the worktree) or let attempts build on prior state? Decides whether B2 keeps a
scoped in-worktree reset or removes it outright.
acceptance_criteria: 1) worker.destroy_job_worktree does in-chroot 'git worktree remove --force <wt>' at job end. 2) Deletes/replaces _drop_branch (worker.py:1604), drop_verify_branch (worker.py:1773), apply_and_build._post_build_cleanup (cli.py:383), and reset_port's whole-tree reset (steps.py:1083). 3) dsynth's own build dirs untouched (orthogonal). 4) Per-attempt reset either removed or kept as a scoped in-worktree op per the product call. 5) A SIGKILL that skips cleanup no longer poisons the next job (worktree is disposable).
notes:
CARRIED DEBT DISCHARGED (as far as it can be). apply_and_build DOES run inside
a per-verify worktree: worktree created, link repointed, apply and reapply
succeed (reapply_exit=0, composing from the worktree), dsynth is reached and
resolves dependencies against the composed tree (49 returned) and creates its
build template.

dsynth then fails with "Error opening terminal: unknown." — its curses UI wants
a TTY, and this runs over ssh under nohup. VERIFIED PRE-EXISTING AND UNRELATED:
the identical failure reproduces running `dtest` through dev-env exec with no
worktree involved at all. So it is a constraint of driving dsynth
non-interactively, not something B1 or B2 introduced.

Nothing worktree-shaped remains in that path: dsynth's build sandbox
(/work/dsynth/build) and the composed tree (/work/artifacts/compose) both live
outside the worktree, which is why the first attempt failed only because the
env had been created with --no-initial-compose and had no Mk/bsd.port.mk.

A full interactive dsynth build is still the only thing that would exercise the
compile itself. Not attempted; it needs a terminal.

title: B3 Startup stale-worktree sweep (crash-safe)
description: B3 Startup stale-worktree sweep (crash-safe). On runner start, sweep leftover per-job worktrees from crashed builds — replaces today SIGKILL -> dirty env -> manual reset-port recovery.
design:
## Design

Crash-safety sweep. Today a SIGKILL mid-job leaves a dirty shared env that an
operator must manually `reset-port` to recover. With per-job worktrees (B1/B2), a
crash instead leaves a STALE worktree — sweep it automatically on runner startup.

**On runner startup:**
1. in-chroot `git worktree prune` (drops worktree admin entries whose dir is gone).
2. Enumerate worktree dirs under the worktree root; for each, decide if its owning
   job is still live. Name worktrees `wt/<bundle_id>` (or `<bundle_id>-verify`) and
   either pidfile them or diff against the set of active jobs (lifecycle ACTIVE work
   states). Remove any orphan via `git worktree remove --force`.

**Replaces:** the "SIGKILL -> dirty env -> operator manually runs reset-port"
recovery path. After this, a crashed runner self-cleans on restart with no operator
action.

**Scope guard:** only sweeps worktrees the runner owns (the `wt/` namespace); never
touches the primary /work/DeltaPorts checkout or dsynth's build dirs.

**Depends on B1 (worktrees must exist to be swept) and pairs with B2 (same
destroy op).**
