acceptance_criteria: 1) On runner startup: in-chroot 'git worktree prune' + remove orphaned wt/ dirs whose owning job is not live. 2) Worktrees named wt/<bundle_id>; orphan decided via pidfile or active-job diff. 3) Replaces the SIGKILL->dirty-env->manual reset-port recovery; crashed runner self-cleans on restart. 4) Only sweeps the wt/ namespace; never touches primary /work/DeltaPorts or dsynth dirs.
notes:
RE-REVIEWED 2026-08-23 against the code as B1/B2 actually shipped. The design section is stale in three places and the scope shrank.

STALE:
  * Names worktrees wt/<bundle_id>. B1 shipped job-<kind>-<id> directly under /work (worker.py:1512), so the sweep namespace is /work/job-*.
  * Scope guard says 'never touches the primary /work/DeltaPorts checkout'. After B1 that path is not a checkout, it is the relative symlink. Restate as: never touch /work/ports-main, and repoint the link to the idle target BEFORE removing anything it might point at.
  * 'decide if its owning job is still live' via pidfile or active-job diff — unnecessary under a single runner. With poly-bg1 criterion 4 (exclusive startup lock), at startup no job of ours is live by definition, so every /work/job-* is stale. That remains the cheapest unblock; ownership recording (7d4b337) does NOT unblock this, because B3 must DECIDE liveness, not log it.

ALREADY DONE BY B1, drop from scope: create_job_worktree force-removes and prunes any leftover at the job's exact path before worktree add (worker.py:1572-1577). Path-collision recovery already exists, lazily, per job.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY LEFT:
  1. Orphan worktrees for bundles never re-enqueued — nothing ever reclaims them. This is the real remaining item.
  2. Stranded inflight/*.job files. reap_orphans only touches DB rows, so a crash leaves the files behind while their rows go DEAD. Same startup, same crash-safety theme.

CORRECTION TO MY OWN EARLIER FRAMING: I called a stale /work/DeltaPorts symlink the sharpest remaining item here. On re-review it is not, and it is not a B3 item at all. Every reader of the link runs inside a job that repoints it first (creation at runner.py:3802, 4031, 4183 precedes any worker.* call), and no startup path reads the ports tree — the health probe does not touch it. The plain stale-link case self-heals on the next job. The real hazard is the soft-fail path, filed separately as its own P1; do not bury it in this deferred bead.

MULTI-ENV: the sweep is per-env. poly-s9m makes 'is this worktree live' hard again unless the in-process-pool option wins, where the runner holds its live set in memory. Do not build the sweep in a way that assumes one env.
AUDIT 2026-08-23. Line numbers in the notes above are stale — the runner lock (c67416a) shifted runner.py by ~113 lines. The worktree-creation call sites cited as runner.py:3802/4031/4183 are the calls inside process_patch_job, the verify dispatch, and the confirm path; find them via _checkout_bundle_branch_for_job and _checkout_verify_branch_for_job. Cite functions, not line numbers.

Also: of those three call sites I verified the ordering claim ('creation precedes any worker.* call') by reading the patch and confirm paths. I did NOT read the verify dispatch as carefully. Treat that third one as unconfirmed.
IMPLEMENTED 2026-08-23. Two sweeps, both at startup, both decidable only because the runner lock (poly-bg1) guarantees no other runner and nothing has been claimed yet.

1. sweep_stranded_inflight — moves inflight/*.job to failed/ with an error note. reap_orphans marked the rows DEAD but never touched the files, and claim_next_job_batch only globs pending/, so those files were invisible forever. Moved rather than deleted: the payload is the only record of what the job was.

2. sweep_stale_worktrees / worker.sweep_job_worktrees — removes /work/job-* in the runner's env, restoring the ports link to ports-main FIRST because it may point at a directory about to be removed.

DESIGN POINT THE BEAD DID NOT ANTICIPATE: the sweep works on directory NAMES, not bundle ids, so destroy_job_worktree is the wrong tool. _job_worktree_name sanitizes any character outside [A-Za-z0-9._-] to '_', so the mapping is lossy and a swept directory name cannot be turned back into the bundle it came from.

SINGLE ENV, deliberately. Sweeping envs the runner does not own would mean rm -rf inside a tree an operator might be sitting in — verified that dev-env shell/exec do NOT mark an env busy, so the lock says nothing about them. When a runner owns several envs (poly-s9m) this loops over the set it owns.

VERIFICATION: the shell is where the risk is, so the generated script is executed against real directories in a test rather than only asserted on as a string — it removes the stale worktrees, keeps the keep-list entry, and leaves ports-main and DeltaPorts alone. Five mutations, each caught: widening the glob to all dirs, ignoring the keep list, ignoring a failed link restore, deleting inflight files instead of moving them, and sweeping with no env resolved.

CORRECTION TO A GUESS I MADE EARLIER: shlex.quote leaves shell-safe names bare, so an assertion that the keep list appears quoted was simply wrong. The test now pins the behaviour (safe name bare, unsafe name quoted) rather than a spelling.

NOT VERIFIED IN A REAL CHROOT (poly-4kr). In particular 'git worktree remove --force' and 'worktree prune' against a real repo are stubbed out in the test; only the glob, keep-list and rm logic run for real.
VERIFIED ON x6 2026-08-23 against the live env 2026Q3-editors_vim.

Stranded inflight sweep: a .job file placed in inflight/ was moved to failed/ with its .error note on the next --once start.

Worktree sweep: simulated a crashed job by creating job-patch-faketest (with content) and job-verify-faketest and pointing /work/DeltaPorts at the patch one. On startup the runner logged 'swept 2 stale worktree(s)', both directories were gone, and the link was back on ports-main. ports-main and polytropos untouched.

Also confirmed the B1 cycle end to end on hardware, which the sweep depends on: create_job_worktree moved the link to job-patch-livetest-b1 and destroy_job_worktree put it back on ports-main.

title: D4 Fingerprint-rule versioning
description: D4 Fingerprint stability. Version the error-line normalization rule; apply new rules only to new occurrences so history doesn't spuriously regroup/regress. Prior art: Sentry grouping versioning; ClusterFuzz frame-based.

title: dev_env.delta_root should be a setting; the env var is allowlisted as per-exec but names a fixed checkout
description:
`dports-dev-env create` takes the DeltaPorts checkout from --delta-root
or $DPORTS_DEV_DELTA_ROOT, and there is no setting for it. The
[dev_env] table carries deltaports_branch but no root.

DPORTS_DEV_DELTA_ROOT sits in ALLOWED_NON_SETTINGS in
tests/test_settings_unification.py, in the group commented:

    Inter-process arguments spelled as environment: a parent telling a
    child about this one exec. Better as CLI flags, but not config.

alongside DPORTS_DEV_TOOL_ROOT, DPORTS_DEV_ENV_CMD and DPORTSV3_CMD.

THE TENSION. The project's own rule is that a value earns an
environment variable only if it "cannot be known when the config file is
written". A DeltaPorts checkout on a fixed install is entirely knowable
then -- it is a stable path an operator would write once and never
change. That is a setting by the stated test, not a per-exec argument.

The reason it is not one looks historical rather than considered. Per
builder.default_delta_root's own docstring it replaced a
Path(__file__).parents[4] walk that, after the repo split, silently
resolved to the tool's own repository -- so an env would have been built
against the wrong tree "without a word of complaint". The fix was to
make the operator name it. Turning that into a setting was never the
question being answered.

It is genuinely arguable: TOOL_ROOT really is per-exec (bin/dportsv3
exports it for the checkout it lives in, and an installed copy has no
repository above it). DELTA_ROOT is not the same shape -- nothing
exports it for you, so every operator either types --delta-root forever
or puts the export in a shell profile, which is the "settable only by
exporting a variable no sample mentions" state the settings unification
existed to end.

Raised by an operator hitting the error while setting up a dev-env only
install, with no services deployed: they had a polytropos.toml and asked
why this one value could not go in it.
design:
Add Setting("dev_env.delta_root", "path", None, ...) and resolve in
builder.default_delta_root with the precedence the rest of the codebase
uses:

    --delta-root  >  $DPORTS_DEV_DELTA_ROOT  >  dev_env.delta_root

Keep the env var. It is what bin/dportsv3 and the runner already pass
down, and dropping it would break every current invocation. Declaring it
as env= on the setting is the shape CLAUDE.md asks for -- "the reader
finds it next to what it overrides" -- and it also takes the name out of
ALLOWED_NON_SETTINGS, since _declared_env_names() then covers it.

Keep the raise when nothing names a root. The whole point of the
original change was that guessing is worse than refusing; a setting adds
a third place to look, not a default to invent.

Not obviously worth doing on its own -- it is one line of shell in a
profile today. Worth doing if a second dev-env-only install shows up, or
alongside any other work in that resolver.

title: the artifact reader shows two vertical scrollbars on a diff: .diff-view's height cap nests a scroller inside .a-body
description:
On the bundle page, selecting a diff artifact renders a scrollbar
inside a scrollbar -- the diff pane appears to be a frame within a frame.

Reproduce: open any bundle with a changes.diff longer than 70vh and select
that artifact in the reader, e.g.

  /agentic/bundles/<bundle_id>?artifact=analysis%2Fchanges.diff

MECHANISM

Two rules combine, progress.css:

  .reader .a-body { overflow: auto; }              outer scroller
    .a-body-inner
      .diff-view  { overflow-x: auto; max-height: 70vh; }   inner scroller

`overflow-x: auto` does not leave the other axis alone: CSS computes an
`overflow-y: visible` to `auto` when the opposite axis is not visible. So
.diff-view is scrollable vertically as well, and `max-height: 70vh` then
guarantees it actually overflows. Meanwhile .reader is a fixed 588px frame
whose .a-body already scrolls. Two vertical scrollbars, nested.

THE CAP IS IN THE WRONG SCOPE

The rule's own comment states the intent:

  "Bundle-page inline preview caps height; standalone artifact view lets the
   renderer take whatever vertical space it needs."

The selector is unscoped, so the cap applies inside .reader too -- where it is
not wanted, because .a-body is the frame. The standalone view
(agentic_artifact.html) does not use .reader at all, so it is unaffected and
renders a single scrollbar today.

SCOPE

Diffs only. .artifact-content and .artifact-markdown carry no max-height, so
they scroll in .a-body alone as intended. That is why this shows on
changes.diff and not on triage.md or patch_audit.json.

FIX

A scoped override, following the existing .reader .artifact-error precedent:

  .reader .diff-view { max-height: none; }

Horizontal scrolling stays -- long diff lines need it inside the frame. The
vertical cap goes, leaving .a-body as the only vertical scroller. The
standalone page keeps its 70vh.

title: Reviewing a fix before accepting it: rebuild_ok cannot tell a fix from a silencing
description:
OPTIONAL. Filed for the record, not queued. Nothing here blocks other work.

rebuild_ok is the only thing that decides agent_fixed, and it cannot tell
a fix from a silencing. `dsynth build` proves the port compiles, links,
packages and matches its plist. It cannot see that a deleted patch was
load-bearing, that a define lies about the platform, or that the code it
just compiled will hang. verify_fix.py replays changes.diff in a fresh
env and asserts dsynth_exit == 0 - an independent verification stage that
asks the same weak question.

MEASURED over all 13 agent_fixed bundles on 2026-08-29..09-01.
About half are sound: devel/json-glib (MAKE_ENV LC_ALL=C for a docutils
locale failure), devel/nspr (refreshes a drifted patch, adds
__DragonFly__ to the ifdef), graphics/dcp2icc (adds defined(__DragonFly__)
to an endian check), math/arpack-ng (drops PLIST_FILES conflicting with a
%%MPI%% guard), shells/bash-completion x2 (gates FreeBSD-only completions
behind an option), irc/ircd-ratbox (moves -I${OPENSSLINC} behind
.if ${PORT_OPTIONS:MOPENSSL}).

The rest fail the same way - they make the build exit 0 without touching
the cause:

  deletes dragonfly/patch-* or diffs/*.diff        4  devel/level-zero,
                                                      devel/libpciaccess x2,
                                                      devel/libunwind 08-29
  define that lies about the platform              1  devel/gamin,
                                                      -D__FreeBSD__=9
  post-patch re-invoking dfly-patch                1  devel/libunwind 09-01
  REINPLACE whose replacement re-matches itself    1  devel/libunwind 09-01
  silently drops a USES entry                      2  devel/gamin,
                                                      graphics/dcp2icc

devel/level-zero and devel/libpciaccess are the clearest: both deleted the
patch that adds __DragonFly__ to a platform conditional. That still
compiles, links and packages - the code just takes another branch - so the
signal reports success while DragonFly support quietly goes away.

NOT PRIMARILY THE MODEL. The same model in the same session produced
bash-completion's option gating and arpack-ng's PLIST analysis, both
non-trivial. Capability is not the binding constraint; the reward is.
Deleting and silencing score identically to fixing and are much cheaper to
find. A stronger model would raise the average and would not change that.
design:
Two tiers, and the useful one needs no model.

TIER 1 - deterministic policy checks in verify_fix.py, which already has
changes.diff in hand. Each is a grep, so there is no sycophancy, no blind
spot shared with the generator, and no rubber-stamping. Five rules cover
roughly 7 of the 13 measured fixes:

  1. deletes dragonfly/patch-* or diffs/*.diff -> refuse unless patch.md
     justifies it with evidence (e.g. quotes the upstream line that now
     carries the change)
  2. adds a define asserting a foreign platform (-D__FreeBSD__, -D__linux__)
  3. adds `mk target set post-patch` invoking dfly-patch - Mk/bsd.port.mk
     already orders 880:dfly-patch, so this double-runs it
  4. REINPLACE whose replacement text still contains its own match pattern
     - not idempotent, and dfly-patch can run more than once
  5. removes a USES entry without saying why

TIER 2 - an LLM critic, only for what rules cannot express, and expect
less of it. Same model means correlated blind spots, critics default to
approving, and "did deleting this patch remove DragonFly support" needs
exactly the understanding the generator just failed at. If built: ask
evidence questions that require a quote ("does this diff remove a platform
conditional? cite the line"), never "is this fix good".

SCORE IT BEFORE SHIPPING IT. The 13 bundles above are a labelled eval set,
roughly half known-bad with documented reasons. Run any rule set or critic
against them first. If it does not flag the four deletions and gamin's
-D__FreeBSD__=9, it is not worth shipping.

COST. A reviewer can only reject, so the effect is fewer bogus agent_fixed
and more escalated_manual, on a queue already carrying 34 gave-up and 16
escalated. Worth paying only because a wrong agent_fixed that reaches
upstream costs far more than an escalation.
notes:
Optional. Not queued, not claimed, nothing blocks on it.

Related: poly-dq5 (the libunwind run this came out of), poly-7jw
(the truncation class). Neither depends on this.

Evidence lives in the bundles named in the description; each carries its
own analysis/changes.diff, so the eval set is reproducible with
  dportsv3 tracker fetch-artifact <bundle> analysis/changes.diff

title: dbuild cannot be driven non-interactively: it always exits 1 on the repository prompt
description:
The dev-env `dbuild` helper is the supported way to build a port in an
env, but it cannot be used from a script: it always exits non-zero even
when every port built as intended.

OBSERVED, overnight run 2026-08-31:

  dports-dev-env exec --quiet 2026Q3 -- dbuild <8 origins>
  ...
  Duration: 00:00:18
  Rebuild the repository? exit=1

The build itself was fine — all 8 ports processed, hooks fired, 8 triage
jobs enqueued. The failure is only the trailing prompt.

WHY

helpers.py:87 maps `dbuild` to the dsynth `build` directive, and
helpers.py:114 execs `dsynth -p "$DPORTS_DSYNTH_PROFILE" build "$@"` with
no `-y`. `build` asks "Rebuild the repository?" at the end; with stdin not
a terminal dsynth reads EOF and returns 1. Caller sees failure, and the
repository is left unrebuilt.

CONSEQUENCE

Any automation around dbuild has to ignore its exit status, which also
throws away the ability to notice a real failure. `set -e` around it stops
a script dead after a successful build.

SCOPE, one of:
  - pass `-y` (dsynth then answers the prompt itself), or
  - use the `just-build` directive, which skips the post-build steps and
    has no prompt, or
  - a `--no-repo` style flag on the helper so the caller chooses.

`just-build` is probably right for the agentic flow, which only wants the
build to run and the hooks to fire, and never consumes the repository.

title: Preflight the model in config check, and for the chat role
description:
validate_model() exists and the runner calls it at startup for triage
and patch. Two gaps remain.

1. `config check` does not call it. The rc scripts run `config check` at
   service start, and it is where an operator looks BEFORE starting, so
   it is the natural home for the check. Today it only consults the
   hardcoded RETIRED_MODELS table.

2. The chat role is not preflighted at all. _preflight_models covers
   triage and patch; a wrong llm.chat.model surfaces as a 502 in the
   panel instead of a line at startup.

WHAT THIS IS NOT

Not a replacement for RETIRED_MODELS. That table looked redundant --
difflib reproduces its advice almost exactly, suggesting
deepseek-v4-pro and deepseek-v4-flash for "deepseek-v4", which is what
the table hardcodes -- but it earns its place for a reason the table's
own comment does not state: preflight needs a working API key.
list_models() returns None ("could not ask", deliberately not a
verdict) whenever the endpoint is unreachable or the key is wrong or
missing. On such a host preflight says nothing and the table is the
only thing that fires. Deleting it would trade a check that always
works for one that usually works.

The table's stated objection -- "a checker that guessed would
eventually reject a name that had just become valid" -- does not apply
here: preflight does not guess, it reads the provider's own /v1/models.

VALUE

Modest and worth being honest about: one gap closed, and the table
stops needing to grow. Nobody has to add an entry for the next
retirement, because anywhere a key works, preflight catches any absent
model on any provider rather than the two names someone remembered.

Keep it non-fatal and silent when it cannot ask, matching the runner.
A spurious ERROR trains people to ignore ERRORs.

title: The agent re-reads files already in its own context
description:
Measured on hardware 2026-08-29, devel/glib20, one 30-turn attempt.
Duplicate calls, all returning ok:

  4x  materialize_dports  origin=devel/glib20
  2x  get_file  .../devel/glib20/overlay.dops
  2x  get_file  .../dragonfly/patch-gmodule_gmodule-dl.c
  2x  get_file  .../dragonfly/patch-gio_meson.build
  2x  list_dir  /work/dsynth/logs
  2x  env_verify

Every one of those files was already verbatim in the prompt from the
earlier call. Re-reading does not add information; it costs a turn, the
model output that requested it, and re-adds the content as fresh
uncached input.

materialize_dports is the clearest: called four times in one attempt,
idempotent, ok every time. Nothing tells the model it already ran.

Cheap fixes worth weighing:
  - have the tool answer "already done, unchanged" instead of redoing
    the work, so the result is small and the model learns it is a no-op
  - a one-line note in the tool result when a path was already returned
    this attempt

Also seen, a different shape of the same waste: the agent probing paths
the chroot does not usefully expose --

  grep pattern='libelf' path=/usr/lib   matches=0  FAIL
  list_dir /lib                                    FAIL

Two turns spent discovering the filesystem model. That is a playbook or
tool-description gap rather than a code bug.
notes:
CORRECTION 2026-08-29: the materialize_dports count was overstated.

dsynth_build REFUSES unless materialize_dports succeeded for the origin
in the current attempt (worker.py stale-compose guard, blocked_by=
stale_compose). So the pairs in the trace are mandatory, not waste:

  T10 materialize_dports -> T11 dsynth_build
  T18 materialize_dports -> T19 dsynth_build

Two of the four calls are the design working. The genuinely redundant
ones are T3 (before any build) and T30 (last turn, nothing follows).

The duplicate get_file calls stand as reported -- overlay.dops,
patch-gmodule_gmodule-dl.c and patch-gio_meson.build were each read
twice, and the content was already verbatim in the prompt.

So the remedy narrows: a no-op-detecting materialize_dports would save
little and could fight the guard. A note on a repeated get_file is
where the value is.
FIXED (the get_file half) 2026-08-29.

get_file now elides the content when the same window of the same file
is requested twice in one attempt and the sha256 is unchanged, returning
unchanged=true plus the metadata (sha, size, line range) and a note
saying the bytes are already above in the conversation.

Two things make it safe:
  - the sha is compared, so a file changed by put_file is returned in
    full rather than withheld
  - the cache is cleared at every attempt start (worker.
    reset_attempt_caches, called from attempt_loop). A retry begins from
    a fresh message list, so carrying it across attempts would refuse
    the model content it has never seen -- worse than the waste.

The tool description says unchanged=true is success rather than an
error; a model reading it as failure would retry and turn a saving into
a loop.

NOT DONE: materialize_dports. Per the correction above, two of its four
calls are mandated by the stale-compose guard, and a no-op-detecting
version risks fighting that guard for little gain.

STILL OPEN: the agent probing paths the chroot does not usefully expose
(grep /usr/lib, list_dir /lib -- two turns). That is a playbook or
tool-description gap, not this fix.

title: devel/skalibs is fixed with -D__BSD_VISIBLE where patching the source was the right shape
description:
Moved out of error-bsd-types-visibility.md, which carried it as an
"## Examples" entry. It was never guidance - it is a standing note
about one port, and it sat where bd could not see it.

VERIFIED STILL TRUE 2026-08-28. ports/devel/skalibs/overlay.dops is a
single op:

  mk add CFLAGS "-D__BSD_VISIBLE"

The original note, from 2026-06-01, commit a8d053f050f:

  upstream make/exports.sh adds -D_POSIX_C_SOURCE=200809L
  -D_XOPEN_SOURCE=700 for portability. First-pass agent emitted
  mk add CFLAGS "-D__BSD_VISIBLE". Compiled and shipped, but Option 1
  (patch make/exports.sh to drop the POSIX flags on DragonFly) would
  have been the right shape.

Why it is worth redoing rather than leaving: the two flags are in
opposition. Upstream asks for a strict POSIX namespace and we force the
BSD one back on top. It builds, but any future change to how upstream
sets those flags lands on a port whose fix is a counterweight rather
than a correction, and the failure will not point here. Patching
make/exports.sh to not add the POSIX flags on DragonFly leaves one
coherent intent instead of two fighting ones.

Not urgent. It builds today. Do it next time the port is touched for
any other reason - which is exactly why it needs to be a bead and not
a line in a playbook nobody greps.

title: Scan the overlay for dragonfly/ patches against generated files
description:
Moved out of error-prefer-dops-over-static-patches.md, which carried it
as a "a future scan should..." line. A playbook is instructions for an
agent working a specific failure; a standing task for us is not that,
and it sat there invisible to bd.

The scan: flag every ports/*/*/dragonfly/patch-Makefile.in and
ports/*/*/dragonfly/patch-configure. Those target autotools-generated
files, so they decay on every upstream bump rather than on drift, and
each one is a recurring failure waiting to happen. The playbook already
documents the conversion (dops text replace-once against the generated
file, or patch the autotools source instead) - this is just finding
them all rather than waiting for each to break.

Cheap to do: a find over the overlay, no tooling needed.

title: Store dedup is unmeasured: the ratio only exists as a hand-run query
description:
Nothing in the system computes or reports how much the content-addressed
store is saving. blob_objects and artifact_refs hold every number needed,
but the only way to see it is to open state.db and write the query by hand.

Measured that way on x6 2026-08-28:

  refs (logical artifacts)   104
  blobs (distinct objects)    78
  logical bytes        1,354,418
  physical bytes         830,784
  saved                  523,634  (39%, 1.63x)

What actually dedups is port-tree snapshots, not logs — the same port
failing in two bundles ships an identical pkg-plist, Makefile and
distinfo. One 473,216-byte port/pkg-plist stored twice is ~90% of the
whole saving on its own. full.log.gz never dedups; every build log
differs.

That last point is the reason to surface it rather than leave it to a
manual query: the intuition is that log volume drives store growth, and
the measurement says otherwise. Retention decisions made on the wrong
axis will target the wrong data.
design:
The whole metric is two sums against tables that already exist:

  SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*)  FROM artifact_refs WHERE backend='blob') AS refs,
         (SELECT COUNT(*)  FROM blob_objects)                       AS blobs,
         (SELECT SUM(size) FROM artifact_refs WHERE backend='blob') AS logical,
         (SELECT SUM(size) FROM blob_objects)                       AS physical;

No new schema, no counters to maintain, nothing to keep in step with
put_blob. Both tables are already written on every put.

Surface it on an existing tracker page rather than adding an endpoint —
this is an operator-curiosity number, not something to poll. Cost is a
full scan of artifact_refs, fine at this size and not fine forever; if
that ever matters it is the same reverse index poly-326 needs, so build
it there rather than here.

Note for poly-326: its description records "zero dedup" from the
2026-08-27 measurement. That is no longer true, which strengthens its
argument — the most-shared blob is exactly the one a naive delete would
drop.

title: patch.md is a truncated mid-sentence fragment when the budget runs out
description:
On the glib20 attempt, analysis/patch.md was 221 bytes and read in full:

  'Now I understand the real situation. Let me verify my understanding of
   the two conflicting patches and check the FreeBSD files/ patch content
   for gresource-tool.c (which the dragonfly overlay may also interact
   with):'

That is the agent's last mid-turn narration, captured verbatim because the tool loop stopped before the next dispatch. It is the artifact an operator opens to find out what the patch attempt concluded, and it concludes nothing.

Compare the same run's manual_handoff.md (3771 bytes) and triage.md (2075 bytes), both of which are proper documents. patch.md is the odd one out because it is written from whatever the agent last said rather than from a required final report.
design:
When an attempt ends without a result — budget-exhausted, gave-up, error — patch.md should say so in its own words rather than preserving a dangling sentence: what was tried, what was ruled out, where it stopped, and what it would have done next. The tool trace already holds the detail; this is the summary an operator reads first.

Cheap version: when status != ok, replace patch.md with a generated stanza (status, attempts, billable tokens, last action, and the mid-flight text demoted to a quoted 'last narration' section) instead of letting the fragment stand alone.
acceptance_criteria: 1. patch.md never ends mid-sentence. 2. A budget-exhausted attempt says it was budget-exhausted in patch.md itself.

title: dev-env create exits 1 on any compose error, so its exit code is unusable
description:
create runs an initial compose as step 7/7 and propagates its failure: 'create FAILED for 2026Q3-editors_vim after 621s (exit 1)'. But the same run also prints 'environment remains ready for inspection', writes status=ready, and produces a usable tree — editors/vim, devel/glib20 and Mk/ all present.

Compose is not expected to be error-free against a live FreeBSD branch; overlay bit-rot is the normal state and is what the tool exists to surface. Observed on a fresh create: 136 errors (E_COMPOSE_STALE_OVERLAY=32, E_COMPOSE_COMPAT_FAILED=32, E_COMPOSE_APPLY_FAILED=3) across origins like devel/valgrind, lang/ghc, java/openjdk8 — none of them the env's own origin.

So create will essentially always exit non-zero while succeeding. Anything scripting it has to ignore the exit code, which means it cannot distinguish this from a create that genuinely failed to produce an env.
design:
Separate 'the env was created' from 'the compose was clean'. Exit 0 when the env reaches status=ready, and report compose errors as part of the summary — the compose step already prints its own error codes and hints. Reserve a non-zero exit for a create that leaves no usable env.

If a caller does want compose to gate creation, that is a flag, not the default.
acceptance_criteria: 1. A create that yields a ready env exits 0. 2. Compose errors are still visible and counted. 3. A create that fails to produce an env still exits non-zero.

title: dev-env dsynth defaults ignore the host: 2 builders x 2 jobs on any machine
description:
config.py hardcodes DPORTS_DEV_DSYNTH_BUILDERS and DPORTS_DEV_DSYNTH_JOBS to 2 and 2, and write_dsynth_config bakes them into every env's dsynth.ini. There is no host sizing anywhere.

On x6 that is 2x2 = 4 parallel compile slots on a 16-core, 16 GB machine — a quarter of the box. dsynth's own heuristic for a host that size would be several times that. Nothing warns; the env just builds slowly and the operator has to know to look.

Found while running a real build: raising it to 6 builders x 4 jobs via the env vars is a one-line change, but you have to know the env vars exist, and hand-editing the generated dsynth.ini afterwards is the obvious-but-wrong route because create/refresh rewrites it.
design:
Derive the defaults from hw.ncpu and physmem when the env vars are unset, and keep the vars as the override.

Memory is the real constraint, not cores: each builder is a concurrent port, and heavy ones (gcc, glib, rust) want a couple of GB. Something like builders = min(ncpu/2, physmem_gb/2.5), jobs = ncpu/builders, floored at the current 2x2 so small machines are unaffected.

Print the chosen values at create time. A silent default that is wrong by 4x on the target hardware is worse than a loud one that is approximate.
acceptance_criteria: 1. A 16-core host gets more than 4 slots without the operator setting anything. 2. The env vars still override. 3. The values are visible at create time, not only by reading dsynth.ini.

title: Step 21 — one constructor for the write connection, and schema-drift tests
description:
Rescoped from the backlog doc's "Step 21 — DB layer consolidation pass".
The doc described a codebase that no longer exists, and its headline
remedy — centralize every write into dportsv3.db.writes — is now the
expensive part with the least evidence of pain. What is kept here is the
fifth of it that earns its keep.

WHAT THE DOC MEASURED, AND WHAT IS THERE NOW

    120 conn.execute sites across six files   ->   232 across 22
    dportsv3.db.writes to be created          ->   still does not exist

The debt is real and it has roughly doubled. Its own soft dependency has
also already failed: Step 21 wanted to land before Step 17 because
"remote runners adds a runners table — would prefer to plug it into 21b's
helpers rather than add a sixth ad-hoc INSERT site". The runners table
was added anyway, ad-hoc, as exactly that site.

THREE CORRECTIONS FROM READING THE CODE

1. There is no accidental fourth connection pattern. 21a asks to "audit
   for accidental fourth patterns (e.g. one-off sqlite3.connect calls in
   helpers)". The 15 inline `write_conn = sqlite3.connect(...,
   isolation_level=None)` blocks in the tracker's route handlers ARE
   pattern 3 — the dedicated autocommit connection — which has spread out
   of lifecycle.apply by copy-paste. agentic_api.py states why verbatim:
   "lifecycle.apply runs explicit BEGIN IMMEDIATE / COMMIT and is
   incompatible with sqlite3's default deferred-transaction wrapper."

   So the remedy is not "document each pattern". Pattern 3 needs a
   CONSTRUCTOR, so it stops being copy-pasted.

2. The PRAGMA drift across those 15 sites is cosmetic, not a bug. Three
   set PRAGMA busy_timeout=5000 and none set foreign_keys=ON, against
   open_db which sets both. Measured, not assumed:

       connect() default, no PRAGMA   -> blocked, failed after 5.21s
       connect(timeout=0), no PRAGMA  -> failed after 0.00s

   Python's sqlite3.connect already defaults to timeout=5.0, so the three
   sites that set the PRAGMA are setting the value they already had. And
   the only FK constraints in the schema are on build_runs,
   build_results and port_status — legacy build-tracker tables written
   through open_db, which does set foreign_keys. The agentic tables the
   ad-hoc connections write have none.

   It misleads a reader about which PRAGMA is load-bearing. It does not
   break anything. Worth fixing for that reason and no stronger one.

3. 21d's WAL item is done — journal_mode=WAL is set in both
   dportsv3/db/schema.py and dportsv3/tracker/db.py.

WHY 21b IS DROPPED RATHER THAN DEFERRED

At 232 call sites across 22 files, "centralize writes into typed helpers,
no behaviour change" is not a ~200 LOC refactor and is not one unit of
work. More importantly the pain it targets — schema drift meaning grep
and manual fix in N places — is better addressed by the drift TESTS below
than by the centralization, at a fraction of the cost. If a future change
makes the centralization pay for itself, file it then with the evidence.
design:
Two things, plus the hygiene tail.

A — ONE CONSTRUCTOR FOR THE WRITE CONNECTION

Add the missing sibling to tracker/db.py's open_db:

    def open_write_db(db_path) -> sqlite3.Connection:
        """Autocommit connection for code that issues its own
        BEGIN IMMEDIATE — lifecycle.apply and the operator action
        handlers. sqlite3's default deferred-transaction wrapper
        fights an explicit transaction; isolation_level=None gets
        out of its way."""

Roughly eight lines: connect(isolation_level=None, check_same_thread=
False), row_factory, and the same PRAGMA set open_db applies — not
because the current sites are broken without them, but so there is one
answer to "what does a write connection look like here" instead of
fifteen slightly different ones.

Then replace the 15 inline blocks: 8 in tracker/routes/bundle_actions.py,
3 in agentic_api.py, 2 in issue_actions.py, and the ones in
delivery_sync.py. Pure substitution, no behaviour change.

Document the three patterns where they live — one short paragraph each at
the top of runner.py (long-lived singleton), tracker/db.py (per-request,
already documented) and lifecycle.py (autocommit + explicit
transaction) — saying why this one and not the others. That is 21a's
actual deliverable; the audit half is done and its answer is above.

B — SCHEMA-DRIFT TESTS

The cheap half of what 21b was for. For each table, assert that the
INSERT statements against it name every column schema.py declares NOT
NULL. That catches the failure centralization was meant to prevent —
a new NOT NULL column landing while one of N writers still omits it —
without moving any code.

C — HYGIENE TAIL (independent; split it out if it gets in the way)

- synchronous=NORMAL. Safe with WAL, faster commits. WAL itself is done.
- Periodic VACUUM, or a runner-startup one-shot past a size threshold.
- Retention: archive or drop bundles and their activity_log/job_events
  rows past ~6 months. artifact_refs are kept regardless.
- Write down the Postgres trigger criteria: direct-writer remote runners
  (poly-fij routes writes through the tracker, so SQLite stays fine even
  with N builders), activity_log past ~10M rows, or a multi-host
  deployment with no central tracker.

SEQUENCING — NOT A PREREQUISITE FOR poly-g19

The doc ordered this 21 -> 31 -> 17, on the grounds that folding the
artifact-store into the tracker would otherwise mean "physically
relocating artifact_store.py's still-scattered write code and
re-consolidating later".

That does not hold. ArtifactStore is a cohesive class whose public
methods already map almost one-to-one onto the six endpoints —
upsert_run_bundle, apply_transition, put_blob, put_fs_ref, get_artifact,
upsert_user_context. It already IS the write surface for its half, and
poly-g19's 31c keeps the class rather than relocating it. So 31a is
"mount six routes onto an existing class" and needs nothing from here.

poly-g19 is unblocked by this bead. Soft relation only: poly-fij.4 (auth)
adds columns and write sites, and would rather find a constructor than a
sixteenth copy — the same preference Step 21 expressed about the runners
table, and lost.
acceptance_criteria: 1. There is one way to open a write connection in the tracker, and the 15 inline sqlite3.connect blocks use it. 2. Each of the three connection patterns is documented where it lives, with why-this-one-not-the-others. 3. A NOT NULL column added to schema.py fails a test rather than a runtime write. 4. No behaviour change: the suite stays green throughout.

title: 17f Per-runner tracker UI
description:
Once more than one builder exists, the dashboard has to say which. Columns on /agentic and /agentic/jobs for the builder that produced each bundle and the one that currently owns each claimed job; a per-runner status card (online/offline, last-seen, current job, token-revoked badge); a /agentic/runners page for enrollment, revocation and display names.

Last, deliberately: everything it reflects has to be stable first. Note the existing runner_status table is a hard singleton (CHECK (id = 1)) and is the 'what is the runner doing' panel — the per-runner view reads runners, not that.
acceptance_criteria: 1. The dashboard attributes every claimed job and every bundle to a named builder. 2. An operator can revoke a builder from the UI.

title: A dead job records its category but not its cause
description:
Observed on the first job ever processed: triage failed with 'Authentication Fails, Your api key: ****e-me is invalid'. The job row got state=dead, retire_reason=triage_failed, and last_error EMPTY (length 0). The tracker UI shows 'triage_failed' and nothing else.

The message exists in two places the operator is not pointed at: the runner log, and queue/failed/<job>.job.error. docs/AGENTIC_BUILDS.md's troubleshooting table sends them to the tracker job view for last_error, which is blank.

An invalid API key is a config error with an obvious fix, and it is the single most likely first-run failure. Surfacing only the category turns a one-line fix into a log hunt.
acceptance_criteria: 1) A job retired for a machinery/API failure carries the cause in last_error, truncated. 2) The tracker job view shows it. 3) The troubleshooting table matches what the UI actually has.

title: dev-env create needs a git checkout; say so at the boundary
description:
L3 of the repo-coupling review (2026-08-25). Recorded as a boundary to
document rather than a coupling to remove.

`dev-env create` does not merely read a source tree, it requires a GIT
one:

  * RepoCache.refresh_local_mirror("polytropos", tool_root) makes a
    `git clone --mirror` of it.
  * clone_branch() then clones the tool_branch into the chroot.
  * builder.current_branch(tool_root) reads the branch to track, so the
    env matches the branch the operator is working on — the property
    X5 (poly-15g.5) was built for.
  * validate_source_repo requires bin/dportsv3 and pyproject.toml at
    the root.

A tarball-extracted tree therefore cannot create an env, and that is a
reasonable place to draw the line rather than something to fix: making
create copy instead of clone would cost the branch-tracking.

The seam that makes this liveable, and the reason it is only P3:
tool_root is consumed by cmd_create ALONE. cmd_exec never touches it.
So the three services — which only ever exec into an env that already
exists — need no checkout at all once the sibling beads land. Creating
an env stays a developer action.

Work: document the boundary (deploy/README.md and OPERATOR_SETUP.md),
and make `dev-env create` fail with that explanation when --tool-root is
not a git repository, instead of whatever git says when the mirror step
fails.
notes:
## Implemented 2026-08-25

The check already existed — validate_source_repo ran
`git -C ROOT rev-parse --git-dir` through run_git — but its failure said

    command failed: git -C /path rev-parse --git-dir

which names the command, not the reason, and discarded git's own
explanation. It is a poor answer to 'why can't I point this at an
installed copy?', which is exactly the question this bead is about.

Now the probe is explicit and the message explains the boundary: not a
git repository, create clones the tool tree into the env and tracks the
branch it is on, so it needs history rather than files, and a tarball or
installed copy cannot be used — point --tool-root at a clone.

Also stopped run_git discarding stderr generally, so any other git
failure in the builder now carries git's own words.

The shape check still runs first, so a directory that is not the tool
tree at all keeps the clearer 'does not look like' complaint rather than
being told it is not a repository.

Documented in docs/OPERATOR_SETUP.md section 3 and deploy/README.md,
both stating the limit explicitly: the requirement applies to CREATING
an env; the three services only exec into envs that already exist, so a
packaged install runs the whole stack with no source tree.

Tests: tests/test_dev_env_git_boundary.py (7), including a real
git init/commit for the passing case and a tarball-shaped tree (all
files, no .git) for the failing one. Mutation tested. Suite 2291.

title: Ship deploy/ as package data so it survives packaging
description:
From the repo-coupling review (2026-08-25).

paths.deploy_dir() resolves $DPORTS_DEV_TOOL_ROOT/deploy, so
`dportsv3 deploy install` only works from a checkout. Move deploy/ under
the package as package data and resolve it the way BUNDLED_CONFIG_DIR
and the playbooks directory already are — both are precedents in
paths.py for "tool-owned data that ships inside the package".

Then `deploy install` works from a packaged install too, and
deploy_dir() stops depending on the tool root entirely. Keep --tool-root
as an override for anyone installing from a checkout they have edited.
notes:
## Implemented 2026-08-25

deploy/ stays at the repo root, where an operator browsing the checkout
finds it, and hatch force-include lands a copy inside the wheel:

    [tool.hatch.build.targets.wheel.force-include]
    "deploy" = "dportsv3/data/deploy"

paths.BUNDLED_DEPLOY_DIR names that location and deploy_dir() resolves:
explicit --tool-root, then the bundled copy, then $DPORTS_DEV_TOOL_ROOT.

Both of the last two are load-bearing. A wheel carries the files, which
is what lets a packaged install deploy with no source tree. An EDITABLE
install has no bundled copy — the package directory is the source tree
and force-include only applies to a built wheel — so a checkout resolves
through the tool root. Preferring the bundled copy means a packaged host
never needs an environment variable to find data it already carries.

Verified by building and installing, not by reading the config:

  * uv build --wheel -> the wheel contains all six files under
    dportsv3/data/deploy/ (three rc.d scripts, three samples, README).
  * installed into a clean venv, then with DPORTS_DEV_TOOL_ROOT and
    DPORTSV3_CMD both unset: deploy_dir() returned
    .../site-packages/dportsv3/data/deploy and listed the scripts.

Side note worth keeping: installing the wheel needs --no-deps, because
dports-dev-env is a sibling source tree and not on any index. That is
the documented arrangement (CLAUDE.md), not a packaging bug, but a real
port will have to satisfy that dependency some other way.

Tests: tests/test_deploy_dir_resolution.py (8), including two that read
pyproject.toml so the packaging declaration and BUNDLED_DEPLOY_DIR
cannot drift apart. Mutation tested. Suite 2284 passed.

title: Service logging and rotation
description:
Run under daemon(8) and the services' stdout/stderr has to go somewhere
bounded.

The runner already writes its own structured runner.log under the queue
root (see log() / activity_log in dportsv3/agent/runner.py), so this is
about the process-level stream — tracebacks, uvicorn's access log, and
anything written before the log file is open — not about replacing the
existing logging.

Decide between daemon(8) -o/-t redirection and syslog, then ship a
newsyslog.conf.d entry so the files are rotated. Untended growth on a
build box is how the disk fills.
notes:
## Implemented 2026-08-25

deploy/newsyslog.conf.sample, installed to
/usr/local/etc/newsyslog.conf.d/polytropos.conf — a directory
/etc/newsyslog.conf already includes on DragonFly (verified on x6; the
directory itself does not exist yet, so deploy install creates it).
Seven rotations, ~1 MB, flags CZ.

THE FINDING, measured rather than read. daemon(8) recommends rotation by
'creating a PID file with the -p option and configuring newsyslog to
send SIGUSR1 to the process ID in this file'. Following that literally
kills the service: -p holds the CHILD's pid, and SIGUSR1's default
disposition terminates a process. On x6:

    SIGUSR1 -> child pid       child alive: NO    supervisor alive: NO
    SIGUSR1 -> supervisor pid  child alive: yes   supervisor alive: yes
                               new log file created and growing

So all three services now also pass -P <name>.sup.pid, and the
newsyslog entries signal THAT pid. rc.subr's $pidfile stays the child,
so 'service stop' is unchanged — the two pidfiles serve different
consumers and both are needed.

Tests: 5 more in test_deploy_rc_scripts.py (84 there, 105 across the two
deploy files). Mutation tested: pointing rotation at the child pidfile,
dropping -P, or making rc use the supervisor pidfile each fail a test.
Suite 2300 passed.

Not yet exercised through newsyslog itself on x6 — that needs the
services installed and running, which is poly-abr.5.

title: Record the env a job actually ran in on the jobs row
description:
jobs has no env column; the env lives only in the .job file payload as job.dev_env, so the tracker cannot show which env a job ran in.

THE DISTINCTION THAT MAKES THIS WELL-DEFINED even though env is operator-selectable: record the env the job RAN IN, not the env it is configured to use. tracker_active_env is a mutable preference; the outcome of resolve_env_for_job at claim time is a historical fact and does not change when someone flips the selector afterwards.

Same discipline as jobs.owner_id (7d4b337): record what happened, branch on nothing. Follow that shape — column plus a MIGRATIONS ALTER so an existing state.db keeps its rows.
acceptance_criteria: 1. jobs carries the resolved env, stamped at claim. 2. Flipping the active env afterwards does not rewrite finished jobs. 3. An existing state.db migrates without losing rows.

title: pyproject.toml Homepage/Repository still point at DeltaPorts
description: [project.urls] in pyproject.toml still reads Homepage = https://github.com/DragonFlyBSD/DeltaPorts and Repository = the same. The tool now lives at https://github.com/DragonFlyBSD/polytropos. Independent of the pending dportsv3 -> polytropos rename; this is just wrong metadata. Note the related-but-separate rename surface: bin/dportsv3, [project.scripts] dportsv3 = dportsv3.cli:main, distribution name dports-dragonfly, and the operator-facing DPORTSV3_* env vars.
acceptance_criteria: 1) Homepage and Repository point at the polytropos repo. 2) No other DeltaPorts URL remains in packaging metadata.

title: Pre-existing: test_issue_bucket[unresolved-occ6-None] fails since R1
description: tests/test_issue_state.py::test_issue_bucket[unresolved-occ6-None] expects None for (unresolved, accepted+verified occurrence) but issue_bucket returns 'delivering'. VERIFIED pre-existing: fails at commit dcd163f004e (the R1 resolving-state commit) using R1's own issue_state.py + test, i.e. before any C1/C2/A1-A4 work. The R1 change introduced the 'delivering' bucket and the test case was not updated. Deselected during this session's runs.
acceptance_criteria: 1) Decide whether 'delivering' or None is correct for an unresolved issue whose latest occurrence is accepted+verified. 2) Fix the test or the projection accordingly. 3) Full suite green with no deselect.

description: D2 Regression -> introducing commit. Archive build points; bisect a regression to the breaking delta/upstream-sync commit; route or revert instead of re-triage. Prior art: ClusterFuzz regression bisect; TAP culprit-finding.

title: A5 (opt) Pre-deliver dual-invariant
description: A5 (Optional) Pre-deliver dual-invariant. Before Accept, also rebuild the fix previously-green neighbors / reverse-deps (PASS_TO_PASS) so a fix that works by breaking a shared component is caught. Prior art: SWE-bench FAIL_TO_PASS and PASS_TO_PASS; SapFix; GenProg overfitting.
notes: FEASIBILITY (checked 2026-08-18): NOT implemented with A1-A4, deliberately. Blocker: the codebase has NO reverse-dependency capability at all (no dep-graph query, no rdep helper anywhere in dportsv3 or dev-env). A5 therefore requires (a) building a reverse-dep subsystem (parse dsynth's graph or shell make all-depends-list across the tree) and (b) N extra full dsynth builds per confirm, on top of A4 already requiring 2 greens. Larger + riskier than A1-A4 combined, for value that is speculative until the loop runs live and we see whether 'fix works by breaking a shared component' actually occurs. Revisit with real data. Not dismissed - own track.
